Ran all 19 checks embedded in this lane through compile_oracle.py check against the real pinned toolchain and dependencies: 19/19 passed, including the exact controller-limit reproduction (0.29-0.31 climbed, 0.311/0.32 stopped, engine's real STEP_HEIGHT/STEP_MIN_WIDTH/SKIN constants) and the exact --no-growable-memory / misaligned-initial-memory linker-argument reproductions. Every one of the ~45 warrant sources resolved and supported its claim; every cited rapier/parry/dlmalloc file:line matched, down to operator-level detail (is_wall uses >=, the stairs landing check uses strict >, snap uses <=0). Engine facts hold up to a subtle test: PR #44's actual current code fixes wasm memory at 256 pages (16 MiB) in both config.toml and build.mjs, matching recipes 1 and 2 exactly, NOT the 512-page figure in the same-day-amended dispatch pin 10 that recipe 2 also cites separately and correctly as a distinct, not-yet-implemented recommendation. Systemic weakness: nearly every engine_note anchors to an open, unmerged, stacked PR (#44 depends on #43, both open) and to dispatch docs that were amended same-day from KB answers; this is accurate today (2026-09-25) but is a moving target that goes stale the moment either branch merges, rebases, or is amended again, and a handful of dense-scene page-count figures (e.g. 49/147/3,320 pages; the 1,117,808-byte linker error) are the research agent's own unreproduced measurements, taken on faith rather than independently re-run in this pass.

recipes.name: Fix wasm32 memory with -C link-arg=--no-growable-memory or equal, page-aligned --initial-memory/--max-memory
recipes.what: On rustc 1.98.1 (rust-lld, LLD 22.1.8) two stable link args make a wasm32 module's maximum equal its initial size; memory.grow of one page then returns -1 on every host.
recipes.how: Pass -C link-arg=--no-growable-memory (the maximum becomes the initial size wasm-ld computes: 1 MiB stack, data, statics, rounded up to pages) or -C link-arg=--initial-memory=N -C link-arg=--max-memory=N with N a multiple of 65,536 and at least the bytes wasm-ld reports. RUSTFLAGS replaces the [target] rustflags of .cargo/config.toml, so put the argument where it survives: a build.rs printing cargo::rustc-link-arg-cdylib=--no-growable-memory (measured: still 18/18 pages with RUSTFLAGS set), or repeat it in every RUSTFLAGS. Check the result with a decoder: memory limits flag 0x01 with max == min. From Rust, core::arch::wasm32::memory_grow(0, n) returns usize::MAX (-1 as i32) once the maximum would be exceeded.
recipes.gotchas: wasm-ld refuses, verbatim: 'initial memory must be aligned to the page size (65536 bytes)', 'initial memory too small, 1117808 bytes needed' (for the solver), 'maximum memory too small, 4194304 bytes needed' (max below initial). --no-growable-memory alone fixes the memory at the linker's minimum (18 pages for the solver), leaving std's allocator about 60 KB of heap: the product golden printed NAN and 32 of 73 tests failed. The link args change only the memory section; std's allocator keeps its memory.grow instruction (see the fixed-arena allocator recipe). No -Z flag is needed.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs (RUSTFLAGS) and solver/.cargo/config.toml, T3 pin 2. Measured on a copy of solver/: no args gives initial 18 pages and no maximum; --no-growable-memory gives 18/18; --initial-memory = --max-memory = 4194304 gives 64/64; the memory.grow count stays 1 in all three. PR #44 fixes 256 pages with the two explicit args in both config.toml and build.mjs.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle ran all 6 checks (incl. the two link failures) against rustc 1.98.1/wasm32: 6/6 passed. LLD docs match verbatim; PR#44 branch code sets exactly 256 pages (16 MiB) in config.toml+build.mjs.

recipes.name: Remove memory.grow from the law's binary with a fixed-arena #[global_allocator]: dlmalloc 0.2.13 over one span
recipes.what: std 1.98.1's wasm32 System allocator is dlmalloc 0.2.13 and calls memory.grow; a #[global_allocator] that hands dlmalloc one fixed span removes the instruction and left the solver's results bit-identical.
recipes.how: Add dlmalloc = "=0.2.13" and a static Dlmalloc<Arena> built with Dlmalloc::new_with_allocator(Arena { .. }). Arena implements the unsafe trait dlmalloc::Allocator: alloc hands out one span once (a zero-initialised static array, or __heap_base up to memory_size(0) * 65536 under fixed memory) and returns (null, 0, 0) after that; remap returns null; free_part, free and can_release_part return false; allocates_zeros returns true; page_size returns 65536. Forward GlobalAlloc alloc, alloc_zeroed, dealloc and realloc to malloc, calloc, free and realloc, mark the static #[global_allocator], and link with --no-growable-memory or equal initial and max. Size the span from the high-water mark of a growable build (memory.buffer.byteLength after the heaviest run): dlmalloc never releases and wasm memory never shrinks.
recipes.gotchas: Linker limits alone keep the instruction: the fixed-memory builds still contain one memory.grow in <dlmalloc::sys::System as dlmalloc::Allocator>::alloc. dlmalloc 0.2.13 donates the linker's __heap_base..__heap_end span only on its first system request and forfeits it if that request does not fit (src/wasm.rs 39-48). Exhaustion returns null and Rust aborts: an unreachable trap, identical on every host once max == initial. The heap need scales with contacts, not bodies: 49, 147 and 3,320 pages for a settling pile, a dense stack and an all-overlapping world at the same 64/64/256 caps under today's law; 53, 245 and 3,973 under PR #44's per-quantum rebuild.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs (#[global_allocator]) and solver/Cargo.toml, T3 pins 2 and 8. Measured on a copy: dlmalloc over a 32 MiB arena gives 532/532 pages and 0 memory.grow, and goldens fd2f6c03fb982d77 / 0d38671370d12d1e and 73/73 tests are unchanged; the product harness needs 21 pages today. PR #44's src/arena.rs rebuilt here also has 0 memory.grow, but its dense capacity scene peaks at 245 of its 256 pages; 512 pages leaves about 2x.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle: all 3 checks passed on real wasm32 (std grows 65 pages; frees never shrink; the fixed-arena allocator grows 0). solver/src/arena.rs on PR#44 branch matches the dlmalloc(size,align) API exactly.

recipes.name: Lint wasm by decoding every instruction: 0x40 and 0xFD bytes recur in block types, immediates and data
recipes.what: The solver binary's code section holds 16,558 bytes equal to 0x40 against one memory.grow (14,916 of them empty block types) and 277 bytes equal to 0xFD against zero SIMD instructions; i32.const 32893 encodes as 41 fd 80 02.
recipes.how: Walk sections by id and u32 size. In the code section read each body's size, skip its locals vector, then decode instruction by instruction with a table that knows every immediate: block types (0x40, a one-byte value type, or an s33 index), br_table vectors, memarg with the bit-6 memidx, i32/i64 const as signed LEB128, f32/f64 const as 4/8 bytes, 0xFC and 0xFD sub-opcodes as u32 LEB128, 16 bytes for v128.const and i8x16.shuffle, lane indices. Flag only at opcode positions, and refuse any opcode or sub-opcode the table lacks, so a gap can only cause a false refusal. In Rust, wasmparser's FunctionBody::get_operators_reader() does the decoding.
recipes.gotchas: Scanning the whole file adds data-segment and custom-section bytes; scanning only the code section still misfires, because every block, loop or if without results is 02/03/04 40, i32.const -64 is 41 40 and an unpadded index of 64 is the byte 40. A byte-level over-approximation that refuses any 0x40 or 0xFD refuses the pinned binary. The target_features custom section (+relaxed-simd, +simd128) is a cheap second signal, but custom sections are optional.
recipes.engine_note: solver/lint.mjs and solver/lint.test.js, T3 pins 2 and 3. PR #44's lint.mjs decodes this way; run on hand-assembled modules it accepted the four false-positive cases and refused the real ones. Two gaps that do not touch rustc output: 0xFD sub-opcodes below 0x100 missing from its table pass as immediate-free, and table.grow is not refused.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check passed (real wasmparser 0.259.0). Read PR#44's actual solver/lint.mjs: its simd() sub-opcode table silently skips unlisted 0xFD sub-opcodes and never flags table.grow, exactly the two named gaps.

recipes.name: Match relaxed SIMD as 0xFD then u32 LEB128 256..=275 and memory.grow as 0x40 then a memidx, padding allowed
recipes.what: Relaxed SIMD is 0xFD followed by the opcode 0x100..=0x113 as a u32 LEB128 (canonically fd 80 02 to fd 93 02; 0x114-0x12F reserved) and memory.grow is 0x40 followed by a memidx; V8 and wasmparser accept padded encodings such as fd 80 82 80 80 00 and 40 80 00.
recipes.how: After an opcode byte 0xFD read the sub-opcode as an unsigned LEB128 of up to 5 bytes (the fifth carries 4 value bits) and refuse 256 <= sub <= 275. After 0x40 read a u32 LEB128 memidx instead of expecting the byte 0x00. For each defined or imported memory read the limits flag: 0x00 (min only) is growable, 0x01 needs max == min, 0x04/0x05 are the i64 address type and 0x02/0x03 shared; refuse what the law must not produce.
recipes.gotchas: A byte-pattern search for fd 80 02 misses a padded encoding, which the spec allows up to ceil(N/7) bytes (0x03 and 0x83 0x00 both encode 3). 0x114 is not a relaxed opcode: V8 rejects the module and wasmparser reports 'unknown 0xfd subopcode: 0x114'. The spec's own instruction index was cut off before SIMD when retrieved; the numbered list is the relaxed-simd proposal's table.
recipes.engine_note: T3 pin 2 ('the 0xfd prefix with opcodes 0x100 through 0x113') and PR #44's lint.mjs constants RELAXED_SIMD_FIRST/LAST and MEMORY_GROW. Add to solver/lint.test.js: i32.const 32893 (41 fd 80 02) and an empty block, accepted; fd 80 82 80 80 00 and 40 80 00, refused.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check passed (real wasmparser decodes all padded/relaxed encodings as claimed). PR#44's lint.mjs literally exports RELAXED_SIMD_FIRST=0x100, RELAXED_SIMD_LAST=0x113, MEMORY_GROW=0x40, matching exactly.

recipes.name: Don't rely on -C target-feature=-relaxed-simd: a #[target_feature] fn or a relaxed intrinsic still emits
recipes.what: Under -C target-feature=-relaxed-simd a #[target_feature(enable = "relaxed-simd")] function and a plain call to core::arch::wasm32::f32x4_relaxed_madd both compile without unsafe and emit f32x4.relaxed_madd (fd 85 02).
recipes.how: Keep the crate-level -C target-feature=-relaxed-simd: it sets cfg(target_feature = "relaxed-simd") for every crate built, which is what gates the relaxed paths in matrixmultiply 0.3.11 (sgemm muladd becomes f32x4_relaxed_madd) and wide 1.7.1 (u8x16::shuffle becomes u8x16_relaxed_swizzle). Make the binary lint the guarantee, and when adding a dependency grep it for target_feature(enable and for *_relaxed_* intrinsics.
recipes.gotchas: The rustc book: there is no compiler flag that disables SIMD emission once a function enables it with #[target_feature]. On Wasm a safe #[target_feature] fn is callable from safe code, so the call site carries no unsafe marker. The precompiled std is built with the target's default features and ignores -C target-feature. relaxed-simd implies simd128. relaxed_madd may round once or twice depending on the host.
recipes.engine_note: solver/.cargo/config.toml, solver/build.mjs and FLAGS.md: the flag holds for today's graph (0 SIMD instructions in the binary) but is not the guarantee; T3 pin 2's lint is. PR #44's config.toml comment already says this.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle: both wasm32 checks (plain call and #[target_feature] fn) compiled clean under -relaxed-simd and returned 7 as claimed. Rust Reference confirms Wasm safe target_feature fns and relaxed-simd implying simd128.

recipes.name: Expect Rapier 0.35.3 to stop T4's fast box at a fixed slab with ccd_enabled(false); max_ccd_substeps 0 tunnels
recipes.what: In rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 every dynamic body moving more than half its thinnest half-extent per step is swept against fixed colliders even with ccd_enabled(false); ccd_enabled(true) only adds kinematic and dynamic targets.
recipes.how: IntegrationParameters::max_ccd_substeps is the switch: 1 (the default) sweeps fast dynamic bodies against fixed colliders and clamps next_position to the first time of impact, 0 disables all CCD. RigidBodyBuilder::ccd_enabled(true) makes a bullet that also sweeps kinematic and dynamic bodies, never another bullet. Fast means max point velocity * dt > 0.5 * ccd_thickness, and a cuboid's ccd_thickness is its smallest half-extent: a 0.05 box at dt = 1/64 is fast above 1.6 u/s. To show a tunnelling test failing, run it with max_ccd_substeps = 0.
recipes.gotchas: The clamp moves the pose only; velocities are kept and the next step's speculative contacts absorb the approach. A body already overlapping a target is not clamped in 3D (only fractions > 0 are accepted). Non-bullets never sweep moving bodies, bullets never sweep bullets, heightfield targets are one-sided, and mesh-shaped fast bodies are never swept. Linear speed is capped at 400 u/s per substep. Pre-0.35 advice that CCD is off unless ccd_enabled no longer holds. Measured envelope at dt 1/64: no tunnelling for 1 to 1,000 u/s against fixed slabs of half-thickness 0.02 to 0.0001.
recipes.engine_note: T4 pin 2 and its acceptance line: rapier_law.rs build_world makes dynamic bodies with ccd_enabled(false) and inherits max_ccd_substeps = 1, so the fast-body test already passes. Through solver_step 14/14 start phases stay on the near side, a copy with max_ccd_substeps = 0 tunnels in 10/14, and ccd_enabled(true) left every result identical; it only adds sweeps against the kinematic walker.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check passed against real rapier3d_f64 0.35.3: exact 'near/FAR' pattern for all three CCD settings. ccd_solver.rs/integration_parameters.rs/rigid_body_components.rs lines match citations exactly, incl. FAST_BODY_SAFETY_FACTOR=0.5.

recipes.name: Keep max_ccd_substeps = 1 so Rapier CCD carries no state between quanta; it hashed alike on x86-64 and wasm32
recipes.what: At max_ccd_substeps = 1 the CCD pass reads only values written in the same step and the CCDSolver holds a rebuildable cache; a 24-body CCD-heavy scene hashes identically on x86-64 release and debug and on wasm32 under V8, with a fresh CCDSolver swapped in mid-run.
recipes.how: Set world.integration_parameters.max_ccd_substeps = 1 explicitly and keep the parallel feature off (the per-body sweep map is then a serial iterator). Snapshot pose, velocities and sleep state as today; nothing CCD-specific needs recording. On restore, build bodies with the law's ccd_enabled value.
recipes.gotchas: With max_ccd_substeps > 1 the pre-solve pass runs the fast-body test on the previous quantum's ccd_vels (crate-private, not settable), which a restore cannot reproduce, and the step splits at the first time of impact. Cross-platform identity also needs IEEE 754-2008 targets and the same insertion order; ARM64 was not measured here.

recipes.name: Set T4's step heights around max_height + offset: KinematicCharacterController climbs 0.31 at max_height 0.3
recipes.what: handle_stairs evaluates max_height + offset and min_width + offset, so with max_height 0.3 and offset 0.01 the engine's box walker climbs steps up to 0.3101, and its feet rest one offset above every surface.
recipes.how: Autostep runs only on a wall hit (angle to up >= max_slope_climb_angle) and, with include_dynamic_bodies = false, never onto a collider whose parent is dynamic (the step casts then exclude dynamic bodies). It needs a free up-cast of max_height + offset, a free forward cast of min_width + offset from the raised pose, and a landing no steeper than the climb angle (strict >). Put the course pair clear of max_height + offset, e.g. 0.29 and 0.33, and measure feet as y - hy - offset.
recipes.gotchas: Asserting the feet at the step top within 1e-3 fails by the 0.01 skin. The limit barely moves with speed: 0.3100989 at 0.4 u/s, 0.3100939 at 2 u/s. Relative lengths evaluate against the shape's AABB (height, or for min_width the horizontal diagonal); the engine uses Absolute. The current Rapier guide says autostep needs floor contact first; the pinned 0.35.3 code does not check that.
recipes.engine_note: harness/course.test.js, T4 pin 5: rapier_law.rs controller() sets STEP_HEIGHT 0.3, STEP_MIN_WIDTH 0.2 and SKIN 0.01. Through solver_step with the product walker (0.25 box) a 0.31 step is climbed, 0.311 is not, and the stopped walker waits 0.0101 short of the riser.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle-reproduced the exact controller-limit claim: 0.29/0.30/0.31 climbed, 0.311/0.32 stopped, via the engine's real STEP_HEIGHT=0.3/STEP_MIN_WIDTH=0.2/SKIN=0.01 from live rapier_law.rs. handle_stairs adds offset to both exactly.

recipes.name: Keep T4 slope and ledge cases off the controller's comparisons: >= at 45 degrees, nudge creep, speed-set snap
recipes.what: is_wall is angle >= max_slope_climb_angle and is_nonslip_slope is angle <= min_slope_slide_angle; snap needs a grounded start and translation.up <= 0; the 1e-4 normal nudge lifts a walker blocked on a 46 degree slope by about 6e-5 per quantum; the snap-or-fall threshold moves with speed (0.2105, 0.2097, 0.2058 at 0.4, 1, 2 u/s).
recipes.how: Test slopes at 44 and 46 degrees with the speed and quantum count stated: at 2 u/s 46 degrees gains 0.018 by 320 quanta and 0.038 by 640 while 44 degrees reaches the top; never test exactly 45. Test drops at 0.19 and 0.22: 0.19 has a longest ungrounded run of at most 1 and lands within 2 quanta of clearing the edge, and 0.22 falls for 12 quanta at 0.4, 1 and 2 u/s. Snap casts down snap_to_ground with offset as target distance, and only when move_shape started grounded (a contact within offset + 0.05 with normal.up >= 1e-3).
recipes.gotchas: Exactly 45 degrees is a wall (>=) but its landing check is strict (>), and the walker creeps up (0.169 in 160 quanta at 2 u/s). The 46 degree 'gain below 0.05' holds only for bounded runs: 0.077 by 1,280 quanta, 0.61 by 10,000. A 0.21 drop is snapped at 0.4 u/s, the product walker's speed, after sliding down the corner while counted grounded, but falls for 12 quanta at 2 u/s; at 0.4 and 2 u/s the quantum that clears the edge is ungrounded for every drop. normal_nudge_factor = 0 removes the creep, but the walker then climbs nothing. Past a ramp's top the walker walks off and its end height drops back to the floor, so assert the maximum height or give the ramp a landing.
recipes.engine_note: harness/course.test.js, T4 pin 5, and rapier_law.rs controller() (CLIMB_ANGLE pi/4, SLIDE_ANGLE 50 degrees, SNAP 0.2, normal_nudge_factor 1e-4); integrate() zeroes vy on movement.grounded, which is how a test reads 'grounded' from the body record.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle ran both checks against real rapier3d_f64 0.35.3, matching exact stdout for slope gains and ledge-drop runs. Source confirms is_wall>=, landing check is strict>, snap needs translation.dot(up)<=0.

lanes.title: Rust CI, reproducible binaries & supply chain
lanes.verifier_note: Checked all 10 recipes' warrant sources by retrieval (WebFetch/gh api against doc.rust-lang.org, the rustup/cargo/rustc/clippy/edition-guide books, docs.rs at the pinned rapier3d-f64/parry3d-f64 versions, cargo-deny/cargo-vet/cargo-mutants/rust-fuzz books, and GitHub READMEs/PRs/issue comments/changelogs), cross-checked every engine_note against si-rpg-engine's main branch read-only via gh api (ci.yml, solver/build.mjs, solver/FLAGS.md, solver/src/lib.rs, solver/src/rapier_law.rs, solver/Cargo.toml, solver/Cargo.lock, solver/.cargo/config.toml, docs/dispatch-t3-platforms.md, docs/PHASE-2.md) and against the actual raw log of CI run 36121826863, and independently reproduced four load-bearing claims myself: the exact rustc rejection text for unstabilized trim-paths (three variants, byte-for-byte), the exact cargo-tree output for the wasm32 dependency graph (rapier3d-f64/parry3d-f64/simba/wide feature lists matched verbatim, plus the rayon-absent error), and the invalid_reference_casting lint firing on a direct &T-to-&mut-T cast but staying silent when the cast and dereference are split across two loops (compile_oracle.py, both PASS). Every one of the 61 warrant sources was reachable and dated 2021 or later. Two genuine defects surfaced: recipe 6 cites the wasm32-unknown-unknown platform-support page for '-Ctarget-feature=-foo disables a feature', but that page only documents the '+foo' enable form and target-cpu=mvp — the disable syntax is real and current, just documented on rustc/codegen-options/index.html instead; and recipe 7's engine_note places canon_zero in solver/src/lib.rs when the live repository shows it defined in solver/src/rapier_law.rs (js_min is correctly in lib.rs). The systemic weakness of this lane is exactly that kind of citation drift: individual numeric/version/API claims are exceptionally well-grounded (dozens of exact-string, line-number and CI-log matches, including exact byte counts and a rustc commit hash that verified against this rig's own toolchain), but a claim occasionally borrows the authority of a citation that supports an adjacent fact rather than the specific one asserted, or misattributes which file in a multi-file crate a function lives in — the kind of small slippage that only shows up by actually opening the cited page or the cited file rather than trusting the surrounding rigor.

recipes.name: Install the solver's pinned toolchain in CI with rustup toolchain install, not a second version pin
recipes.what: Inside solver/, rust-toolchain.toml outranks whatever default toolchain a CI action sets, and rustup 1.29.1 auto-installs a missing pinned toolchain on a proxy call by default; running `rustup toolchain install --no-self-update` in solver/ installs exactly the channel, targets and components the file names, so the file stays the one pin.
recipes.how: Keep one pin in solver/rust-toolchain.toml (`channel = "1.98.1"`, `targets = ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]`, `profile = "minimal"`) and add `components = ["clippy", "rustfmt"]` once lint jobs exist, because minimal means rustc, rust-std and cargo only (measured: `cargo clippy` in the solver prints `'cargo-clippy.exe' is not installed for the toolchain '1.98.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc'`, and likewise cargo-fmt). CI step: `working-directory: solver` then `rustup toolchain install --no-self-update`. The ubuntu-24.04 image (20260920.314.1) already ships rustup 1.29.1 and Rust 1.98.1. Measured with rustup 1.29.1 on scratch copies: the solver's file with no components gave `info: using existing install for 1.98.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`; with components added, the same command went to sync the 1.98.1 channel to fetch them. In a directory whose file named an uninstalled 1.97.0, `RUSTUP_AUTO_INSTALL=0 cargo --version` printed "error: toolchain '1.97.0-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc' is not installed" and "help: run `rustup toolchain install` to install it". With the default setting the proxy started `syncing channel updates for 1.97.0-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. A `rustup toolchain list` run there installed the toolchain and warned `auto-installation is deprecated for most rustup commands`, pointing to rust-lang/rustup#4836. If an action stays, dtolnay/rust-toolchain's README says to use @master with a `toolchain` input. On the @stable branch the input defaults to `stable`, and an explicit value overrides it. The action runs `rustup toolchain install 1.98.1 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --profile minimal --no-self-update`, then `rustup default`, and exports CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 when unset.
recipes.rust_version: rustup 1.28.1+ (auto-install on by default), measured on rustup 1.29.1; Rust 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: rustup 1.28.0 (2025-03-04) stopped auto-installing and 1.28.1 (2025-03-05) restored it behind RUSTUP_AUTO_INSTALL (default 1). rustup#4836 is closed for the 1.30.0 milestone, which is not out yet: the changelog's newest entry is 1.29.0 and this rig runs 1.29.1. From v1.30 the toolchain, show, target and component subcommands stop auto-installing, while run, doc and man keep it. A maintainer comment says #4840 influenced only the rustup and rustup-init commands, so the cargo and rustc proxies keep auto-installing. So 'rustup never auto-installs' and 'CI ignores rust-toolchain.toml' are both wrong. A plain `rustup toolchain install` also checks for a rustup self-update, so pass --no-self-update. `cargo +toolchain`, RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN and `rustup override` all outrank the file, so one `cargo +stable` step in solver/ silently leaves the pin. Adding rust-src to the 1.98.1 toolchain changes the artifact's bytes (see the path-remap recipe).
recipes.engine_note: .github/workflows/ci.yml job `engines` pins 1.98.1 twice: once with `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` (`toolchain: "1.98.1"`, `targets: wasm32-unknown-unknown`; run 36121826863 resolved @stable to commit 6bed0761) and once in solver/rust-toolchain.toml. A bump that edits only one of them still builds inside solver/ with the file's version, while the action's `rustup default` names the other. Replace the action step with the no-argument install run in solver/. T3's ARM lane builds no Rust, but any aarch64 rebuild job must install 1.98.1 itself.
recipes.verify_note: CI run 36121826863 log: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable resolved SHA 6bed0761...; exact install/default commands match. rustup CHANGELOG.md newest entry is 1.29.0 (rig runs 1.29.1) as claimed.

recipes.name: Cache solver deps with Swatinem/rust-cache@v2 and build with --locked; build.mjs's flags never reach the key
recipes.what: rust-cache@v2 keys on the runner OS and CPU, the `rustc -vV` release, host and commit, any job env var whose name starts with CARGO, RUST, CC, CFLAGS, CXX or CMAKE, and the solver's Cargo.lock, Cargo.toml, rust-toolchain.toml and .cargo/config.toml. It never sees flags a script sets for its own child process, and it skips the save on a full key match. Cargo's fingerprints keep a restored cache correct, but only `--locked` stops a stale Cargo.lock being rewritten silently.
recipes.how:
Measured in the engine's CI run 36121826863 (main f84c98b):
- The key was `v0-rust-engines-Linux-x64-6ff13d87-a62750e7`.
- Env considered: CARGO_HOME, CARGO_INCREMENTAL, CARGO_TERM_COLOR.
- Lockfiles considered: solver/.cargo/config.toml, Cargo.lock, Cargo.toml, rust-toolchain.toml.
- The restore reported `full match: true`, `node solver/build.mjs --check` printed the pinned ede99ea1… about 1.4 s later, and the post-job step printed `Cache up-to-date.` with no save.

Add `--locked` to build.mjs's cargo arguments (today: `build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`) and to every cargo step. Measured on cargo 1.98.1 after bumping si-solver's version without regenerating the lock: `--locked` failed with `cannot update the lock file ... because --locked was passed to prevent this`, while plain `cargo build` or `cargo tree` rewrote the root `version` line of Cargo.lock without a message. An offline `cargo generate-lockfile` re-resolved smallvec 1.16.1 to 1.16.2 from the local cache. `--frozen` is `--locked` plus `--offline`; run `cargo fetch --locked` first if the build must be offline. When build.mjs's flags change, add `key: ${{ hashFiles('solver/build.mjs') }}` to the rust-cache step.
recipes.gotchas: A flag change made only inside build.mjs leaves the key unchanged. Each run then restores deps built with the old flags, Cargo rebuilds them (its fingerprints include rustflags), and the full-match rule never saves the new ones. The build stays correct but slow. A job-level RUSTFLAGS or CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS does enter the key through the RUST/CARGO prefixes, and it also replaces the solver's config rustflags. rust-cache never caches workspace crates, drops artifacts older than a week and sets CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0. The Cargo CI guide's latest-dependencies job (`cargo update`, then build) is the opposite of a pinned artifact: run it only as a separate, non-gating scheduled check.
recipes.engine_note: ci.yml runs `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2` with `workspaces: solver`, and solver/build.mjs calls `spawnSync(cargo, ['build', '--release', '--target', 'wasm32-unknown-unknown'])` without `--locked`. In run 36121826863 the cached build still reproduced fixtures/solver.sha256. The weekly uncached rebuild (scheduled-jobs recipe) is what proves the cache hides nothing.
recipes.verify_note: CI log matches exactly: key v0-rust-engines-Linux-x64-6ff13d87-a62750e7, full match true, env/lockfiles considered, digest ede99ea1... 1.37s later, post-step 'Cache up-to-date.' with no save.

recipes.name: Remap CARGO_HOME to make the solver digest path-independent, then scan the wasm for any leaked build path
recipes.what: Dependency source paths reach the wasm as panic-location strings. Remapping the cargo home alone made the 1.98.1 solver build byte-identical across four checkout directories, one of them containing a space. Cargo passes the workspace member's own source to rustc as a relative path (`src\lib.rs`), so build.mjs's solver and repo remaps change no bytes today.
recipes.how:
Measured on this Windows host (rustc and cargo 1.98.1, scratch copies of solver/, build.mjs's flags):
- A/repo, B/x, D/r and a path containing a space all gave 1,524,412 bytes, sha256 b21c7f15…. The space-containing path went through CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS.
- With no remap (config rustflags only): 1,526,380 bytes, c8782b06…. The data section held 132 strings `C:\Users\<user>\.cargo\registry\src\index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f\<crate>-<version>\src\...`.
- `--remap-path-prefix=<CARGO_HOME>=/cargo` alone (plus the pin) gave build.mjs's exact bytes, b21c7f15…. Reversing the three remaps gave them too.
- The remapped strings read `/cargo\registry\src\...`; 12 std strings keep `/rustc/48a229ceaefd4985c50990b14116b6d856af0985/library/...`.

rustc applies the last matching remap, textually and as a best effort. `--remap-path-scope` (stable since 1.95.0; the 1.98.1 compiler lists scopes macro, diagnostics, documentation, debuginfo, coverage, object, all) only narrows where remapping happens. After each build, fail if the wasm contains the absolute CARGO_HOME, the checkout root, the user name, `/home/runner` or the output of `rustc --print sysroot`. That makes a remap that silently stopped matching a build failure on every host.
recipes.gotchas: Remapping is strictly textual. A FROM spelled differently from the path Cargo passes (a symlink, a short name, other separators) remaps nothing and prints nothing. Since 1.83.0, when the rust-src component is installed rustc replaces `/rustc/$hash` with a real path into the local rust-src; the cargo-home remap does not cover that. Keep rust-src off the 1.98.1 toolchain, or remap the sysroot too. `-C strip=symbols` does not remove these strings, because they are data (see the checks). The rustc book warns that code generated by build scripts can still hold un-remapped paths.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs passes three remaps (cargoHome=/cargo, solver=/solver, root=/repo), and solver/FLAGS.md says they strip the cargo home and user name. Only the cargoHome remap moved bytes in the measured build. Keep the other two as insurance for path dependencies outside the workspace or OUT_DIR paths (a judgment, not measured). Add the leak scan to build.mjs next to the digest compare.
recipes.verify_note: All 3 checks PASS under the oracle and semantically test the prose (default Location leaks build dir; -C strip=symbols does not remove it). build.mjs's 3 remaps and FLAGS.md's 132-string count match the repo exactly.

checks.label: a panic's Location names the absolute source path rustc was given
in a wasm32 cdylib the Location data still names the build directory
-C strip=symbols keeps that path: it is data, not a symbol

recipes.name: Re-pin the solver digest only from x86_64 Linux CI: host, toolchain, lock, version and crate-type all move it
recipes.what: Under Cargo 1.98.1 a wasm crate's -C metadata leaves out the host triple but mixes in every dependency's metadata. Proc-macros and build scripts are host units that keep it. So si_solver.wasm's bytes follow the build host's OS and CPU, not only its path separators. The same hash also takes in the package version and crate-type, and trim-paths is still nightly-only.
recipes.how:
Write and enforce fixtures/solver.sha256 only from the x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu CI job: in build.mjs, gate on `process.platform === 'linux' && process.arch === 'x64'`. Bump policy, written into solver/FLAGS.md:
- A toolchain bump, a crate bump (`cargo update -p <crate> --precise <version>`, a conservative update) or a version or crate-type change is one PR.
- The new digest comes from the x64 CI log, never from a laptop.
- The goldens must not move.
- Rapier-specific reruns belong to the rapier-core lane.

Evidence:
- Cargo's compilation_files.rs at rust-1.98.0 hashes the `host:` line only when `unit.kind.is_host()`, and mixes in the metadata of all dependencies.
- rust-lang/cargo#14107 (merged for 1.81.0) dropped the host line for cross-compiled units.
- rust-lang/cargo#15477, still a draft, says wasm -C metadata contains host-dependency metadata, so symbols differ across platforms.

Measured on Windows with 1.98.1:
- Changing only the host units' profile (CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_BUILD_OVERRIDE_OPT_LEVEL=1) changed -C metadata for rapier3d_f64 (68b2f4be… to fd2e5617…) and for si_solver. The wasm went from b21c7f15… to fc5cce1c…, 56 bytes smaller, and the type, function, element, code, data and name sections all differed.
- Built with `-C strip=symbols`, the pair still differed in the function, element, code and data sections (d9f38d6a… vs 99d31c85…).
- Rewriting the 1,025 backslashes in the Windows build's path strings as '/' gave 64518814…, not the pinned ede99ea1….
- si-solver's version 0.1.0 to 0.1.1 gave adf377ab…; crate-type ["cdylib", "rlib"] gave da3d1d11….
- Cargo 1.98.1 refused `trim-paths = "object"` with "feature `trim-paths` is required", then "requires a nightly version of Cargo" once cargo-features was added, and refused `-Ztrim-paths` because -Z is only accepted on nightly.
recipes.rust_version: Cargo 1.98.1 (host line dropped for target units since 1.81.0; host-dependency leak unfixed); v0 mangling default since 1.97.0
recipes.gotchas: The 182,205-byte `name` section holds v0 symbols whose crate disambiguators (e.g. `CsiW7JDTFDBaP_12rapier3d_f64`) derive from -C metadata. Stripping it does not remove the host dependence, because function order moves too (measured, and reported on cargo#8140 in 2026-01). The workaround reported there is a RUSTC_WRAPPER that rewrites -C metadata, which is one more build input to pin and maintain. Profile `strip` is itself hashed, so changing it moves the digest once. A shipcheck-style bump of solver/Cargo.toml's version (e.g. to 1.0.0) moves the digest: re-pin in the same PR. The golden hash, which three JS engines agree on, is the cross-host invariant; the digest is not.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs sets `const linux = process.platform === 'linux'`, which lets an aarch64 Linux machine write fixtures/solver.sha256. Tighten it to x64. solver/FLAGS.md says 'Windows still writes backslashes ... so the two hosts never produce identical bytes'. That conclusion stands, but host-unit metadata is a second cause that no remap removes, so correct the explanation. solver/Cargo.toml's `version = "0.1.0"` and `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` are pinned inputs too.
recipes.verify_note: hash_rustc_version in compilation_files.rs confirmed line-by-line (host line hashed iff unit.kind.is_host()). Independently reproduced all 3 trim-paths stable-Cargo error strings verbatim via `cargo +1.98.1 build`.

recipes.name: Give the ARM lane the x64-built solver and check sha256 of its embedded bytes against fixtures/solver.sha256
recipes.what: Free arm64 Linux runners (ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm) have been generally available for public repositories since 2025-08-07. An aarch64 rebuild is expected to give different bytes, so the ARM lane runs the module the x64 job built and proves it is the pinned binary by hashing the embedded wasm, not by trusting the artifact's name.
recipes.how: x64 job: after `node solver/build.mjs --check`, record the byte length and SHA-256 of si_solver.wasm and upload solver/dist/solver.mjs with actions/upload-artifact. The current major is v7; its `artifact-digest` output is the SHA-256 of the artifact, and artifacts are immutable since v4. ARM job: `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm`, `needs:` the x64 job, a `timeout-minutes`, and the same concurrency group. It downloads with actions/download-artifact (v8 verifies the server hash, `digest-mismatch: error` by default). Then, before any trace, it hashes the module's exported `bytes` (the Uint8Array build.mjs emits) with node:crypto SHA-256, compares the result to fixtures/solver.sha256, and prints the length. For public repositories the docs list 4 CPU / 16 GB / 14 GB runners under ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm and ubuntu-26.04-arm. Length plus digest also gives a first diagnosis, as T3 plans for snapshots. Measured: removing the remap changed the length (1,526,380 vs 1,524,412), the host-unit profile changed it by 56 bytes, and a separator swap cannot change it (one byte for one). An informational aarch64 rebuild may print its own digest to gather evidence, but must never write or gate the pin.
recipes.rust_version: rustc 1.98.1 artifact; GitHub arm64 runners GA 2025-08-07
recipes.gotchas: download-artifact's check covers the artifact archive, not the wasm inside it, so without the byte hash the lane proves only that some x64 job uploaded something. The arm64 partner image's inventory lists Node.js 20.20.0 and Rust 1.93.0 with rustup 1.28.2, so install Node 22 as T3 plans. rust-cache keys include the CPU architecture, so an ARM Rust job never reuses the x64 cache. The evidence that aarch64 bytes differ is a mechanism in Cargo's source plus user reports on rust-lang/cargo#8140; it was not measured on this rig.
recipes.engine_note: docs/dispatch-t3-platforms.md pin 1 says the ARM job 'does not rebuild the solver: it downloads the x64 job's solver/dist/solver.mjs artifact'. Keep that, and add the sha256(bytes) == fixtures/solver.sha256 assertion. Keep the ARM job inside .github/workflows/ci.yml: the studio caps push-triggered workflow files at two, and ci.yml plus pages.yml already fill both slots. ci.yml still references actions/upload-artifact@v4.
recipes.verify_note: upload-artifact: artifact-digest = 'SHA-256 digest of an Artifact', v7 current. download-artifact digest-mismatch defaults 'error', v8 current. Partner arm64 image (Node 20.20.0, Rust 1.93.0, rustup 1.28.2) exact.

recipes.name: Pass build.mjs's flags via CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS and refuse relaxed-simd in code: the bytes hide the pin
recipes.what: Cargo uses only the first rustflags source it finds: CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS, then RUSTFLAGS, then target rustflags, then build rustflags. RUSTFLAGS is split on whitespace. An inherited CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS, even an empty one, drops every flag build.mjs sets. And on 1.98.1, losing `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd` changes no byte, so only a compile-time guard notices a lost pin.
recipes.how:
In build.mjs, set `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS: flags.join('\x1f')` in the child env and delete any inherited RUSTFLAGS or CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS. Measured on 1.98.1:
- With a checkout path containing a space, the space-joined RUSTFLAGS failed before compiling: `--remap-path-prefix must contain '=' between FROM and TO`.
- The same flags joined with 0x1f in CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS built the identical b21c7f15….
- An empty `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS=` beside build.mjs's RUSTFLAGS produced the unremapped c8782b06…, and si_solver's rustc line carried neither the pin nor any remap.
- RUSTFLAGS without the pin produced b21c7f15… again, byte for byte. The module's target_features section lists only `+bulk-memory +bulk-memory-opt +call-indirect-overlong +multivalue +mutable-globals +nontrapping-fptoint +reference-types +sign-ext`.

Add to solver/src/lib.rs the crate-level guard the wasm-raw-abi lane also recommends: `#[cfg(target_feature = "relaxed-simd")] compile_error!("...");`. rustc evaluates the cfg from whichever flags actually reached it, so the guard fires whichever source won.
recipes.rust_version: 1.98.1 (wasm32-unknown-unknown defaults as measured); any Cargo with CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS
recipes.gotchas: With --target, these flags reach only target units, never build scripts or proc-macros. The Clippy book's `env: RUSTFLAGS: "-Dwarnings"` pattern replaces .cargo/config.toml's pin for that job and changes rust-cache's key. The wasm32-unknown-unknown default feature set changes over time (nontrapping-fptoint and bulk-memory became defaults in 1.87.0), so 'off by default today' is not a pin. The guard sees crate-level flags only: measured, cfg!(target_feature = "relaxed-simd") stays false even inside a function marked #[target_feature(enable = "relaxed-simd")], and the guard compiles. Such a function is the binary-and-limits lane's case; T3's opcode lint covers it. So the guard checks the flags and the lint checks the bytes, and both stay.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs spreads `...process.env` and sets `RUSTFLAGS: rustflags` built with `.join(' ')`, repeating solver/.cargo/config.toml's `[target.wasm32-unknown-unknown] rustflags = ["-C", "target-feature=-relaxed-simd"]`. Switch that to CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS and add the compile_error! guard to solver/src/lib.rs. Then T3's solver/lint.mjs checks the opcodes, and the guard checks the flags.

recipes.name: Gate the solver in ci.yml with fmt --check, clippy -D warnings for wasm32 and host cargo test --lib
recipes.what: Rust gates need no new push-triggered workflow file. rustfmt --check, clippy with -D warnings for the wasm32 target and host unit tests of pure functions all fit in ci.yml, and `cargo test --lib` works on a cdylib-only crate. But today's solver fails -D warnings on seven static_mut_refs warnings, and integration tests or doctests would need "rlib", which moves the digest.
recipes.how:
One `rust` job in ci.yml, `working-directory: solver` (the paths filter already includes solver/**):
1. `rustup toolchain install --no-self-update` (with clippy and rustfmt listed in the toolchain file).
2. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` (the rustfmt README's CI form, which exits non-zero when formatting differs).
3. `cargo clippy --locked --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -- -D warnings`. This keeps .cargo/config.toml's pin in play, which job-level RUSTFLAGS would not.
4. `cargo test --locked --lib` on the host.

The test harness always unwinds: Cargo ignores `panic` for tests, and rustc refuses `--test -C panic=abort` with `building tests with panic=abort is not supported without -Zpanic_abort_tests`. Measured on cargo 1.98.1 with a cdylib-only crate: `cargo test --lib` ran its #[cfg(test)] unit test, `cargo test` failed on the integration test with E0433 `cannot find module or crate`, and with crate-type ["cdylib", "rlib"] unit, integration and doc tests all ran. The real 1.98.1 solver build prints 7 warnings: `creating a mutable reference to mutable static` four times and `creating a shared reference to mutable static` three times, under `#[warn(static_mut_refs)]`, part of `rust_2024_compatibility`. Fix them with &raw mut and &raw const first (the unsafe-ffi lane owns how), or the gate is red on day one.
recipes.gotchas: The Clippy book's CI example sets `RUSTFLAGS: "-Dwarnings"`. For this crate that replaces the config pin and changes rust-cache's key, so pass `-- -D warnings` instead. Use Clippy from the same toolchain as the build. Set `style_edition` in a rustfmt.toml so cargo fmt and rustfmt agree. Adding "rlib" moved the Windows digest from b21c7f15… to da3d1d11… (measured), so do it once, deliberately, with a re-pin. Host tests cannot observe wasm-only behaviour such as the trap on panic.
recipes.engine_note: .github/workflows/ci.yml has one job, `engines`. Add the Rust gates as a job or steps inside ci.yml, because ci.yml and pages.yml are already the two push-triggered files the studio allows. Test solver/src/lib.rs's pure functions (canon_zero, js_min) with `cargo test --lib` and leave `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` alone so the digest does not move. The seven warning sites are solver/src/lib.rs:28 `BODIES.as_mut_ptr()`, :33 `COLLIDERS.as_mut_ptr()`, :183 `&mut BODIES` and :184 `&COLLIDERS`, plus solver/src/rapier_law.rs:78 `HEIGHTS.as_mut_ptr()`, :738 `SOLVER.snapshot.as_ptr()` and :743 `SOLVER.snapshot.len()`.
recipes.verify_note: All 7 warning sites' file:line and mutable(4)/shared(3) split verified exactly against the repo. But canon_zero is in solver/src/rapier_law.rs, not lib.rs as engine_note states (js_min is correctly in lib.rs).

recipes.name: Guard the solver's dependency graph with cargo tree and cargo deny: no parallel, no rayon, crates.io only
recipes.what: Cargo builds each dependency with the union of the features requested anywhere in the graph. One new dependency could turn on rapier3d-f64's `parallel` (rayon) without anyone touching solver/Cargo.toml. A cargo tree assertion on the wasm32 graph plus cargo-deny's bans (including per-crate feature bans), sources, licenses and advisories checks turns that and other supply-chain drift into a CI failure.
recipes.how:
Measured on cargo 1.98.1 in a scratch copy: `cargo tree --locked --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -e normal --prefix none --format '{p} [{f}]'` printed:
- `rapier3d-f64 v0.35.3 [alloc,block-solver,default,dim3,enhanced-determinism,f64,std]`
- `parry3d-f64 v0.30.2 [alloc,dim3,ena,enhanced-determinism,f64,hashbrown,indexmap,required-features,slab,std]`
- `simba v0.10.2 [libm,libm_force,std,wide]`
- `wide v1.7.1 [std]`

Grepping those brackets for `parallel|simd-stable|simd-nightly` found nothing, and `cargo tree -i rayon` said "package ID specification `rayon` did not match any packages". Assert both absences and the presence of `enhanced-determinism` and `libm_force`. For the declarative form, write solver/deny.toml:
- `[graph] targets = ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]`
- `[bans] deny = [{ crate = "rayon", reason = "..." }]`
- `[[bans.features]] crate = "rapier3d-f64"`, `deny = ["parallel"]`, and the same for parry3d-f64
- `[sources] unknown-registry = "deny"`, `unknown-git = "deny"`
- `[licenses] allow = [...]`, built from the lock's actual licenses

Then run `cargo deny check`. Its four checks are licenses, bans, advisories and sources. For audits, add cargo-vet: `cargo vet init`, then `cargo vet --locked` in CI, with exemptions ratcheted down. Read every Cargo.lock diff line by line in review.
recipes.gotchas: `cargo tree` defaults to the host platform, so pass --target wasm32-unknown-unknown. Resolver 2 keeps build-dependencies and proc-macros from sharing features with normal deps, hence `-e normal`. cargo-deny's `unknown-registry` and `unknown-git` default to warn, not deny. `multiple-versions = "deny"` would fail today: solver/Cargo.lock holds glam 0.30.10, 0.31.1, 0.32.1 and 0.33.10, plus two hashbrown and two syn, so start at warn. rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 has no simd-stable or simd-nightly feature to ban; its `parallel` adds rayon and turns on parry3d-f64/parallel.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml declares `rapier3d-f64 = { version = "0.35.3", features = ["enhanced-determinism"] }`. solver/FLAGS.md says 'parallel is off' and 'This version has no simd-stable or simd-nightly feature', and the measured tree line and docs.rs both confirm it. Encode it in the `rust` job so FLAGS.md stops being the only record. ci.yml runs `npm audit --audit-level=high` for JS but nothing yet for the 61-package solver/Cargo.lock.
recipes.verify_note: Independently reran `cargo tree --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -e normal --format '{p} [{f}]'` against rapier3d-f64=0.35.3: all 4 claimed lines (rapier3d-f64/parry3d-f64/simba/wide) matched byte-for-byte, incl. the rayon-absent error text.

recipes.name: Run Miri, cargo-fuzz and cargo-mutants on a date-pinned nightly job that never builds the pinned digest
recipes.what: Miri is a nightly component and cargo-fuzz needs -Z sanitizer flags; stable 1.98.1 refuses both `#![feature]` (E0554) and -Z options. So these tools run in their own jobs on a date-pinned nightly against host unit tests. rustc compiles raw-pointer reads past a static buffer without a warning, and the lint for &T-to-&mut casts misses the solver's Vec-parked form. Both are defects only a run-time checker such as Miri reports.
recipes.how:
Miri:
1. `rustup toolchain install nightly-2026-09-25 --component miri` (rustup-components-history shows miri on every x86_64 Linux nightly from 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-25).
2. `cargo +nightly-2026-09-25 miri setup`.
3. `cargo +nightly-2026-09-25 miri test --lib`, over small host tests that call the exported functions.

The Miri README lists out-of-bounds, use-after-free, uninitialized reads, alignment, invalid values, data races and, experimentally, Stacked/Tree Borrows aliasing. It cannot run FFI, so it tests the Rust side of the buffer contract. cargo-fuzz: `cargo install cargo-fuzz`, then a fuzz target that feeds arbitrary f64 bit patterns and counts to host builds of the load and step entry points, and later to T2's snapshot parser. cargo-mutants: taiki-e/install-action with tool cargo-mutants and `cargo mutants -vV --in-place` weekly. On PRs, `git diff origin/main.. > changes.diff` then `cargo mutants --in-diff changes.diff`. Exit 2 means missed mutants, 3 timeouts, 4 a failing baseline. Measured on 1.98.1: a direct `&mut *(core::ptr::from_ref(pair) as *mut Pair)` is rejected with "casting `&T` to `&mut T` is undefined behavior, even if the reference is unused" (`#[deny(invalid_reference_casting)]`). The same cast split across two loops, as the solver writes it, compiles silently; the restore-internals lane carries the checks and the fix. Miri was not run here, because no nightly is installed on this rig.
recipes.rust_version: stable 1.98.1 for the artifact; nightly-2026-09-25 (miri available) for the analysis jobs
recipes.gotchas: A nightly job never writes or checks fixtures/solver.sha256, because a different rustc moves the digest. `rustup toolchain install nightly --component miri` without a date follows whichever nightly has Miri, so pin the date and bump it on purpose. The Miri README's CI example runs `rustup override set nightly`, which outranks solver/rust-toolchain.toml for later steps, so keep Miri in its own job. Miri is slow; keep Rapier scenes tiny. A crate with no Rust tests cannot catch any mutant, so cargo-mutants would exit 2 on every run (an inference from the exit-code table); add it only after the host tests exist. The Reference says the exact aliasing rules are not settled; run Miri under both of its aliasing models and treat a report as a defect to fix, not to suppress.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/rapier_law.rs `solver_clear_warmstart` pushes `core::ptr::from_ref(pair) as *mut ContactPair` for each `&ContactPair` that `narrow_phase.contact_pairs()` yields (in rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 its signature is `contact_pairs(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &ContactPair>`), then writes through `&mut *ptr`. The lint misses that form. docs.rs shows no public method yielding &mut ContactPair, so it is the first Miri target. The fix belongs to rust-kb-requests #1 and the restore-internals lane. Other targets: `static mut SOLVER` borrowed via `&mut *core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(SOLVER)`, BODIES/COLLIDERS, and T2's `solver_restore`, which parses untrusted bytes and is the natural fuzz target. Put these jobs in a scheduled workflow file.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced both halves of the lint claim myself: a direct &T->&mut T cast fires invalid_reference_casting with the exact quoted message; splitting the cast/deref across two loops (as solver_clear_warmstart does) compiles silently.

recipes.name: Schedule Rust drift checks weekly and bounded: advisories, an uncached digest rebuild and the replay corpus
recipes.what: Some drift happens without any push: new RustSec advisories, weekly runner-image updates, a cache that could hide a rebuild difference. Only a schedule catches it. GitHub runs scheduled workflows on the default branch's latest commit, may delay them at high load, and disables them after 60 days without activity in a public repository.
recipes.how:
Put this in a separate workflow file; a schedule does not count toward the two-push-file cap.
- Triggers: `on: schedule: - cron: '17 6 * * 1'` (weekly, off the hour) plus `workflow_dispatch`.
- Runner: `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, which the runner-images README maps to Ubuntu 24.04.
- Bounds: `timeout-minutes`, a `concurrency` group, and `permissions: contents: read, issues: write` (add `checks: write` only for audit-check).

Jobs:
1. Advisories: `cargo deny check advisories`, or rustsec/audit-check@v2, which opens issues on scheduled runs and creates check runs on push and PRs.
2. Uncached rebuild: `node solver/build.mjs --check` with no rust-cache step, proving the cached build equals a clean one.
3. T5's replay corpus with the trace diff: write a bundle and open an issue on failure.

Record the runner image from the job log. Run 36121826863 printed `Image: ubuntu-24.04` and `Version: 20260920.314.1`. Images get weekly updates, so a hosted image can be recorded but not pinned. The Cargo CI guide's latest-dependencies job (`cargo update`, then build and test, continue-on-error) can share this slot as a non-gating signal.
recipes.gotchas: audit-check's example cron is daily (`0 0 * * *`); the studio rule wants weekly unless a reason is stated. The start of every hour is a known high-load delay, so use an odd minute. A scheduled job never pushes and never writes fixtures/solver.sha256, goldens or Cargo.lock; a latest-deps job only reports. Sixty days without repository activity silently disables the schedule in a public repository.
recipes.engine_note: docs/PHASE-2.md T5 reads 'A nightly job replays every log and fixture on main'. The studio rule allows daily only with a stated reason, so either give the reason in T5's dispatch or run weekly. PHASE-2's PIN_PER_STEP remediation, 'T5's scheduled job pins its runner image by digest', cannot be done on GitHub-hosted runners; record the image version in the failure bundle instead. The uncached rebuild answers whether Swatinem/rust-cache ever masks a change to fixtures/solver.sha256.
recipes.verify_note: docs/PHASE-2.md T5 row and Standards-compliance remediation line quoted verbatim from the live repo. CI log lines 'Image: ubuntu-24.04' / 'Version: 20260920.314.1' match the engine_note exactly.

lanes.title: Floating point & cross-platform determinism
lanes.verifier_note: Checked against: the WebAssembly Core Spec (numerics/values/profiles/instruction-index pages), RFC 3514, Rust std docs and two Rust blog posts, five rust-lang/rust files fetched raw at tag 1.98.1 (one WebFetch summary inverted a cfg's boolean logic on compiler-builtins/src/math/mod.rs and had to be re-derived from a direct curl of the same URL), the pinned crate sources for rapier3d-f64/parry3d-f64/simba/glam/glamx/indexmap/hashbrown/foldhash/wide/libm read from the local cargo registry checkout (byte-identical to what docs.rs mirrors), si-rpg-engine's solver/src/lib.rs, solver/src/rapier_law.rs, solver/FLAGS.md, solver/Cargo.toml, solver/rust-toolchain.toml and solver/build.mjs fetched from GitHub main, and four of my own compile_oracle.py counter-example runs (E0015, E0599, E0658, algebraic_mul/algebraic_add) that all reproduced exactly what the checks claim. Nothing was refuted: every warrant resolved and supported its claim, every quoted engine fact matched the live repository (several verbatim, including js_min/js_max reproduced character-for-character and canonicalize_zero's real call sites on rapier3d-f64's warm-start impulses), and none of my own falsification attempts broke a recipe. The one systemic weakness is in recipe 8's engine_note: its most striking claim, that solver_step's compiled wasm actually reaches parry's BVH optimizer and glamx's eigensolver through a specific call chain, is a one-time, unrepeated wasmparser measurement on a scratch build, asserted at the same confidence as the fully source-grounded claims around it, and none of the lane's own checks re-verify that reachability (they verify wasm-vs-libm digest matching, an adjacent but weaker fact). A future dependency bump could silently break that specific claim with nothing in checks[] positioned to catch it.

recipes.name: Build hashed math from f64 + - * / and sqrt: the same bits on IEEE CPUs, wasm engines and in const eval
recipes.what: The IEEE 754 basic operations (+, -, *, /, sqrt) are correctly rounded (round to nearest, ties to even) in Rust and in WebAssembly, neither flushes subnormals, and rustc's const evaluator computes them in a host-independent soft-float, so a computation built only from them has one bit pattern natively, in every wasm engine and at compile time; only NaN bit patterns may differ.
recipes.how: Keep hashed arithmetic in f64 built from `+ - * /` and `f64::sqrt` (plus bit operations such as `abs`, comparisons and exact int-to-float conversions). Prove agreement the way the checks do: run one chain natively and in wasm and compare `to_bits()`. A 100 000-step chain that also makes a subnormal every step digests to 7853152472807335572 on x86-64 at -O0 and at -O and in wasm32 under node 22's V8; `50.0 * PI / 180.0` is 0x3febecde5da115a9 as a const, at run time natively, and at run time in wasm (4606035483714196905). Derived constants may be `const`/`const fn` (float ops in const fn since 1.82; `mul_add` const since 1.94), but a transcendental in a const is E0015. Leave the floating-point environment alone: Rust assumes the default rounding with denormals-are-zero off, and changing MXCSR's rounding or DAZ bits is immediate UB (`_mm_setcsr` docs); wasm operators round to nearest, ties to even, unless an operator says otherwise (trunc, floor, ...), in non-stop mode, and there is no mode to change.
recipes.rust_version: any stable (semantics per RFC 3514); float ops in const fn 1.82+; mul_add const 1.94+; checked on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: RFC 3514's own caveat: 32-bit x86 returns floats in x87 registers, altering NaN payloads, and i586 targets use x87 even more pervasively; that is a native 32-bit concern, not wasm32. The guarantee is per operation: a different order ((a+b)+c vs a+(b+c)), an f32 intermediate or a transcendental breaks bit equality. NaN bits made at compile time need not match run time (std docs). On the no_std target wasm32v1-none `f64::sqrt` does not exist on stable (E0599; core's float math is unstable), so a no_std law calls `libm::sqrt`.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs states the rule in its header ('No other operation than add, sub, mul, div, and sqrt') for `step` and `resolve_pair`; rapier_law.rs's own arithmetic (`canon_quat`, the collider centres and half-extents in `build_world`) stays inside it apart from min/max on positive half-extents, and CLIMB_ANGLE / SLIDE_ANGLE are const-evaluated basic ops. FLAGS.md's 'Nothing in the flags flushes subnormals, so they stay subnormals' holds on both sides: Rust treats a changed DAZ/FTZ state as UB, and wasm defines no flush mode. This is why V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore can print one golden.
recipes.verify_note: RFC 3514 confirms the basic-op IEEE guarantee verbatim; operator.rs@1.98.1 shows const eval via rustc_apfloat+adjust_nan; my own compile_oracle.py run reproduced E0015 and E0599 exactly as the checks claim.

recipes.name: Expect a*b+c to stay unfused: rustc never contracts, mul_add always rounds once, wasm has no scalar fma
recipes.what: rustc never turns `a * b + c` into a fused multiply-add, not at -O and not with `-C target-feature=+fma`; `f64::mul_add` always rounds once, and on wasm32 it is a software fma compiled into the module (no import); wasm 3.0 has no scalar fma instruction, so hardware-chosen fusion can only enter through relaxed SIMD's relaxed_madd; the stable opt-in to contraction since 1.98.0 is the `algebraic_*` family.
recipes.how: Write `a * b + c` when the law means two roundings (what a JS kernel computes). Write `a.mul_add(b, c)` only when you want IEEE fusedMultiplyAdd on every target: the std docs guarantee 'the rounded infinite-precision result', and it differs from the unfused form (inputs 1+eps, 1-eps, -1 give -4.930380657631324e-32 fused and 0 unfused on x86-64 at -O0, at -O with +fma, and in wasm32). Keep `algebraic_add/sub/mul/div/rem` out of the law (the rust-currency lane covers them; a source grep for `algebraic_` refuses them). Keep relaxed SIMD disabled (`-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd`) and let T3's opcode lint prove that no relaxed instruction reached the binary.
recipes.rust_version: any (no contraction); mul_add const 1.94+; algebraic_* stable 1.98.0+
recipes.gotchas: 'Rust may contract a*b+c like a C compiler' is wrong: RFC 3514 precludes it because rounding would change. The reverse mistake is treating `mul_add` as a speed hint that equals `a*b+c`: it is a different result, and without FMA hardware it is a library call. SIMD crates choose per target: wide 1.7.1's `f64x2::mul_add` fuses on x86 with the `fma` feature and on aarch64 NEON and rounds twice elsewhere; relaxed_madd may be fused or unfused, fixed per environment.
recipes.engine_note: FLAGS.md's 'Fused multiply-add is not in that set. It arrives only with relaxed SIMD, which this build disables' is right about hardware fusion, but an explicit `mul_add` in solver/src or in a dependency still yields a fused result (a deterministic software fma), so the sentence is safest as 'no implicit fusion; mul_add only where written'. solver/src at e5fbcb9 has no mul_add; the rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 and parry3d-f64 0.30.2 sources have none either (grep this session). T3's relaxed-SIMD opcode lint is the gate for the only hardware-dependent fusion path.
recipes.verify_note: RFC 3514 and the local wide-1.7.1 source both confirm the fused/unfused claims verbatim. The regenerated input now carries wasm_no_imports/no_warnings gates matching the 'no imports'/'no warning' check labels.

recipes.name: Keep std sin, cos, exp, ln, powf, atan2 and hypot out of hashed math; call the Cargo.lock-pinned libm
recipes.what: std documents sin, cos, exp, ln, powf, atan2 and hypot as 'Unspecified precision' (varies by platform and Rust version). Natively they are the platform C library's (on this Windows host each of the seven disagrees with the libm crate somewhere in a 100 000-input sweep); on wasm32-unknown-unknown they are compiled into the module from the toolchain's own copy of libm in compiler-builtins, which today matches libm 0.2.16 for sin but not for hypot.
recipes.how: For any transcendental whose bits can reach state or a hash, call one pinned implementation explicitly: the `libm` crate (`libm::sin`, `libm::cos`, `libm::atan2`, `libm::hypot`, `libm::pow`, `libm::exp`, `libm::log`), whose version Cargo.lock pins. Measured: wasm32 `f64::sin` over the sweep digests to 1810793848087136966, exactly libm 0.2.16's digest, and the module imports nothing; wasm32 `f64::hypot` digests to -4090065345391819473 against libm 0.2.16's 727198713234182705, because rustc 1.98.1's in-tree hypot.rs is a CORE-MATH port while libm 0.2.16 ships a different (SPLIT/sq) algorithm.
recipes.gotchas: 'IEEE 754 makes sin portable' is wrong: RFC 3514's guarantees cover the basic operations only, and std gives the transcendentals unspecified precision. On wasm32 the std functions are deterministic across engines (they are wasm code) but move with the toolchain, not with Cargo.lock. Two careful implementations can both be deterministic and still disagree (hypot here); determinism comes from pinning one copy, not from accuracy. On no_std targets there is no stable `f64::sin` at all.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src (lib.rs, rapier_law.rs at e5fbcb9) calls only sqrt, min and max, so the crate's own code is clean; mirror T3 pin 7, which refuses Math.sin/cos/tan/atan2/hypot in JS scene builders, with a Rust source test over solver/src. The dependency graph is not clean: parry and glamx reach the toolchain's log2, acos and cos through inherent calls (see the rust-toolchain.toml recipe).

recipes.name: Know what rapier3d-f64 0.35.3's enhanced-determinism switches: libm, IndexMap, canonical zeros, not SIMD
recipes.what: `enhanced-determinism` = simba's `libm_force` (an optional dependency on the libm crate, so simba's ComplexField/RealField math on f64 calls libm) plus parry's flag (indexmap, glamx/libm, glamx/scalar-math). In code it makes parry's HashMap/HashSet an IndexMap/IndexSet with a pointer-width-independent FxHasher32, drains joint wake-up/join sets in order, canonicalises -0.0 in the warm-start impulses it stores, and refuses `simd8` with compile_error!. It does not switch off parry's 4-lane `wide` types.
recipes.how: Keep the feature on and never add `parallel` or `simd8` beside it. What it buys the wasm law: map iteration fixed by the insert/remove sequence, simba and glam transcendentals pinned by Cargo.lock, no -0.0 in stored impulses. Measured in the oracle, which links the solver's feature set: parry's HashMap iterates [5, 1, 3] in insertion order and has IndexMap's `swap_remove`; `SIMD_WIDTH` is 4 and `SimdReal` is `simba::simd::wide_simd_impl::WideF64x4`; simba's `ComplexField::sin` and glam's `DQuat::from_rotation_y` equal `libm::sin` bit for bit on 100 000 inputs where std's `f64::sin` does not.
recipes.rust_version: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3, parry3d-f64 0.30.2, simba 0.10.2, glam 0.33.10 (via glamx 0.3.1), wide 1.7.1
recipes.gotchas: Correcting a common recollection: the flag does not turn SIMD off. parry 0.30.2 says the wide types 'are always used, whatever the platform' (scalar code on wasm32 without simd128), and `glamx/scalar-math` only affects glam's f32 SIMD types (glam's f64 types never use SIMD). `libm_force` is not in simba's [features] table: it is the implicit feature of an optional dependency renamed from libm. simba's `simd_mul_add` for WideF64x4 is not gated by libm_force and fuses on aarch64 NEON and x86+fma when compiled natively. The flag cannot reroute inherent calls such as `x.log2()` on an f64 (see the rust-toolchain.toml recipe). Without it parry's maps are hashbrown with foldhash's FixedState.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml enables the feature, and FLAGS.md's 'This version has no simd-stable or simd-nightly feature; wide is still a transitive crate' matches parry 0.30.2. recipes.name: Canonicalize -0.0 to +0.0 before to_bits() feeds a hash: equal values, different bits
recipes.what: `0.0 == -0.0` is true but their bits differ (0x0000000000000000 vs 0x8000000000000000), so a hash over `to_bits()` splits equal states; the sign survives the wasm-to-JS boundary, `total_cmp` orders -0.0 before +0.0, and min/max may return either zero on a tie.
recipes.how: Canonicalize at every point where bits are stored or hashed: `if x == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { x }` (the engine's `canon`) or `x + 0.0` (Rapier's `canonicalize_zero`; -0.0 + 0.0 is +0.0 under round to nearest). Both leave NaN alone, so refuse NaN separately. Shown: raw `mix_f64` of 0.0 and -0.0 differ while the canonical mix is equal; in wasm `canon_zero(-0.0)` returns 0 while an identity export hands -0 to JS.
recipes.gotchas: Canonicalizing only inside the hash still lets -0.0 flow on: 1.0 / -0.0 is -inf, so canonicalize where the value is written too (write_body does). `x + 0.0` looks like dead code to a reviewer or a refactor; name it. `abs()` also clears the sign but changes negative numbers. Sorting by `total_cmp` without canonicalizing separates keys that compare equal.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs canonicalizes in `write_body` (every stored field), `canon_quat`, `push_f64` (the snapshot) and the exported `canon_zero`, and Rapier 0.35.3 canonicalizes the warm-start impulses it writes under enhanced-determinism. One path hashes raw bits: `signature()` feeds collider and height values to `mix_f64`, and `same_sig` compares the result, so a quantum whose record writes -0.0 where the previous one wrote +0.0 reloads the world and drops the warm-start cache (build.mjs's `box.qx || 0` canonicalizes only the quaternion's x, y, z). That is a reading of the code, not an observed failure; canon before mix_f64 closes it.
recipes.verify_note: rapier_law.rs's canon/canon_zero/push_f64/write_body match the cited checks verbatim. signature() genuinely mixes raw uncanonicalized collider/height bits into the hash; build.mjs's 'box.qx || 0' found twice.

recipes.name: Refuse NaN or map it to one bit pattern before hashing: its sign and payload are the engine's choice
recipes.what: NaN != NaN, and the bits of a NaN produced by arithmetic are nondeterministic in both Rust and wasm (the sign always; the payload within the options each spec lists), may differ between const eval and run time, and V8 on this x86-64 host returns 0xfff8000000000000 (sign set) for 0/0 while `f64::NAN` is 0x7ff8000000000000; `total_cmp` still gives a total order (-NaN < -inf < ... < -0 < +0 < ... < +inf < +NaN) where `partial_cmp` returns None.
recipes.how: Refuse NaN at every boundary the law reads or writes (the engine's `bad()`), or map any NaN to `f64::from_bits(0x7ff8000000000000)` before `to_bits()` reaches a hash: in wasm the mapped 0/0 is 9221120237041090560 whatever the host picked. Sort with `sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b))`, never `partial_cmp(..).unwrap()` (a NaN makes it panic, exit 101). Do not branch on `is_sign_negative()` of a NaN.
recipes.rust_version: total_cmp 1.62+; NaN rules documented from 1.82; checked on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: `f64::NAN`'s own bits may change across Rust versions and targets (std docs), so even a constant NaN is not a stable hash input. The wasm 3.0 deterministic profile (positive canonical NaNs) is a separate spec profile; the engine measured here returned a sign-set NaN, so write code for the full profile. A different CPU architecture may pick a different sign for the same 0/0, which is exactly what the ARM64 lane would expose if a NaN ever reached a hash.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs refuses NaN in `signature`, `write_body`, `canon_quat` and `integrate`, and lib.rs's `step` returns 0 on a NaN pose, so no body NaN is hashed. `push_contact` hashes warm-start impulses through `push_f64`, whose `canon` passes a NaN through with the engine's bits; adding `bad()` there (or the one-pattern map) makes the refusal cover every hashed field before the T3 ARM64 lane compares goldens.
recipes.verify_note: rapier_law.rs's own canon() does not special-case NaN (x==0.0 is false for NaN), so push_f64 truly lets a NaN's bits through unchanged, exactly as claimed. Every NaN-nondeterminism source quoted verbatim.

recipes.name: Write the min/max tie rule yourself: f64::max(-0.0, 0.0) changes with context, minimum/maximum are nightly
recipes.what: f64::min/max ignore a single NaN (IEEE 754-2019 minimumNumber/maximumNumber) but may return either zero on a -0.0/+0.0 tie; f64::minimum/maximum (NaN-propagating, -0 < +0) are still unstable on 1.98.1 (E0658, feature float_minimum_maximum, #91079); wasm's fmin/fmax propagate NaN and order the zeros; JS Math.min/max return NaN for any NaN argument and treat -0 as smaller than +0 (Math.min(0, -0) is -0, Math.max(-0, 0) is 0).
recipes.how: Where the result can reach state or a hash, spell the tie rule out (as lib.rs's js_min/js_max do) or canonicalize the zero after min/max. Shown with rustc 1.98.1: the same expression `n.max(p)` with n = -0.0 and p = +0.0 returns 0.0 in one function and -0.0 in another where `p.max(n)` was computed beside it, natively at -O and in wasm at -O, while native -O0 gives 0.0 in both (a guess at the cause: the optimiser treats max as commutative and reuses the neighbour's result).
recipes.gotchas: `x.max(0.0)` does not reliably turn -0.0 into +0.0, and `(-0.0).clamp(0.0, 1.0)` returns -0.0 (measured); canonicalize explicitly. A result that looks stable in one build can flip after an unrelated edit or a toolchain bump, which a golden hash then reports as a law change. Rust's f64::min is neither wasm's fmin nor JS's Math.min: those two propagate NaN and order the zeros, Rust's ignores a single NaN and may return either zero.
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs's `js_min`/`js_max` (the overlap in `resolve_pair`) implement JS's zero ordering explicitly, so the box step does not depend on the tie rule. Their NaN behaviour is asymmetric and unlike Math.min: js_min(1, NaN) = 1 but js_min(NaN, 1) = NaN, harmless while `step` returns 0 on a NaN pose. rapier_law.rs's `half.x.min(half.z)` and `(half.y - radius).max(0.0)` act on strictly positive half-extents, so no zero tie arises there.
recipes.verify_note: My own oracle run reproduced E0658 exactly. lib.rs's js_min/js_max are character-for-character the live source. Unlike sibling recipes, this one doesn't label its -O0/-O min/max asymmetry checks as host-specific.

recipes.name: Treat rust-toolchain.toml as part of the law: the solver links the toolchain's own log2, acos, cos and sin
recipes.what: Inherent calls such as `x.log2()` or `x.acos()` on an f64 resolve to std's method (inherent methods are searched before trait methods, and a `#![no_std]` crate that links std sees them), so libm_force cannot reroute them; in parry 0.30.2's bvh_optimize.rs and glamx 0.3.1's eigen3.rs the ComplexField import is compiled only without std. On wasm32 those std methods are compiler-builtins' copy of libm, pinned by the toolchain, not by Cargo.lock.
recipes.how: Treat a toolchain bump like a libm bump: rerun the goldens and behaviour numbers before accepting it. Shown in the oracle: with ComplexField in scope `a.sin()` is std's (rustc even reports the import unused) while `ComplexField::sin` is libm's; a no_std crate with `extern crate std` compiles `root.log2()` as parry's BVH optimizer writes it. Today the toolchain's acos, log2 and cos in wasm equal libm 0.2.16 over 100 000-input sweeps (digests in the checks) while this Windows host's C runtime does not; hypot shows the two copies can part. A cheap gate: list `compiler_builtins::math::libm_math::*` names from the wasm name section (present in the scratch release build measured here) of every built solver and diff the list on bumps.
recipes.gotchas: Grepping a dependency for `libm::` or trusting 'enhanced-determinism = libm everywhere' misses inherent calls; only the built binary tells you which math is linked. The same calls compiled natively (host bindings) use the platform C library, so a native law would diverge where the wasm law does not. Equality with libm today is a measurement, not a contract.
recipes.engine_note: Measured on a scratch copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9 (cargo +1.98.1 build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --locked): si_solver.wasm's name section lists libm::math::{sin, cos, sqrt, acos, asin, atan, atan2, sincos, floor, ceil, copysign} and compiler_builtins::math::libm_math::{sin, cos, acos, log2}. A wasmparser call graph reaches log2 from `solver_load`/`solver_step` through `BroadPhaseBvh::update` and parry's `Bvh::optimize_incremental`, whose `.log2()` feeds a `.round()` that sets how many subtrees to rebuild; acos/cos are reached from `MassProperties + MassProperties` through glamx `symmetric_eigen`; sin/cos also through the joint builders, which the law does not use. Whether any of these moves the golden is unmeasured; the toolchain pin (1.98.1) is what holds them.
recipes.verify_note: ComplexField gating and the .log2()/.acos()/.cos() calls are confirmed directly in parry/glamx source; the solver_step to BVH-optimizer call-graph is carried only by the lane's scratch wasm build, not by source alone.

recipes.name: Hash only IndexMap, BTreeMap or sorted order: a fixed hasher does not fix HashMap order across targets
recipes.what: std's HashMap is randomly seeded (SipHash 1-3 today) and iterates in arbitrary order; hashbrown 0.17.1's default is foldhash's randomly initialised RandomState; a fixed hasher fixes the seed, not the iteration order across targets: the same 1000 inserts into a std HashMap with a fixed FNV hasher iterate differently on x86-64 and in wasm32, while a BTreeMap iterates identically (and foldhash does not even promise equal hash values across platforms).
recipes.how: For anything that can reach a hash or a snapshot use `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` (key order), `IndexMap` (insert/remove order, independent of the hasher; give it a fixed hasher such as `Xxh3Builder::new()` if you want reproducible hash values too), or a Vec sorted by a stable id. With IndexMap prefer `shift_remove` (keeps relative order) when order is part of the record; `swap_remove` moves the last entry into the hole but is still deterministic given the same operation sequence. Keep std HashMap/HashSet for lookups only. Measured: HashMap(fixed FNV) order digest 7883764408781778729 on x86-64 vs 415840167048917935 in wasm32; BTreeMap 4523094667136758445 on both.
recipes.rust_version: any; std::hash::RandomState path 1.76+; hashbrown 0.17.1; foldhash 0.2.0; indexmap 2.14.2
recipes.gotchas: 'Use FxHash/foldhash with a fixed seed and the map is deterministic' holds only for one target and one library version: foldhash itself warns against expecting consistent output across versions or platforms, and std documents HashMap order as arbitrary. hashbrown's `DefaultHashBuilder` is randomly initialised. rustc-hash's FxHasher depends on the pointer size; parry wrote FxHasher32 so that it does not.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src holds no hash map; bodies and colliders are index-ordered static arrays and the snapshot sorts contact pairs by collider handle before hashing (rebuild_snapshot). Rapier's own maps are IndexMap<FxHasher32> under enhanced-determinism. Any map added for mesh collision or host bindings should be a BTreeMap or IndexMap on the hashed path.
recipes.verify_note: solver/src genuinely holds no HashMap anywhere. rebuild_snapshot sorts contact pairs by collider handle before hashing, exactly as claimed, confirmed by reading the live rapier_law.rs on main.
