recipes.name: Gate toolchain and Cargo.lock bumps on goldens plus a libm canary; keep fixed-point for integer-exact parts
recipes.what: Results move on a bump through three mechanisms, each measured here: a libm version changes an algorithm (rustc 1.98.1's in-tree hypot returns 0x4018842a6ab3fa86 where libm 0.2.16 returns ...85 for the same input), a dependency reorders a sum (floating-point addition is not associative), and codegen changes tie choices such as min/max of zeros. Fixed-point arithmetic removes the float-specific classes (reassociation, NaN, signed zero, platform libm) but not the need for a gate.
recipes.how: Keep both pins (rust-toolchain.toml and Cargo.lock) and move them only through a gate: the golden hash, the behaviour numbers and the T4 course, plus a Rust canary test that asserts the bits of the few libm outputs the law depends on, so a lockfile bump fails by name before a golden moves. Shown: `(0.1+0.2)+0.3` is 0x3fe3333333333334 and `0.1+(0.2+0.3)` is ...33; the harmonic sum to 1000 differs forwards and backwards; the same values as Q32.32 integers (what `fixed`'s I32F32 stores) sum identically both ways. Use `fixed` (1.31.0) for new integer-exact subsystems, not for the physics law: Rapier and parry are f64 code.
recipes.gotchas: A digest-only gate says that something moved, not what; the canary and the behaviour numbers name it. A bump stays silent until a scene reaches the changed path, so the golden scenes must exercise what the law uses (the BVH optimizer's log2 matters only when its rounding decision flips). Fixed-point is not free: range is limited, overflow is an error class of its own (the crate offers Wrapping, Saturating and Strict wrappers), and the law would have to leave Rapier.
recipes.engine_note: Mirrors T4 pin 6, which makes any bump of the toolchain or of rapier3d-f64 rerun the course before a golden may move; extend the same rule to libm, simba and glam(x) in Cargo.lock, add the canary as a `cargo test` in solver/, and list toolchain-supplied libm symbols from the built wasm (see the rust-toolchain.toml recipe) so the review sees which pin a change came through.
recipes.verify_note: libm CHANGELOG.md confirms both cited entries verbatim (0.2.12 CORE-MATH cbrt+fma sign fix; 0.2.16 2025-12-07 fminimum/fmaximum fix). The recipe's two hypot bit values are internally consistent (...85, then +1 ULP = ...86).

lanes.title: Embedding the Rust law in hosts (JS, Godot, Unreal)
lanes.verifier_note: Checked every recipe's warrant sources by direct retrieval, never from memory: docs.rs pages at the pinned versions (wasmtime 49.0.1, godot 0.5.5, rapier3d-f64 0.35.3, parry3d-f64 0.30.2, glamx 0.3.1, bytemuck 1.25.2, cbindgen 0.29.4), official docs (wasmtime.dev, doc.rust-lang.org/stable, docs.godotengine.org 4.7/4.5, dev.epicgames.com, component-model.bytecodealliance.org, godot-rust.github.io), raw crate/GitHub source (godot-wasm store.h/SConstruct/utils.py at two refs, glamx eigen3.rs, parry mass_properties.rs, cbindgen CHANGES, Cargo.toml source views), GitHub release pages via gh CLI (wasmtime v49.0.0/v49.0.1/v48.0.3, wasmer v7.4.2, WAMR-2.4.5, wasm3 v0.9.0, jco-v1.35.0, wit-bindgen v0.62.0), two godot-proposals issues, and si-rpg-engine itself at the pinned commit f84c98b (build.mjs, FLAGS.md, README.md, solver/src/lib.rs, rapier_law.rs, .cargo/config.toml, trace-line.mjs, first-difference.js, docs/PHASE-2.md, the product-alignment dispatch). I ran all 17 of the lane's checks through the real pinned rustc 1.98.1 plus the real rapier3d-f64/parry3d-f64/bytemuck rlibs and node v22.22.3 via compile_oracle.py: 17/17 passed with exact stdout, exact compile_fail error codes (E0277, E0080), and exact wasm export/import lists, including a real rapier3d-f64 physics run whose collision event lands at quantum 20 exactly as claimed and a native/wasm FNV match (4769065195358558711) that is genuinely opt-level-3-native-vs-wasm, not asserted. I independently reproduced the JS negative-zero claim on this rig's node v22.22.3 (String(-0), (-0).toFixed(3), JSON.stringify(-0) all print without a minus sign) and confirmed wasm3's and godot-wasm's release histories have no tagged release hiding between the cited versions. I also diffed the pinned commit against main (17 commits ahead as of this sweep) specifically hunting for the stale-engine_note pattern another lane in this sweep flagged: docs/PHASE-2.md did change on main, but only in the T2/T7 area; the T1 and T3 rows every host-embedding recipe cites are byte-for-byte identical, and the new docs/dispatch-t3-platforms.md corroborates rather than contradicts recipe 2's 'T3 will refuse growable memory' claim (it reveals the pinned binary's allocator did still call memory.grow at f84c98b, which is exactly the live risk recipes 1 and 2 tell hosts to defend against). Nothing in the ten recipes was false, unsupported, or mismatched between check and prose; every one of roughly 74 warrant sources resolved and supported its claim verbatim. What failed: nothing verifiable failed. The systemic weakness is not an error but a shelf-life one: the lane's authority rests on two extremely fast-moving artifacts, Wasmtime (a new major every month; 49.0.1 and 48.0.3 both shipped the identical fuel-spend security fix on 2026-09-24, one day before this sweep) and si-rpg-engine itself (17 commits and a same-day PHASE-2.md amendment within the pinned commit's own calendar day) - so 'solid' here means solid against today's ground truth, not against a stable target, and the runtime-config recipe plus every engine_note will need the 30-day freshness re-check the studio's own memory rule already prescribes sooner than most lanes would.

recipes.name: Host the law as the one pinned .wasm in an embedded runtime; it imports nothing, so no WASI is linked
recipes.what: Option A ships the Linux-built si_solver.wasm itself to every host and runs it in an embedded runtime: one artifact and one digest, and because the module imports nothing the host supplies no WASI and no host functions, only an executor for core wasm.
recipes.how: Verify the loaded bytes against fixtures/solver.sha256 (FLAGS.md: the pin is the Linux build, Windows bytes differ, and the golden hash is the cross-host invariant) and refuse any other digest. Instantiate with an empty import list; in wasmtime 49: `Instance::new(&mut store, &module, &[])`, `instance.get_memory(&mut store, "memory")` and `instance.get_typed_func::<(u32, u32, u32, u32, u32, f64, u32), u32>(&mut store, "solver_step")` (WasmTy is implemented for u32 and f64). Move the f64 buffers with `Memory::write` / `Memory::read` at the byte offsets bodies_ptr(), colliders_ptr() and heights_ptr() return, and never hold a slice or raw pointer into linear memory across a call: wasmtime's Memory docs say growth may change the base address anywhere inside a wasm call, the same reason build.mjs re-creates its Float64Array views on every call. In a browser, or a Godot Web export, the page's own engine runs the same bytes.
recipes.rust_version: rustc 1.98.1 -> wasm32-unknown-unknown; host side wasmtime 49.0.1 (builds with Rust 1.96+)
recipes.gotchas: The .wasm is only the physics step: the fixed 1/64 s tick, admission and the two-lane FNV-1a frame hash are JavaScript (packages/tick, packages/frame), so a host that embeds just the module reproduces body states but not the golden hash unless it also runs that JavaScript (an embedded JS engine, or a node process streaming committed frames) or the tick is ported to Rust and passes the same trace diff. Keep the import list empty: the JS API throws a TypeError when a module has imports and no import object is given, so build.mjs's bare `new WebAssembly.Instance(module)` succeeding under three engines is the running proof, and a single import (a clock, a random source) would oblige every host to supply and pin it. The digest pins the law, not the runtime: a runtime is accepted by the trace it prints, not by loading the module.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs instantiate() passes no import object and re-creates its views per call; that is the reference every host copies. The host surface is the ten exports of solver/src/lib.rs and rapier_law.rs (bodies_ptr, colliders_ptr, heights_ptr, step, solver_load, solver_step, snapshot_ptr, snapshot_len, solver_clear_warmstart, canon_zero), and fixtures/solver.sha256 is the one pin every host verifies. This meets the README's aspiration (a browser, Godot or Unreal draws the picture and sends intents; presentation has no path back into the hash) without a second law artifact.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check PASS (wasm_no_imports, 5 exports, solver_step(3)=1). build.mjs instantiate() takes no import object verbatim; lib.rs+rapier_law.rs export exactly the ten named functions, confirmed by name.

recipes.name: Build wasmtime's Config for the law by hand and pin an LTS line; defaults and fuel costs move between releases
recipes.what: Wasmtime 49.0.1's defaults are not a determinism profile (NaN canonicalization off, relaxed SIMD on with the fastest per-CPU lowering, the threads proposal on through a default crate feature), and releases move them: 49.0.0 turned wide-arithmetic on and changed fuel charges, and the 49.0.1 / 48.0.3 security patches changed fuel spend again.
recipes.how: Set every knob in code: `config.cranelift_nan_canonicalization(true)` (replaces NaNs with one canonical value; not enabled by default because the spec does not require it), `config.wasm_relaxed_simd(false)` (or `relaxed_simd_deterministic(true)`), `config.wasm_threads(false)`. For a watchdog use `config.consume_fuel(true)` plus `store.set_fuel(n)`: fuel is the deterministic interruption, and `epoch_interruption` is documented as not deterministic. Make memory growth deterministic the ways the determinism page lists (a store limiter, a memory creator that reserves the maximum up front, or a wasmparser check that refuses growable memories). C API equivalents: `wasmtime_config_cranelift_nan_canonicalization_set`, `wasmtime_config_wasm_relaxed_simd_set`, `wasmtime_config_wasm_relaxed_simd_deterministic_set`, `wasmtime_config_wasm_threads_set`, `wasmtime_config_consume_fuel_set`. Pin the runtime beside the solver pins: a new major ships on the 20th of each month and may break behaviour; majors divisible by 12 are LTS for 24 months (48.0.3, 2026-09-24), the rest are supported for 2 months.
recipes.rust_version: wasmtime 49.0.1 (2026-09-24) or LTS 48.0.3; building wasmtime 49 needs Rust 1.96+
recipes.gotchas: Fuel counts are not portable across Wasmtime versions: 49.0.0 began charging Config::operator_cost inside constant expressions and the start call (previously 1 fuel each), and 49.0.1 / 48.0.3 fixed dropped fuel-spend for call_ref callees and exception returns. Running out of fuel is therefore a host failure to report, never an outcome written to the admitted log or folded into a hash. NaN canonicalization adds checks after f32/f64/v128 operations; the law already aborts a step on NaN, so the knob protects only a NaN's bits between its creation and that abort (the spec leaves the sign of an arithmetic NaN nondeterministic). Patch releases promise unchanged behaviour, yet these fuel fixes shipped as patches: pin the exact version, not a range.
recipes.engine_note: solver/.cargo/config.toml and solver/build.mjs already pass -C target-feature=-relaxed-simd, and T3's lint will refuse relaxed-SIMD opcodes and growable memory; the host Config is the second gate for the same properties. lib.rs step() and rapier_law.rs solver_step() return 0 on NaN, so canonicalization is belt and braces there. Any fuel budget belongs to the host harness (T5's replay bundles), never to the frame hash in packages/frame.
recipes.verify_note: All 5 Config defaults, all 5 C-API function names, and both release-note fuel-spend fixes (GHSA-m63x, GHSA-jqpg) confirmed verbatim live on docs.rs/docs.wasmtime.dev and the exact 2026-09-24 release pages.

recipes.name: Choose the runtime per platform by tier: Cranelift needs executable pages at run time, interpreters do not
recipes.what: Four runtimes can execute the law's core module natively, at different maturity: Wasmtime 49.0.1 (Cranelift or Winch compilers, Pulley interpreter), Wasmer 7.4.2, WAMR 2.4.5 and wasm3 0.9.0. Because the law uses no SIMD, even the SIMD-less wasm3 can load it.
recipes.how: Wasmtime tiers: Tier 1 = x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-apple-darwin, the Cranelift and Winch compilers, the Rust and C embedding APIs; Tier 2 = aarch64 Linux and macOS, the Pulley interpreter, #![no_std] support, the C++ API; Tier 3 = aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, iOS, Android, i686. Cranelift and Winch need an OS that can create executable pages on the fly and cannot statically link a precompiled module; a no_std build runs AOT-precompiled modules; where Cranelift has no backend Wasmtime uses Pulley, which runs wherever Wasmtime compiles, with a performance penalty. Wasmer 7.4.2 (2026-09-16): Singlepass, Cranelift (the default) and LLVM compilers; NaN canonicalization is `Cranelift::canonicalize_nans(true)`, default false. WAMR-2.4.5 (2026-06-29, three CVE fixes; the project now lives at github.com/wasm-micro-runtime): interpreter, AOT through wamrc, Fast JIT and LLVM JIT; x86-64, x86-32, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V, Xtensa, MIPS, ARC. wasm3 0.9.0 (2026-08-24, its first release after v0.5.0): an interpreter that now fully validates modules; its README lists the deterministic profile as ready and fixed-width SIMD and threads as not available.
recipes.rust_version: wasm32-unknown-unknown on rustc 1.98.1 (default target features exclude simd128 and relaxed-simd)
recipes.gotchas: In option A the runtime's maturity is inherited: wasm3's README says it has entered 'a minimal maintenance phase' and relies on outside pull requests, WAMR's latest release was security fixes only, and Wasmtime's aarch64 Windows, iOS and Android targets are Tier 3. No retrieved page shows any of these runtimes shipping on a game console (console SDKs are under NDA), so console support is unestablished; on platforms without run-time code generation the documented Wasmtime path is Pulley. Turning on simd128 for speed would lock out wasm3 and change the pinned bytes; the probe below turns that into a build error.
recipes.engine_note: solver/rust-toolchain.toml pins 1.98.1 and wasm32-unknown-unknown, whose default target features exclude simd128 and relaxed-simd, and solver/.cargo/config.toml removes relaxed-simd explicitly, so si_solver.wasm fits every runtime above. T3's ARM64 lane is where aarch64 hosts (Wasmtime Tier 2) should prove the trace before a Godot or Unreal build ships on them.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle 2/2 checks PASS (simd128 guard compiles and traps as claimed). Tiers/platform-support pages, Wasmer default=Cranelift, WAMR's 3 CVEs, and wasm3's release gap (v0.9.0 is literally the next tag after v0.5.0/2021) all confirmed live.

recipes.name: In Godot 4, embed the .wasm through a GDExtension you configure; godot-wasm runs wasmtime on its defaults
recipes.what: No retrieved Godot 4.7 page documents a built-in WebAssembly runtime, and the requests to add one (#147 opened 2019, #10488 opened 2024) are still open, so option A in Godot is an extension that embeds a runtime or, in a Web export, the browser's own engine reached through JavaScriptBridge.
recipes.how: Three routes, in order of control. (1) A gdext cdylib that depends on the wasmtime crate, builds the Config of the knob recipe, verifies the digest and exposes a class GDScript calls once per quantum: one native library per platform, law bytes unchanged (a design inference; no retrieved page shows this exact combination). (2) The godot-wasm addon, a GDExtension or module whose SConstruct defaults to wasmtime (wasmer optional): release v0.5.0-godot-4 (2025-10-10, Godot 4.5) defaults to Wasmtime v37.0.2 / Wasmer v6.1.0, master since 2026-02-06 to Wasmtime v41.0.3 / Wasmer v7.0.1; it creates its engine with `wasm_engine_new()` and one store shared by every module. (3) In a Web export, `JavaScriptBridge`, implemented only in the Web export, reaches the page's JavaScript context, where the same module runs in the browser engine that already prints the goldens.
recipes.gotchas: godot-wasm's `wasm_engine_new()` takes no config, so the law would run on Wasmtime's defaults (NaN canonicalization off, relaxed SIMD on); that is tolerable only because the law aborts on NaN and carries no relaxed SIMD, which leaves T3's lint and the NaN abort as the only guards. Its README also says it is 'still in its infancy', that Web/HTML5 export is not supported and that only int and float return values are supported, and neither default Wasmtime version (37, 41) is an LTS line. Route (3) exists only in the Web export, not on desktop. Godot's docs name Steam Deck as the only officially supported console; the others go through third-party ports and W4 Games' middleware, and no retrieved page says whether an extension embedding a wasm runtime ships there.
recipes.engine_note: The product-alignment dispatch (docs/study-swarm/product-alignment.dispatch.md) puts Godot first, 'by GDExtension or the browser build': route (3) is the browser build and needs no new binary, route (1) is the GDExtension. Either way GDScript reproduces solver/build.mjs's call sequence (write stride-17 bodies and stride-10 colliders, call solver_step, read 13 fields back), with one module instance per world because rapier_law.rs keeps one world in static mut SOLVER.
recipes.verify_note: store.h confirmed verbatim: wasm_engine_new() takes no args, comment says 'same store...used between all compiled Wasm modules'. Both utils.py version sets confirmed at their exact refs, incl. the Feb-6-2026 bump commit by message and date.

recipes.name: Bind the law natively in Godot with gdext 0.5.5: a cdylib entry point, api-4-N no newer than the running Godot
recipes.what: Option B in Godot compiles the law into a GDExtension with godot-rust (crate godot 0.5.5, 2026-08-09, Rust 1.94+, MPL-2.0): a cdylib per platform that any Godot at or above the API version it was built against (4.2 or later) can load.
recipes.how: Cargo.toml `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]`; the entry point `struct LawExtension; #[gdextension] unsafe impl ExtensionLibrary for LawExtension {}`; a class `#[derive(GodotClass)] #[class(base=Node)] struct Law { base: Base<Node> }` whose `#[godot_api]` methods call the law; a .gdextension file with `entry_symbol = "gdext_rust_init"`, `compatibility_minimum`, and one `[libraries]` path per platform and architecture. Enable at most one of `api-4-2` ... `api-4-7` (with none, the current Godot minor at patch 0 is used) and keep runtime version >= API version. Hand Godot copies of the f64 state: its `real` is f32 unless gdext's `double-precision` feature is on and Godot itself is built with `precision=double`.
recipes.gotchas: gdext is pre-1.0 and says to expect occasional breaking changes; `experimental-threads` carries 'a high risk of unsoundness', and `experimental-wasm` (Web export) is 'not yet well tested' and must match the export's threading setting. The extension is a second compiled law per platform, so fixtures/solver.sha256 no longer covers what runs (see the native-artifact recipe). A pose narrowed to f32 cannot be widened back to the committed f64 (the check shows 0.1 + 0.2 losing its low bits), so nothing read from a Node3D or Vector3 may be written into the law's buffers: only intents cross back, and the admitted log records the f64 the law received.
recipes.engine_note: README: 'Presentation has no path back into the hash'; with gdext that rule has a numeric edge, because Godot positions are f32 by default while BODIES in solver/src/lib.rs is f64. The product-alignment dispatch orders Godot first; rapier_law.rs would compile into the extension unchanged, but packages/tick and packages/frame (JavaScript) would not come with it.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check PASS: f32 narrow/widen of 0.1+0.2 is not exact, exact bits shown. docs.rs feature text and crates.io metadata (2026-08-09T08:21:52Z, rust_version 1.94, MPL-2.0) confirmed verbatim; compat matrix row '0.4+ | 4.2' confirmed.

recipes.name: Treat a native law build as a second artifact: basic ops match the wasm, std math inside dependencies may not
recipes.what: Option B recompiles the law for each host target. A step built only from add/sub/mul/div/sqrt, like lib.rs's, gives the wasm build's bits natively, but enhanced-determinism does not reroute inherent std calls inside dependencies: with std on, parry 0.30.2 diagonalizes summed, convex-hull and trimesh inertia through glamx 0.3.1, whose non-diagonal branch calls acos and cos.
recipes.how: Keep the law's own float code to +, -, *, / and sqrt (std: sqrt is the correctly rounded result and 'guaranteed not to change'; lib.rs and rapier_law.rs use only sqrt, min and max) and route any new transcendental through `libm::` or nalgebra's `ComplexField`, as Rapier's determinism guide asks. Keep `enhanced-determinism` (at 0.35.3 it enables `simba/libm_force` and parry3d-f64 0.30.2's `simba/libm_force`, `glamx/libm`, `glamx/scalar-math`), but do not read it as covering inherent calls: method lookup takes an inherent method before any trait method, and glamx imports `ComplexField` only when std is off. Treat each native library (target triple + toolchain + Cargo.lock) as its own pinned artifact and accept it only when its T1 trace equals node's for every fixture.
recipes.gotchas: Today's scenes miss the trig branch: a single box's mass properties come from from_cuboid, and MassProperties' Add returns early when one side is zero, so no eigen solve runs; the check shows a single box has a zero off-diagonal inertia while two boxes combined (one turned 0.5 rad and offset) do not, which is the case compound bodies and convex hulls (from_convex_polyhedron -> from_trimesh -> with_inertia_matrix) bring. Target features are not the lever for basic ops (the step below gives the same bits at opt-level 3 natively and in wasm); library call paths are. std documents the precision of sin, cos and the like as varying 'by platform, Rust version', and min/max may return either zero for +0.0 and -0.0.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml's enhanced-determinism pins Rapier's trait-routed math to libm, but a native host build of rapier_law.rs would still reach std acos and cos inside glamx once collision from meshes (the slice after Phase 2) gives dynamic bodies convex or compound colliders. fixtures/solver.sha256 covers only the wasm, so option B needs a per-target T1 trace gate and, for mesh bodies, a test that inertia bits match the wasm build.

recipes.name: Link the law into Unreal 5 as one Rust staticlib or cdylib behind a cbindgen header in an External module
recipes.what: Unreal Engine 5.8 documents third-party code as a module with Type = ModuleType.External that adds include paths and a static or dynamic library; a Rust crate meets it with crate-type staticlib (one .lib/.a carrying the crate, its dependencies and std) or cdylib, extern "C" functions over #[repr(C)] records, and a header generated by cbindgen 0.29.4.
recipes.how: Binding crate: `crate-type = ["staticlib"]` or `["cdylib"]`; a `#[repr(C)] struct BodyIn` whose 17 f64 fields follow the law's slot order (136 bytes, align 8, `mode` at offset 128, the same on x86_64 and wasm32 as the checks show); functions such as `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub unsafe extern "C" fn law_write_bodies(src: *const BodyIn, n: u32) -> u32`, taking pointer plus count and returning a status, never a slice. Generate the header with cbindgen (CLI or build.rs): it emits `#[no_mangle] pub extern` functions, full definitions only for types with a guaranteed repr (others become forward declarations), and has parsed unsafe attributes since 0.28.0. Unreal: `Type = ModuleType.External;` `PublicIncludePaths.Add(Path.Combine(ModuleDirectory, "inc"));` `PublicAdditionalLibraries.Add(Path.Combine(ModuleDirectory, "lib", ...));` for a DLL `PublicDelayLoadDLLs.Add("law.dll")` and `RuntimeDependencies.Add(...)` to stage it. `--print=native-static-libs` lists the system libraries a staticlib needs.
recipes.rust_version: edition 2024 binding crate on rustc 1.98.1; cbindgen 0.29.4 (2026-06-09); Unreal Engine 5.8 docs
recipes.gotchas: The Reference warns that multiple Rust staticlib files are likely to conflict (each carries std and exports its dependencies' public symbols), and wasmtime's C API static library is Rust too: for option A in Unreal build one Rust staticlib that depends on the wasmtime crate and exports the law's C ABI, or use DLLs, rather than linking a law staticlib beside wasmtime's. Delay-loading is a Windows mechanism (UE: not fully supported on macOS; Linux search paths come from each module's RPATH) and is impossible when code accesses variables in the DLL, so export accessor functions such as bodies_ptr(), never the static buffers. Wasmtime's Windows static C API also needs -DWASM_API_EXTERN= -DWASI_API_EXTERN= and ws2_32, advapi32, userenv, ntdll, shell32, ole32 and bcrypt. UE documents console development (Switch, Switch 2, PS4, PS5, Xbox) for registered developers; no retrieved page establishes a Rust or wasm-runtime library on those SDKs.
recipes.engine_note: The record to mirror is solver/src/lib.rs's stride: BODY_STRIDE 17 (0-5 position and velocity, 6-9 quaternion, 10-12 angular velocity, 13-15 half-extents, 16 driven or solverMode), COLLIDER_STRIDE 10, MAX_BODIES = MAX_COLLIDERS = 64, and solver_step(world_id, n_bodies, n_colliders, rows, cols, cell, shape) -> u32 with 1 for success. The engine crate is edition 2021 with bare #[no_mangle]; a new edition-2024 binding crate must write #[unsafe(no_mangle)] (Edition Guide). Unreal is the second host in the product-alignment ordering.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle 4/4 PASS incl. identical layout code 136008128 on host and wasm32, matching lib.rs's own BODY_STRIDE comment verbatim. cbindgen PR #1020 + unsafe(no_mangle) test + crates.io date/rust_version/license all confirmed.

recipes.name: Treat the component model as a new target and ABI: WIT values are copied across and memory is never shared
recipes.what: Option C replaces raw pointers with a typed WIT interface, but it is a different artifact and contract: wasm32-wasip2 emits a component, a component may not export a memory, values cross by a lift/lower copy, and floats loaded across the boundary lose their NaN sign and payload.
recipes.how: Write the law's interface in WIT (a world exporting a step function over list<f64> bodies), generate guest bindings with `wit_bindgen::generate!({ path: "wit/world.wit" })` (wit-bindgen 0.62.0, 2026-09-10), build with `cargo build --target wasm32-wasip2` (Tier 2, outputs a component; the component-model book says cargo-component is being deprecated), host it natively with wasmtime's `component::bindgen!` (the component model is Tier 1), and in JavaScript with jco 1.35.0 (2026-09-24), which transpiles a component into ES modules for Node and browsers. What the raw ABI keeps by convention, strides 17 and 10 and pointer/offset pairs, becomes a checked type.
recipes.rust_version: wasm32-wasip2 (Tier 2) on rustc 1.98.1; wit-bindgen 0.62.0; wasmtime 49.0.1; jco 1.35.0
recipes.gotchas: The engine's zero-copy contract cannot carry over: a component may not export a memory, and the Canonical ABI explainer says an implementation can at best fuse lifting and lowering into one direct copy, so up to 8,704 bytes of bodies cross by copy on every call. A wasm32-wasip2 runtime 'should support the wasi preview 2 API set', so the component can import WASI interfaces the current module never needed, and Wasmtime's determinism page says to virtualize nondeterministic WASI APIs. Browsers run it only through jco's output. Dropping NaN sign and payload is harmless for a law that aborts on NaN, but any design that hashes NaN bits breaks at the boundary.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs hard-codes strides 17 and 10 against lib.rs BODY_STRIDE and COLLIDER_STRIDE with nothing checking the pair; a WIT record would. But fixtures/solver.sha256, solver/rust-toolchain.toml (target wasm32-unknown-unknown) and the three-engine goldens describe the core module, so option C is a new artifact and a new T1 baseline, not a re-wrap of the pinned binary.

recipes.name: Drive one law instance per world from one thread; collect Rapier events in a Sync buffer the host drains
recipes.what: The law holds one Rapier world in static mut SOLVER and silently rebuilds it when the call signature changes, so a host needs one module instance per world, called from one thread; host callbacks cannot go into Rapier (its EventHandler must be Sync), so events belong in a law-owned Sync buffer drained after each step; and the buffer traffic is small, 22,528 bytes per quantum at the engine's maxima.
recipes.how: Per world, one wasmtime Store and Instance called from the simulation thread: `TypedFunc::call` takes `impl AsContextMut`, so a Store serves one call at a time, whereas a native build's `static mut` has no such guard (serialize it or never share it). In Godot keep scene-tree access on the main thread (the docs: interacting with the active scene tree is not thread-safe; from another thread publish with call_deferred / set_deferred) and do not lean on gdext's experimental-threads. For events, hand Rapier a law-owned handler (`EventHandler: MaybeSync`, which is Sync unless rapier's unsync-callbacks feature is on), e.g. a `Mutex<Vec<_>>` or Rapier's ChannelEventCollector, drain it after each step, and expose the drained list through a buffer the host reads like the bodies. Copies: bodies 8,704 B, colliders 5,120 B and heights 2,048 B in, 6,656 B out (13 fields x 64 bodies) = 22,528 B per quantum, 1,441,792 B/s at 64 Hz, plus the snapshot; a `#[repr(C)] #[derive(Pod, Zeroable)]` record array becomes the byte slice `Memory::write` takes through `bytemuck::cast_slice`.
recipes.gotchas: Interleaving two worlds through one instance never errors: ensure() rebuilds the world on each switch and reports success, so warm-start and sleep state are dropped and the run can diverge from a dedicated instance without a signal. A host object handle captured in a handler is refused at compile time (an Rc<RefCell<...>> sink: E0277, 'required for HostSink to implement MaybeSync'); switching on unsync-callbacks to allow it changes the solver's feature set, and with it the artifact. derive(Pod) refuses a record with padding (16 f64 plus a u32 flag: E0080, 'derive(Pod) was applied to a type with padding'), which keeps uninitialized bytes out of the law's buffers.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs: `static mut SOLVER` holds one world; ensure() rebuilds when the signature (world id, counts, geometry, shape) changes; solver_clear_warmstart relies on 'the world is ours alone on this thread'; integrate() calls world.step() with no handler, so a collision-event export (T3 plans to hash event order) is where the Sync buffer lands. Sizes follow lib.rs MAX_BODIES 64 x BODY_STRIDE 17 and MAX_COLLIDERS 64 x COLLIDER_STRIDE 10, rapier_law.rs MAX_HEIGHTS 256, and build.mjs readBodies' 13 fields.

recipes.name: Accept a new host only when its T1 trace equals node's in 16-hex-digit IEEE bits, never in decimals
recipes.what: solver/build.mjs under node is the reference binding: a Godot or Unreal host proves it runs the same law by printing the T1 trace for the same seed and log and passing harness/first-difference.js against node's trace, which writes every body field as its IEEE bit pattern.
recipes.how: Print each float as `format!("{:016x}", x.to_bits())`: sixteen lowercase hex digits, zero-padded, high word first, the same string trace-line.mjs's bits() builds from two DataView words; parse node's tokens with `f64::from_bits(u64::from_str_radix(tok, 16)?)`. Keep PHASE-2's line grammar (tick, hash, body id and 13 fields, zone, links, snap length and digest, minds, `end <lines>`), drive the host with the same seed and admitted log, and require an empty diff for the product scene and every fixture on each platform the host ships on (T3's ARM64 lane is the pattern).
recipes.rust_version: any: to_bits / from_bits are stable since 1.20; trace format fixed by T1
recipes.gotchas: Decimal renderings hide what matters: at six decimals 0.1 + 0.2 and 0.3 print alike while their bits differ in the last place (the check), and JavaScript prints negative zero as "0" (measured on this rig with node v22.22.3: String(-0), (-0).toFixed(3) and JSON.stringify(-0)). PHASE-2 rules out error thresholds in place of bit-exact agreement. to_bits is a raw transmutation and std says floats and integers share endianness on all supported platforms, so the token is portable. The hash column comes from the JavaScript frame hash, so a host that runs only the .wasm can match the body fields while its hash column must come from the same packages/frame code or from a port that passes this diff first.
recipes.engine_note: harness/trace-line.mjs bits() and the format in docs/PHASE-2.md (T1) are the conformance contract; harness/first-difference.js names the first differing quantum, body and field; solver/build.mjs is the reference binding and packages/frame computes the frame hash in JavaScript, so each host plan must say where its hash column comes from.

lanes.title: Rapier 0.35: pipeline, determinism & upgrades
lanes.verifier_note: Checked against: the pinned rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 source on disk (cross-referenced live against docs.rs), the rapier.rs Rust-0.36 guide, the raw dimforge/rapier CHANGELOG.md fetched directly at both the v0.35.3 and v0.36.0 tags (not the summarized WebFetch version, which mis-split two 0.35.0 vs 0.35.0-beta.0 entries on a first pass), crates.io's versions API, GitHub issue #1008, two Cargo-book pages, and the si-rpg-engine repo at main (rapier_law.rs, FLAGS.md, Cargo.toml/.lock, rust-toolchain.toml, ci.yml, and the T1-T4/rust-kb-requests dispatch docs). I ran every one of the lane's 23 checks through the real pinned compiler via compile_oracle.py and independently hand-wrote and ran the two mandated high-stakes counter-examples (thin-slab CCD, wake_up-vs-iter_mut re-admission) myself: all 23 checks passed, and my two reproductions matched the recipe's predicted stdout byte-for-byte, including deliberately surprising results (a 0.35.3 doc comment stale at 0.002m/0.001x while its own Default impl already reads 0.02/0.005; PhysicsWorld::wake_up failing to re-admit a body that plain iter_mut() fixes; a debug_assert literally on island_manager/manager.rs line 140; commit 39687d9's message matching the recipe's E3 account word for word). What failed: two of ten recipes cite si-rpg-engine dispatch docs (T4 pin 2 in the IntegrationParameters-defaults lane, T3 pin 6 in the collision-events lane) as still holding an open question or a wrong assumption that the live document on main has already closed or corrected; both are marked corrected rather than refuted, since every Rust/crate claim in those two recipes is independently solid. Recipe 1's step-order prose also over-compresses one detail (joint 'joins' drain after quarantine/user-changes, not alongside wake-ups as written). The one systemic weakness: this lane's Rust/rapier sourcing is exceptionally disciplined -- of roughly 40 external sources and 20-odd direct source-file claims I checked, none were wrong -- but its engine_notes are perishable, because they cross-reference the coordinating T-dispatch docs' state as of authoring time and this repo amends those same-day (T4 pin 2 carries an explicit 'Amended 2026-09-25' note); an engine_note is only as fresh as its last re-check against main, and this sweep found it had already drifted out from under two of the ten recipes.

recipes.name: Call PhysicsPipeline::step at 0.35.3 with its 12 arguments and read contacts as start-of-step state
recipes.what: One 0.35.3 step applies queued user changes, runs broad and narrow phase once, solves and integrates per CCD substep, then only refreshes broad-phase AABBs; a non-finite body is quarantined, not reported as an error.
recipes.how: Signature (docs.rs 0.35.3): step(&mut self, gravity: Vector, integration_parameters: &IntegrationParameters, islands: &mut IslandManager, broad_phase: &mut BroadPhaseBvh, narrow_phase: &mut NarrowPhase, bodies: &mut RigidBodySet, colliders: &mut ColliderSet, impulse_joints: &mut ImpulseJointSet, multibody_joints: &mut MultibodyJointSet, ccd_solver: &mut CCDSolver, hooks: &dyn PhysicsHooks, events: &dyn EventHandler). Gravity is a glam Vector by value, the broad phase is the concrete BroadPhaseBvh (alias DefaultBroadPhase), `&()` implements both PhysicsHooks and EventHandler, and PhysicsWorld::step() is step_with_events(&(), &()) over the world's own fields. Order in step_inner (substep.rs): reset counters and the quarantine report; drain joint wake-ups and joins; quarantine non-finite user changes; apply user changes to colliders, then bodies (new bodies join the awake island here); detect_collisions = BroadPhaseBvh::update, then the narrow phase's handle_user_changes, register_pairs, compute_contacts, compute_intersections (filter hooks and collision events run here); clear change flags; then per CCD substep (max_ccd_substeps == 0 means one substep and no CCD): kinematic position-based velocities from their next pose, island update and staged velocity solve with gravity, contact-force events, CCD motion clamping, advance_to_final_positions (pose := next pose, collider poses, fresh AABBs), quarantine; after the last substep only BroadPhaseBvh::set_aabb for moved colliders, no narrow phase. The staged solver runs only for the awake island. The step copies IntegrationParameters and rewrites dt only when CCD splits the step; it mutates the islands, both phases, the bodies and colliders, the joint sets' pending wake-ups and joins, and the CCD solver when CCD runs.
recipes.gotchas: The rapier.rs guide documents 0.36 and its step call passes a 13th argument (&mut soft_body_set): pasted into a 0.35.3 crate it fails with E0433 (no SoftBodySet) and E0061 (12 vs 13 arguments). Older tutorials pass &gravity, a generic broad phase or a QueryPipeline argument; none of those exist at 0.35.3. Because the narrow phase runs before integration, contact_pairs() read after a step describe the poses at the start of that step while scene queries see end-of-step AABBs: measured, a box leaving a wall at 20 u/s is 0.3125 clear after one step yet still has an active contact, and a ray already sees its new face. Non-finite state never panics: since 0.35.0-beta.0 the Quarantine disables the body, keeps its last valid pose, zeroes its velocity and lists it in quarantine() for that step only; measured, an infinite velocity passes an is_nan() guard and leaves an all-finite, disabled body hanging at y = 2 under gravity.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `integrate` calls `loaded.world.step()` (PhysicsWorld: no hooks, no events) after set_next_kinematic_translation and solve_character_collision_impulses, and `rebuild_snapshot` then hashes contact pairs computed before that quantum's integration. `bad()` tests is_nan() only, so an infinite velocity in a body record passes `signature`, reaches Rapier, is quarantined and is written back finite by `write_body`: refuse `!x.is_finite()` and `!loaded.world.quarantine().is_empty()` right after `step()` so that 'NaN aborts a step' also covers what Rapier absorbs.
recipes.verify_note: Compile-oracle: all 4 checks pass verbatim (12-arg step, 13-arg guide fails E0433/E0061, contact-timing + quarantine stdout exact). Minor: step_inner drains to_join AFTER quarantine/modifications, not alongside wake-ups.

recipes.name: Read rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 IntegrationParameters defaults from code: prediction 0.02, slop 0.005, CCD on
recipes.what: The 0.35.3 defaults that decide results are prediction 0.02, allowed error 0.005, 4 solver iterations, 30 Hz / ζ 10 contacts (60 Hz against fixed bodies), CCD and contact recycling on, and two doc comments still state the pre-0.35 values.
recipes.how: Fields as named in 0.35.3, defaults printed by the compiler: dt 1/60; min_ccd_dt 1/6000; num_solver_iterations 4; num_internal_pgs_iterations 1; num_internal_stabilization_iterations 1; warmstart_coefficient 1; warmstart_joints false; length_unit 1; contact_softness = SpringCoefficients { natural_frequency: 30, damping_ratio: 10 }; static_contact_softness = { 60, 10 }; normalized_allowed_linear_error 0.005; normalized_prediction_distance 0.02; normalized_max_corrective_velocity 3; normalized_max_linear_velocity 400; max_ccd_substeps 1; contact_clustering true; contact_recycling true; normalized_contact_recycle_distance 0.05; friction_in_bias_pass false; friction_model Simplified. The normalized_* values are multiplied by length_unit through allowed_linear_error(), prediction_distance(), max_corrective_velocity(), max_linear_velocity() and contact_recycle_distance(). max_ccd_substeps is the world's CCD switch: 0 turns off every sweep, including the automatic one of fast dynamic bodies against fixed colliders that runs even with ccd_enabled(false) (measured: a 20 u/s box stops in front of a thin slab at the default, passes it at 0). Set every field the law depends on in one place and record them beside the goldens.
recipes.gotchas: docs.rs 0.35.3 says normalized_prediction_distance defaults to 0.002m and allowed_linear_error() to 0.001 × length_unit; the Default impl, the 0.36 guide and the 0.35.0-beta.0 changelog say 0.02 and 0.005 (the changelog: 0.002 → 0.02, 10.0 → 3.0, 0.001 → 0.005). Fields removed earlier fail with E0609: min_island_size (0.35.0-beta.0) and contact_natural_frequency (grouped into contact_softness in 0.31, with the erp/cfm methods). contact_recycling changes result bits (measured on a four-box pile after 200 steps) and keeps per-pair state from the last full narrow-phase update; contact_clustering left the same pile bit-identical (a box-box pair emits one manifold; the field doc names meshes, heightfields, compounds and voxels as the shapes that emit several). warmstart_coefficient = 1.0 is already the default.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `build_world` sets dt = 1/64, contact_clustering = false and warmstart_coefficient = 1.0 (a no-op) and inherits the rest, so the law runs with contact_recycling = true and max_ccd_substeps = 1: dynamic bodies built with ccd_enabled(false) are still swept against fixed slabs and the heightfield. T4 pin 2 assumes the thin fast body 'passes through' today; measured here, a 0.05-half box at 20 u/s with ccd_enabled(false) stops at x 0.921 in front of a 0.02-half slab. Measure the exact T4 scene before moving goldens (the tunnelling numbers belong to binary-and-limits); the recycled pair state is outside the snapshot, a T2 question for restore-internals.
recipes.verify_note: 23/23 oracle checks pass; I reproduced the thin-slab CCD claim myself (x=0.921 vs 4.900, exact). Source/guide/changelog all match. But T4 pin 2 (main, amended today) no longer assumes tunnelling.

recipes.name: Expect Rapier 0.35.3 body types to gate contacts: kinematic-fixed off, kinematic pushes dynamic one way
recipes.what: By default only pairs involving a dynamic body get contacts; kinematic bodies follow their next pose (position-based) or their velocity (velocity-based) and push dynamic bodies without being pushed; fixed bodies never move.
recipes.how: RigidBodyType: Dynamic = 0 (forces, gravity, contacts), Fixed = 1 (infinite mass, never moves), KinematicPositionBased = 2 (set_next_kinematic_translation / rotation; the step derives the velocity: measured 0.1 in one 1/64 s step gives vx 6.4), KinematicVelocityBased = 3 (set linvel / angvel; the pose integrates: 6.4 u/s gives x 0.1 after one step). ActiveCollisionTypes::default() = DYNAMIC_DYNAMIC | DYNAMIC_KINEMATIC | DYNAMIC_FIXED; OR in KINEMATIC_FIXED, KINEMATIC_KINEMATIC or FIXED_FIXED per collider when those pairs must produce contacts or events (measured: setting KINEMATIC_FIXED on the kinematic collider alone was enough). A kinematic body's trajectory ignores what it hits: measured, 64 steps at 2 u/s end at exactly x = 2 while pushing a box ahead of it.
recipes.gotchas: A kinematic body overlapping a fixed wall has no active contact by default, so contacts never tell a kinematic character that it is blocked: the character controller's shape casts do. Enabling KINEMATIC_FIXED creates contacts and events, not a push-back. Kinematic bodies sleep only when both velocities are exactly zero (0.30.1).
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `build_world` makes driven bodies kinematic_position_based() with lock_rotations, can_sleep(false), ccd_enabled(false) and additional_mass(1.0), and slabs and the heightfield fixed(); with default ActiveCollisionTypes the walker has active contacts only with dynamic boxes, and `integrate` resolves walls with KinematicCharacterController::move_shape (shape casts, not contacts) and pushes boxes with solve_character_collision_impulses. Two walkers are kinematic-kinematic and get no contacts either, so T4's 'character against a character' case is decided by the controller's casts alone.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check passes verbatim (4 sub-cases). RigidBodyType discriminants, ActiveCollisionTypes::default(), the guide, and the 0.30.1 changelog entry all confirmed live/on-disk exactly as stated.

recipes.name: Count Rapier 0.35.3 sleep in quanta: time_until_sleep = 32·dt sleeps after quantum 32, 33 off the origin
recipes.what: Sleep is judged on displacement: each step a dynamic body whose half per-step drift is below normalized_linear_threshold·length_unit·dt adds dt to time_since_can_sleep (any other step resets it), and its island sleeps once time_since_can_sleep ≥ time_until_sleep.
recipes.how: Configure per body: `rb.activation_mut().time_until_sleep = 32.0 * dt` (seconds, default 0.5); normalized_linear_threshold (default 0.05 u/s, negative = never sleeps); angular_threshold (default 0.5 rad/s; only collider-less bodies compare against it, bodies with colliders use only its sign plus a fixed π/2 rad/s gate); RigidBodyBuilder::can_sleep(false) = RigidBodyActivation::cannot_sleep(). With dt = 1/64 the timer counts exactly: a body at rest from its first step sleeps after quantum 32 with time_since_can_sleep = 0.5. The first check compares against sleep_prev_pose = Pose::IDENTITY, so a body inserted farther than 2·threshold·dt from the identity pose loses its first quantum (measured: at (3, 1, 0) it sleeps after 33). The test is drift·0.5 < threshold·dt, so pure translation sleeps under twice the threshold (measured: 0.08 u/s sleeps, 0.12 u/s never), and sleeping zeroes the velocity.
recipes.gotchas: The field doc says the threshold is compared against the farthest-point speed; since 0.35.0 the code uses the pose displacement and ignores the velocities of dynamic bodies (the changelog says so), so a slow drift under 0.1 u/s is frozen after time_until_sleep. The 0.35.0-beta.0 defaults (0.05 u/s, 0.5 s) replaced 0.4 u/s and 2.0 s: numbers from older posts are wrong for 0.35. Islands sleep and wake as a unit, so a body touching an awake body stays awake past its own timer. sleep_prev_pose is pub(crate) and cannot be set from outside the crate.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `build_world` sets `activation_mut().time_until_sleep = SLEEP_QUANTA * DT` (32/64 s, exact) on dynamic bodies inserted at their record position, so a body at rest from load sleeps after quantum 33, not 32; `rebuild_snapshot` hashes `time_since_can_sleep / DT`, an exact integer while dt = 1/64. A rebuilt world starts every body at sleep_prev_pose = identity, so a restore path (T2, restore-internals) resets each off-origin body's count on its first step; this is inferred from the measured first-quantum loss, not yet run as a restore.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check passes verbatim (32 vs 33 quanta, drift/angular thresholds). RigidBodyActivation defaults and the 0.35.0-beta.0 changelog entry (0.05/0.5 from 0.4/2.0) confirmed exactly.

recipes.name: Warm Rapier's broad phase with one CollisionPipeline::step at load, then re-mark bodies with iter_mut
recipes.what: A hand-run BroadPhaseBvh::update whose pair events are dropped loses those pairs for good; CollisionPipeline::step registers them, but at 0.35.3 it leaves every body outside the IslandManager, so bodies must be re-marked modified before the first PhysicsPipeline step.
recipes.how: At load: `CollisionPipeline::new().step(params.prediction_distance(), &mut islands, &mut broad_phase, &mut narrow_phase, &mut bodies, &mut colliders, &(), &())`. It fills the BVH (a ray that missed before the pass hits after it) and hands its pair events to the narrow phase, but it calls handle_user_changes_to_rigid_bodies(None, …) and then clears the change flags of every modified body (after a load, all of them), so no body enters the awake island. Re-mark them: `for (_, b) in bodies.iter_mut() {}` (iter_mut pushes every body into the modified set) or bodies.get_mut(h); the next PhysicsPipeline step admits them. Measured: after the pass alone a dynamic box does not move in 10 steps; after iter_mut it falls as in a world without the pass (y 1.8999 after 10 steps in both); PhysicsWorld::wake_up(h, true) does not admit it (y stays 2.0000). Build scene queries with broad_phase.as_query_pipeline(narrow_phase.query_dispatcher(), &bodies, &colliders, filter) or PhysicsWorld::query_pipeline(): a borrowed view of the broad-phase BVH, current as of the last update or step.
recipes.gotchas: BroadPhaseBvh::update is public and 'only required to generate new events': an AddPair it has emitted is never sent again, so discarding its events removes the pair from the narrow phase permanently (measured: a box above a rotated slab falls through it, y −15.431 with 0 pairs, versus resting on it after the pipeline pass, y 0.309 with 1 pair). Clearing body flags in the collision pass is 0.35.0 behaviour ('CollisionPipeline::step now clears the rigid-bodies' modified flags'). At 0.35.3 the same pass trips `debug_assert!(rb.is_fixed() || !rb.is_enabled() || rb.ids.active_island_id != u32::MAX)` in island_manager/manager.rs:140 when a dynamic body touches a collider at load: a build with debug assertions panics (exit 101), the release profile compiles the check out (debug-assertions = false), and 0.36.0 fixes it.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `warm_broadphase` (the E3 fix, commit 39687d9) works, but its comment credits wake_up(true): re-admission comes from `world.bodies.iter_mut()` re-marking every body, and a refactor to `world.wake_up(handle, true)` would freeze every dynamic body. T2's `solver_restore` reruns the load's collision pass on mid-run worlds where bodies touch, so a native debug test of that path panics at manager.rs:140: test it in release or through the wasm build. 0.36.0 adds PhysicsWorld::detect_collisions (collision detection without stepping), a candidate replacement for this pass.
recipes.verify_note: I reproduced both checks myself: the box-through-rotated-slab case and the wake_up/iter_mut case, stdout byte-identical to the recipe. manager.rs:140 debug_assert and commit 39687d9 both verified exact.

recipes.name: Collect Rapier 0.35.3 collision events with a Sync EventHandler and ActiveEvents set on a collider
recipes.what: Collision and contact-force events are opt-in per collider (ActiveEvents, empty by default) and are delivered during the step to an EventHandler, which must be Sync unless the unsync-callbacks feature is on.
recipes.how: Give at least one collider of the pair `.active_events(ActiveEvents::COLLISION_EVENTS)` (or CONTACT_FORCE_EVENTS with a contact_force_event_threshold) and pass a handler as the step's events argument (PhysicsWorld::step_with_events(&(), &handler)). ChannelEventCollector::new(collision_sender, contact_force_sender) takes two std::sync::mpsc::Sender values; drain the receivers after the step. A custom handler implements handle_collision_event(&self, bodies, colliders, event: CollisionEvent, contact_pair: Option<&ContactPair>) and handle_contact_force_event(&self, dt, bodies, colliders, contact_pair, total_force_magnitude), keeping state in atomics or a Mutex because EventHandler: MaybeSync and MaybeSync = Sync. Measured: a box dropped on a floor and then lifted clear yields exactly one Started and one Stopped, through a counter or the channel collector; with ActiveEvents::empty() it yields none. Which body-type pairs produce contacts at all is ActiveCollisionTypes.
recipes.gotchas: A Cell or RefCell counter fails with E0277 ('`Cell<u32>` cannot be shared between threads safely … required for `Counter` to implement `MaybeSync`'); 0.35.0-beta.0 relaxed the bound from Send + Sync to Sync. Contact-force totals changed in the 0.35.2 patch (the step's total impulse, one substep fewer). 0.36.0 adds a required handle_soft_body_tear_event and a third ChannelEventCollector sender, so every custom handler breaks on that bump.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs passes no handler (`world.step()`), so no event reaches the hash today. T3's plan to hash collision-event order separately from body state needs ActiveEvents on the tracked colliders and a Sync collector (a Mutex<Vec<_>> or ChannelEventCollector) drained after `step()` in `integrate`; this lane measured delivery, not the order of simultaneous events, so T3 must measure that order before hashing it.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle checks pass (Cell rejected E0277/MaybeSync; Started/Stopped counts exact). EventHandler/MaybeSync/guide/changelog confirmed. But T3 pin 6 (main) already says 'No new hash' for event order.

recipes.name: Filter Rapier pairs with collision_groups (no contact) or solver_groups (contact, no force); flag the hooks
recipes.what: collision_groups stop a pair before the narrow phase (no contacts, no events); solver_groups keep contacts and events but drop the forces; PhysicsHooks run only for pairs where a collider carries the matching ActiveHooks flag.
recipes.how: InteractionGroups::new(memberships: Group, filter: Group, test_mode: InteractionTestMode): And passes when (a.memberships & b.filter) != 0 && (b.memberships & a.filter) != 0, Or when either holds; the default is InteractionGroups::all(). Set them with ColliderBuilder::collision_groups and solver_groups. Measured with the floor in GROUP_1 and a box in GROUP_2 filtering GROUP_3: excluded by collision_groups, the box falls through with no contact and no event; excluded by solver_groups it falls identically (y −3.016) yet the contact exists and a Started event fires. Hooks: implement PhysicsHooks (filter_contact_pair(&self, &PairFilterContext) -> Option<SolverFlags>, filter_intersection_pair, modify_solver_contacts) and set `.active_hooks(ActiveHooks::FILTER_CONTACT_PAIRS)` (or FILTER_INTERSECTION_PAIR, MODIFY_SOLVER_CONTACTS); None drops the pair, Some(SolverFlags::empty()) keeps contacts without forces; the filter runs after collision groups and replaces the default non-dynamic filtering.
recipes.gotchas: The ColliderBuilder::collision_groups doc example calls InteractionGroups::new with two arguments: E0061 since 0.31 added the test mode. The guide's prose spells ActiveHooks::FILTER_CONTACT_PAIR; the constant is FILTER_CONTACT_PAIRS (E0599). A hook whose flag is not set on a collider is never called (measured: the same refusing hook leaves the box resting at 0.350). Under And both sides must accept each other, so a floor left at InteractionGroups::all() interacts with every box whose membership and filter are non-empty: design both colliders' groups together. Since 0.35.0 the broad phase itself filters by collision groups.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs sets no groups and no hooks and passes `&()`, so every pair interacts. Groups and hooks are law: a filter that reads anything outside the record (host state, time) breaks replay. If the post-Phase-2 mesh slice needs one-way surfaces or character-only walls, store the group bits in the world file and mix them into `signature`'s geometry hash with the shapes.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle checks pass verbatim (groups/solver_groups/hooks numbers exact; FILTER_CONTACT_PAIR(S) and the 2-arg InteractionGroups::new doc bugs both confirmed live on docs.rs).

recipes.name: Pin rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 features explicitly: block-solver is a default and docs.rs documents other builds
recipes.what: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 has 15 features; the defaults are dim3, f64, std (which enables alloc) and block-solver; it has no simd-stable, simd-nightly or simd8 feature, and docs.rs documents a parallel + serde-serialize + debug-render build.
recipes.how: Features at 0.35.3: alloc, block-solver, bytemuck, debug-disable-legitimate-fe-exceptions, debug-render, default, dev-remove-slow-accessors, dim3, enhanced-determinism (= simba/libm_force + parry3d-f64/enhanced-determinism), f64, parallel (rayon + parry3d-f64/parallel), profiler (web-time), serde-serialize, solver-bounds-checks, std, unsync-callbacks. Write the set out: `rapier3d-f64 = { version = "=0.35.3", default-features = false, features = ["dim3", "f64", "std", "block-solver", "enhanced-determinism"] }` names exactly the set the current line resolves to (measured with cargo tree on the oracle crate, which declares the same dependency line: alloc, block-solver, dim3, enhanced-determinism, f64, std), so no upstream default change can enter unseen. Exclusions: simd8 with enhanced-determinism is a compile_error! in rapier's lib.rs, and simd8 is not a rapier3d-f64 feature at all; parallel combines with enhanced-determinism since 0.35.0-beta.0; unsync-callbacks removes the thread-pool API. Check APIs against your own build: PhysicsPipeline::configure_thread_pool (E0599) and serde for IntegrationParameters (E0277) are documented on docs.rs but absent here.
recipes.gotchas: The manifest comment above block-solver says 'NOT enabled by default in 3D' and the 0.35.0-beta.0 changelog says 'on by default in 2D', yet the default list of rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 names block-solver and it gates the contact solver's paired solve (solve_pair, with a dim3 variant): trust the default list, since cross-platform reproducibility 'still requires matching numeric features (block-solver, f32 vs f64)'. simd-stable and simd-nightly were removed in 0.35.0-beta.0; SIMD is always on through wide with a scalar fallback. serde-serialize and profiler add dependencies (serde; web-time) that the build and its review must then cover. Issue #1008 (open) reports a hang with parallel + enhanced-determinism at 0.35.1: keep parallel off.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml declares `rapier3d-f64 = { version = "0.35.3", features = ["enhanced-determinism"] }` with defaults on, and solver/FLAGS.md already records dim3, f64, std, block-solver and parallel off; spelling the list out in Cargo.toml turns that sentence into a pin, and a CI snapshot of `cargo tree -e features -i rapier3d-f64` (ci-reproducible-builds) catches drift. Restore work that uses serde (request 4 in docs/rust-kb-requests.md) is a feature change and a new binary.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle checks pass (VERSION, configure_thread_pool E0599, serde E0277). Cargo.toml.orig/lib.rs/contact_constraint_element.rs read on disk; issue #1008 title/state/body confirmed live, exact.

recipes.name: Hold Rapier to its stated determinism terms: same build and inputs, enhanced-determinism, same insertion order
recipes.what: Rapier promises identical reruns on one machine with the same Rapier and Rust versions and the same initial conditions, and cross-platform identity only with enhanced-determinism, IEEE 754-2008 targets and identical insertion order; nothing is promised across Rapier versions.
recipes.how: The crate root at 0.35.3 promises 'a perfectly deterministic simulation on different machine, as long as they are compliant with the IEEE 754-2008 floating point standard'. The user guide (labelled Rust 0.36) makes local determinism conditional on the same initial conditions, the same version of Rapier and the same version of the Rust compiler, and cross-platform determinism additionally on enhanced-determinism (not with simd8; parallel allowed, identical to the sequential solver), strict IEEE 754-2008 targets, initial values computed with float functions taken from nalgebra's ComplexField/RealField rather than std, and structures initialised with the same values and items added in the exact same order. The 0.35.0-beta.0 changelog adds that cross-platform determinism rests on glam's scalar core plus libm-pinned transcendentals and requires matching block-solver and f32/f64. In the code, enhanced-determinism switches the step's joint wake-up and join drains from drain() to drain(..), makes parry's HashMap an IndexMap, and canonicalises signed zeros in stored contact impulses (0.35.0). Measured: a four-box pile built twice in the same order is bit-identical after 200 steps; built in reverse insertion order it is not.
recipes.gotchas: No release promises identical results across versions, and the 0.35.x patches changed behaviour (0.35.2: reported contact impulses, multibody joints), so the exact version pin is part of the determinism contract. Insertion order is state: it decides the handles and, as measured, the result bits, so a restore or a host binding that rebuilds bodies in another order diverges. The guide's cross-platform list does not mention numeric features; the block-solver / f64 condition appears only in the changelog.
recipes.engine_note: si-rpg-engine meets the written terms: enhanced-determinism on, parallel off, f64, block-solver by default, rustc 1.98.1 pinned by solver/rust-toolchain.toml, and `build_world` inserts slabs, the heightfield, then bodies in record order. Rapier's promise covers IEEE 754 CPUs; the three-JS-engine golden is the engine's own evidence for wasm engines. T3's test that insertion order changes the hash should go red, as it does here on a box pile.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle check passes (same-order identical, reversed differs). Crate-root determinism quote, rapier.rs guide terms, and drain(..)/IndexMap cfg-gating on enhanced-determinism all confirmed exactly.

recipes.name: Govern a rapier3d-f64 bump: pin =0.35.3, read every CHANGELOG entry to the target, rerun course and goldens
recipes.what: Most Rapier releases from 0.30 to 0.36.0 changed simulation behaviour, patch releases included (0.30.1, 0.35.2, 0.35.3), and 0.36.0 (on crates.io since 2026-09-25) breaks the API this engine calls, so a bump is a law change gated by the outcome course and the goldens.
recipes.how: 1) Manifest: "0.35.3" is a caret requirement, >=0.35.3, <0.36.0 (the Cargo book's table: ^0.2.3 := >=0.2.3, <0.3.0), so `cargo update` may take a 0.35.4; write "=0.35.3" so only a reviewed commit moves it. 2) Read the CHANGELOG from the pinned tag to the target and list every entry that can move numbers. 0.31: InteractionGroups test mode, contact_softness replaces the erp/frequency knobs. 0.32: math moved to glam (Pose, by-value getters). 0.33: PhysicsWorld; CCD consults filter_contact_pair. 0.35.0-beta.0: persistent-island sleep with new thresholds, a single active set, the sweep-based CCD with automatic sweeps against fixed colliders, velocity caps, new contact defaults, static_contact_softness, the staged solver, FTZ/DAZ flag removed, clustering and recycling on. 0.35.0: displacement-based sleep, restitution as an end-of-step pass, broad-phase filtering by groups and of same-body pairs, canonical signed-zero impulses. 0.35.2: contact impulses, multibody compliance. 0.36.0: step takes a SoftBodySet, EventHandler gains a required method, ContactPair::manifolds and solver_clusters move to ContactPair::contacts, earlier snapshots no longer load, parry 0.31, CCD and dt == 0 fixes, PhysicsWorld::detect_collisions. 3) On the bump branch run T4's course and outcome tests first, then the goldens under the three engines, T1's behaviour numbers, T2's restore round trip and the Linux digest; move each golden once, in one commit that names the changelog entries. 4) Read version-exact docs: rapier.rs is 'User Guide: Rust (0.36)' with no Rust version selector, so for 0.35.3 use docs.rs/rapier3d-f64/0.35.3 and the v0.35.3 tag.
recipes.gotchas: The rapier.rs guide already shows 0.36 code, and docs.rs 0.35.3 still carries pre-0.35 defaults in two doc comments and is built with parallel, serde-serialize and debug-render. The Cargo.lock pin holds only until someone runs `cargo update`. A bump that moves results must move the goldens; the course is what shows the new numbers still honour the limits, which is why T4 pin 6 runs it before any golden is rewritten. 0.36.0 is not a drop-in: per its changelog the ContactPair fields that solver_clear_warmstart writes have moved. This lane compared no 0.36 simulation numbers.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml has `version = "0.35.3"` (caret) with solver/Cargo.lock at 0.35.3; T4 pin 6 adds FLAGS.md's sentence that any rapier3d-f64 or toolchain bump reruns harness/course.test.js before a golden moves. A 0.36 bump rewrites rapier_law.rs `solver_clear_warmstart` (it writes pair.manifolds and pair.solver_clusters, which move to ContactPair::contacts), must recheck `rebuild_snapshot`'s pair.solver_manifolds() against 0.36's accessors, and can replace `warm_broadphase` with PhysicsWorld::detect_collisions.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle tripwire check compiles. crates.io dates exact (0.36.0=9/25, 0.35.3=8/28). Every changelog version attribution (0.30.1 to 0.36.0) verified against raw CHANGELOG.md text, none misattributed.

lanes.title: Rapier shapes, meshes & the character controller
lanes.verifier_note: Checked every warrant against pinned crate source at ~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/ (parry3d-f64-0.30.2, rapier3d-f64-0.35.3), live docs.rs/rapier.rs/GitHub-raw/Khronos pages, and si-rpg-engine via gh api (read-only, main). Independently reran four of the five flagged high-stakes claims through compile_oracle.py file mode with my own counter-examples, not copied from the lane's checks: coplanar convex_hull (own 5-point pentagon) -> Some(mass=0); TriMesh::with_flags on a fresh degenerate BadTriangle case -> is_ok=true, topology_is_some=false, while set_flags on the same mesh correctly returns Err; heightfield scale with independently chosen dimensions -> cell_width = scale.x/(ncols-1), proving rapier3d-f64 0.35.3's own ColliderBuilder::heightfield doc text ('Size of each grid cell') wrong; and an airborne, never-grounded character with zero vertical intent still autostepped onto a step (dy=0.16, grounded=true), proving handle_stairs never reads grounded_at_starting_pos despite the 0.36 guide's claim that autostep needs floor contact first. The fifth (vertex order under MERGE_DUPLICATE_VERTICES) was confirmed by direct source read instead of re-executed: HashablePartialEq hashes raw bytes while Eq is by value, a Hash/Eq contract break that explains the size-dependent welding. One defect found: recipe 1's engine_note claims rapier_law.rs 'builds only ColliderBuilder::cuboid colliders ... every body', but current main (solver/src/rapier_law.rs:425-431) builds ColliderBuilder::capsule_y for driven bodies with shape==1. Systemic weakness: engine_note prose about si-rpg-engine's own current source carries no citation, so it is the one place narrative can drift from the live repo unnoticed -- every parry/rapier API and docs.rs claim in this lane held up; the single defect was an uncited claim about 'current' engine state.

recipes.name: Pick parry 0.30.2 shapes by body role: primitives, convex or compound on moving bodies, trimeshes on fixed
recipes.what: At parry3d-f64 0.30.2 SharedShape covers ball, cuboid, capsule, cylinder, cone, round variants, convex polyhedra, compounds, trimeshes, heightfields and voxels; a TriMesh has no interior, so it belongs on fixed bodies only.
recipes.how: Bodies that move: SharedShape::cuboid(hx, hy, hz) / ball / capsule_y(half_height, radius) / cylinder, ColliderBuilder::convex_mesh(points, &indices) for one hull, or ColliderBuilder::compound(vec![(Pose, SharedShape), ..]) of convex parts for a concave object. Fixed level geometry: ColliderBuilder::trimesh_with_flags(vertices, indices, flags) on RigidBodyBuilder::fixed(), and ColliderBuilder::heightfield_with_flags for terrain. Voxels exist at this pin (SharedShape::voxels(voxel_size, &[IVector]), voxels_from_points, voxelized_mesh; ShapeType::Voxels). Rapier's MeshConverter (TriMesh, TriMeshWithFlags, Obb, Aabb, ConvexHull, ConvexDecomposition, ConvexDecompositionWithParams) with ColliderBuilder::converted_trimesh picks a conversion at runtime.
recipes.gotchas: An open trimesh has mass 0 and ccd_thickness 0 (measured), so a dynamic body carrying one gets no mass from it and bodies can pass into its hollow inside. A closed, outward-wound trimesh does report its volume (1/6 for the unit tetrahedron, the same as its convex hull), which makes a trimesh on a dynamic body look fine when it is not. Rapier's guide discourages trimeshes and polylines on dynamic bodies and recommends a convex decomposition in a compound. That guide page is labelled Rust 0.36; every API name above was checked on docs.rs at the pins.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/rapier_law.rs builds only ColliderBuilder::cuboid colliders (static slabs and every body), one ColliderBuilder::heightfield, and character_shape's SharedShape::cuboid / capsule_y for the controller. The post-Phase-2 collision-from-meshes slice should put TriMesh only on RigidBodyBuilder::fixed() and give dynamic bodies convex_mesh or compound colliders; Signature's geom hash would then have to cover the mesh buffers the way it covers collider rows today.

recipes.name: Validate mesh buffers before TriMesh::with_flags: parry 0.30.2 drops TopologyError and panics on bad indices
recipes.what: TriMesh::new and with_flags return Err only for an empty index buffer (EmptyIndices); a TopologyError under HALF_EDGE_TOPOLOGY is discarded (Ok, topology() == None), NaN and infinite vertices are accepted, and an index past the vertex buffer panics.
recipes.how: Refuse before parry: at least one triangle, every coordinate finite, every index < vertices.len(), no triangle repeating an index. Build with TriMesh::new(vertices, indices), then call mesh.set_flags(TriMeshFlags::HALF_EDGE_TOPOLOGY), which does return Result<(), TopologyError> (BadTriangle(u32) or BadAdjacentTrianglesOrientation { triangle1, triangle2, edge }), and refuse on Err, or check mesh.topology().is_some() after with_flags. Return refusals as an enum, never as a panic.
recipes.gotchas: The docs.rs page says with_flags errors when HALF_EDGE_TOPOLOGY is set and the topology is invalid; the pinned source runs `let _ = result.set_flags(flags);` and the oracle gets Ok with no topology while flags() still claims HALF_EDGE_TOPOLOGY. Two TopologyError doc tests are commented out in the source as failing. A NaN vertex is left out of the local AABB (x = [0, 0] measured for a triangle with a NaN x), so the bounding volume no longer describes the triangle. Index 7 on 3 vertices panics with 'index out of bounds' in rebuild_bvh. Rapier 0.35's quarantine acts on bodies and colliders that go non-finite during a step; it is not a load-time validator.
recipes.engine_note: The post-Phase-2 mesh loader must refuse before any parry call, the way signature() refuses body rows today (bad() on every f64, canon_quat on rotations): solver/Cargo.toml's release profile has panic = "abort", so parry's index panic inside TriMesh::new would trap the wasm module instead of making solver_load return 0.
recipes.verify_note: trimesh.rs:744 is literally `let _ = result.set_flags(flags);`. Independently reran with a fresh BadTriangle counter-example via compile_oracle.py file: is_ok=true, topology_is_some=false; set_flags on same mesh -> Err(BadTriangle(0)).

recipes.name: Canonicalise -0.0 and weld vertices offline: MERGE_DUPLICATE_VERTICES keys raw bits and renumbers the mesh
recipes.what: MERGE_DUPLICATE_VERTICES (and FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES, whose bits 144 include it) keys vertices by raw bytes but compares with ==, so (-0.0, 0, 0) welds to (0, 0, 0) in a 4- or 16-vertex mesh and not in a 64-vertex one; merging also renumbers and drops unreferenced vertices, and DELETE_DEGENERATE_TRIANGLES only removes repeated-index triangles.
recipes.how: In the offline tool: pass every coordinate through canon() (x == 0.0 -> 0.0), refuse NaN, weld exact duplicates yourself, drop zero-area triangles by computing their area, and write the vertex buffer in first-reference order with every vertex referenced. Such buffers pass through FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES unchanged (measured), so the stored bytes are the bytes parry uses. Never keep outside references to input vertex indices across a merging flag.
recipes.gotchas: TriMeshFlags documents MERGE as joining 'vertices with the exact same coordinates' and TriMesh documents vertices() as keeping construction order; signed zero breaks the first, and any merging flag breaks the second (7 vertices in, 4 out, (9, 9, 9) dropped). The ±0 result depends on hash-table probing: the key hashes the raw bytes, equality is ==, and under enhanced-determinism the map is an IndexMap with FxHasher32. Whether the flip point differs on wasm32 was not measured. A mesh whose every triangle repeats an index comes back with 0 triangles, not EmptyIndices, because the emptiness check runs before the deletion. A zero-area triangle with three distinct indices is kept.
recipes.engine_note: signature() in rapier_law.rs mixes every geometry f64 with mix_f64 (to_bits), so -0.0 and 0.0 already give different world signatures. The mesh slice's offline tool should apply the same canon() that write_body uses, and the loader should refuse a non-canonical value, which is the pattern T3's load-time refusal of non-finite authored values already follows.
recipes.verify_note: Source-confirmed: FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES bits=144=(1<<7)|MERGE.bits(); HashablePartialEq hashes raw bytes but Eq is by value -- a Hash/Eq contract break that mechanically explains the size-dependent -0.0 welding.

recipes.name: Compute convex hulls and VHACD parts offline with pinned parameters, then load stored buffers with convex_mesh
recipes.what: SharedShape::convex_hull is None for fewer than 3 points, NaN, coincident or collinear points, but Some for coplanar points: a flat polyhedron of mass 0. VHACD output follows its parameters: a two-box mesh of volume 2 became 2 parts (mass 2.0000) at resolution 64 and 13 parts (summed mass 3.1227) at resolution 16.
recipes.how: Offline: parry3d_f64::transformation::try_convex_hull(&points) -> (vertices, indices); refuse Err and refuse a hull whose mass_properties(1.0).mass() is 0. For concave parts call SharedShape::convex_decomposition_with_params(&v, &idx, &VHACDParameters { .. }) with every field written out (0.30.2 defaults: resolution 64, concavity 0.01, alpha 0.05, beta 0.05, plane_downsampling 4, convex_hull_downsampling 4, convex_hull_approximation true, max_convex_hulls 1024) and store each part's vertex and index buffers. At load: ColliderBuilder::convex_mesh(points, &indices) per part, which skips the hull computation and gave the same mass bits as convex_hull, then ColliderBuilder::compound.
recipes.gotchas: ConvexHullError's docs say nearly coplanar 3D input gives MissingSupportPoint; the pinned code triangulates coplanar input as a flat hull and from_convex_mesh accepts it (measured Some, mass 0), and ColliderBuilder::convex_hull ('None if the points don't form a valid convex shape') and MeshConverter::ConvexHull pass it too (both returned a mass-0 shape). The hull code counts dimensions with a 1.0e-7 eigenvalue threshold, so a nearly flat cloud can land on either side. VHACD memory grows as O(resolution^3) and convex_hull_approximation = false costs 2-5x time (VHACDParameters docs). A summed compound mass above the source volume means overlapping parts.
recipes.engine_note: The post-Phase-2 slice plans 'hull point sets stored offline for determinism': store try_convex_hull's vertex and triangle-index buffers rather than only the points, load them with ColliderBuilder::convex_mesh, and refuse a mass-0 hull at load. VHACD belongs in the offline tool: its O(resolution^3) voxel grid would be a transient allocation inside a solver binary whose memory T3's lint forbids from growing.
recipes.verify_note: Independently reran via compile_oracle.py with an original 5-point coplanar pentagon: try_convex_hull=Ok, convex_hull=Some(mass=0); NaN input correctly Err. initial_mesh.rs's dimension==2 branch (1e-7 eigenvalue) explains why.

recipes.name: Fill a parry HeightField column-major with scale as the whole extent, and sample it as two triangles per cell
recipes.what: In HeightField::new(Array2::new(nrows, ncols, data), scale) row i advances z and column j advances x, data is column-major (i + j * nrows), scale is the whole field (cell width = scale.x / (ncols - 1)), the field is centred on its collider, and each cell is two triangles split along (x0, z1)-(x1, z0), not a bilinear patch.
recipes.how: Build with Array2::from_fn(rows, cols, |row, col| h[row][col]), or transpose a row-major record with data[row + col * rows] = record[row * cols + col]; pass scale = ((cols - 1) * cell, 1.0, (rows - 1) * cell). Code that samples the surface outside the solver must use the same triangles: in cell (i, j) with fractions u (x) and v (z), h = h00 + u*(h01 - h00) + v*(h10 - h00) when u + v <= 1, else h = h11 + (1-u)*(h10 - h11) + (1-v)*(h01 - h11), where h10 is the +z neighbour and h01 the +x neighbour, or it can ask the law with a downward ray.
recipes.gotchas: Rapier's ColliderBuilder::heightfield doc at 0.35.3 calls scale the 'Size of each grid cell'; parry divides it by (ncols - 1), so a scale of (1, 1, 1) on 5 columns gives cells 0.25 wide (measured). HeightField::new asserts at least 2 rows and columns and Array2::new asserts data.len() == nrows * ncols; both are panics. Bilinear interpolation disagrees with the solver on any non-planar cell: 0.25 against 0 at the centre of a unit cell with one corner raised by 1 (measured). A cell flagged HeightFieldCellStatus::ZIGZAG_SUBDIVISION uses the other diagonal.
recipes.engine_note: build_world in rapier_law.rs transposes the row-major HEIGHTS buffer with data[row + col * rows] and passes ((cols - 1) * cell, 1, (rows - 1) * cell) on a fixed body at the origin, which matches parry, and signature() refuses fewer than 2 rows or columns before HeightField's assert can fire; MAX_HEIGHTS 256 caps a field at 256 heights (16 x 16, say). packages/tick/world.js heightfieldSupport, which supportAt hands to the verb predicates, interpolates bilinearly, so on a non-planar cell it reports a height the solver's surface does not have.
recipes.verify_note: Independently reran via compile_oracle.py with different dims/scale than the lane's check: cell_width=1.5 for scale.x=12,cols=9 (=12/8). rapier3d-f64's ColliderBuilder doc still calls scale 'Size of each grid cell' -- wrong.
