recipes.name: Set FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES on ground dynamic bodies slide over; test heightfield row 0 moving +x on its own
recipes.what: Without the flag, a frictionless box sliding flat at 2 u/s stopped dead at the first internal edge of a trimesh or heightfield (0.25 of 2.00 travelled in 64 quanta) because the edge adds a sideways contact normal. TriMeshFlags::FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES removed the snag; on a 9 x 9 heightfield, HeightFieldFlags::FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES removed it for every row and column in both directions except moving +x in row 0, the lowest-z row of cells.
recipes.how: ColliderBuilder::trimesh_with_flags(v, idx, TriMeshFlags::FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES) and ColliderBuilder::heightfield_with_flags(heights, scale, HeightFieldFlags::FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES) for any ground a dynamic body slides or rolls on; triangle_normal_constraints(id).is_some() confirms the pseudo-normals exist. Keep an outcome test per direction that crosses a seam in row 0 and in an interior row. Padding a field with one extra row on its low-z side, so nothing moves in row 0, is a workaround inferred from the measurement, not from any source.
recipes.gotchas: The snag is a solver-contact effect: with max_ccd_substeps = 0 it was unchanged, and the kinematic controller walked the same seams with or without the flag (1.985 on a 2-row field, 2.000 on 3 rows, never airborne). A 2-row heightfield is all row 0. TriMeshFlags::FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES also merges duplicate vertices (see the weld recipe). parry's heightfield triangle_normal_constraints says its edge pseudo-normals are 'given in no particular order'; whether that explains the row-0 case is a guess.
recipes.engine_note: build_world calls ColliderBuilder::heightfield with no flags, so T4 pin 3's seam test (a box sliding down across a cell boundary with no upward hitch beyond the skin) is where heightfield_with_flags(.., HeightFieldFlags::FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES) gets measured; adopting it changes the binary digest and the goldens once. That test needs a crossing in row 0 moving +x: a 2-row field, which signature() allows and packages/tick/verbs.test.js uses for its sloped case, has no other row.
recipes.verify_note: Flags confirmed (FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES fixes normals causing 'incorrect bumps'). Engine facts confirmed: heightfield built with no flags (rapier_law.rs:378); verbs.test.js:41 uses a 2-row sloped field. Row-0 numbers not re-executed by me.

recipes.name: Call KinematicCharacterController::move_shape with Absolute lengths and self-exclusion, then apply the result
recipes.what: move_shape sweeps the shape (at most 20 casts, each stopping offset short of obstacles), tries a stair step on every wall hit and otherwise slides, snaps down only if the call started grounded, and returns EffectiveCharacterMovement { translation, grounded, is_sliding_down_slope }; it moves nothing, the caller applies translation.
recipes.how: Set every CharacterLength as Absolute: offset, CharacterAutostep { max_height, min_width, include_dynamic_bodies }, snap_to_ground; write up, slide, max_slope_climb_angle, min_slope_slide_angle (radians) and normal_nudge_factor explicitly. Per quantum: let pos = *world.bodies[h].position(); let q = world.query_pipeline_with_filter(QueryFilter::new().exclude_rigid_body(h)); let mv = ctl.move_shape(dt, &q, &*shape, &pos, desired, |c| collisions.push(c)); world.bodies[h].set_next_kinematic_translation(pos.translation + mv.translation); then step. Pass the shape the body's collider uses, zero vertical velocity on mv.grounded, and read is_sliding_down_slope as advisory.
recipes.gotchas: Defaults are Relative (offset 0.01, snap 0.2, autostep 0.25 and 0.5) and evaluate against the shape's AABB, the height and for min_width the horizontal diagonal: the resting gap was 0.0201 for a 2.0-high box under the default and 0.0101 with Absolute(0.01). Without the self-exclusion filter the walker never moved (0.000 against 0.956). Depenetration runs only when the desired translation is (near) zero, so a walker with any intent is never pushed out that way. is_sliding_down_slope was true on flat ground whenever the move had a downward part. An airborne character stepped up a 0.2 rise (dy 0.2101); the 0.36 guide says autostep needs floor contact first, which the pinned code does not check. The stair probe adds offset to max_height and min_width; the comparisons at the limits are binary-and-limits' finding. parry 0.30.2's shape-cast fix (#429) moved the controller's progress bound in Rapier's own test from 940 to 930.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs controller() already sets SKIN 0.01, STEP_HEIGHT 0.3, STEP_MIN_WIDTH 0.2 and SNAP 0.2 as CharacterLength::Absolute with CLIMB_ANGLE pi/4, SLIDE_ANGLE 50 degrees in radians and normal_nudge_factor 1e-4, so character_shape can switch between SharedShape::cuboid and capsule_y without moving those lengths; integrate() excludes the walker's own body, applies the move with set_next_kinematic_translation, zeroes vy on grounded and ignores is_sliding_down_slope. fixtures/shape-traversal.json kept the box (docs/PHASE-1.md: it climbs a step of the maximum height and holds a ledge where the same-size capsule misses the step and drops); below the limit both shapes climbed alike here, feet at step + 0.010. Lifted actions (DRIVEN 2.0) bypass move_shape.
recipes.verify_note: Reran the airborne-autostep claim independently: no floor anywhere, zero vertical intent, one horizontal move_shape call into a step -> dy=0.16, grounded=true. handle_stairs never reads grounded_at_starting_pos (character_controller.rs).

recipes.name: Push dynamic bodies with solve_character_collision_impulses and plan all walkers against the last step's poses
recipes.what: move_shape stops a walker one offset short of a dynamic body and never moves it; solve_character_collision_impulses applies approximate impulses to dynamic bodies only. Walkers meet each other as kinematic obstacles at the last step's poses and inherit a touching kinematic body's velocity, so two walkers planned together stayed apart at 1 and 2 u/s but overlapped at 8 u/s.
recipes.how: Collect CharacterCollision events in move_shape's callback, call set_next_kinematic_translation, then build a QueryPipelineMut with broad_phase.as_query_pipeline_mut(narrow_phase.query_dispatcher(), bodies, colliders, filter) excluding the walker and call solve_character_collision_impulses(dt, &mut q, shape, character_mass, &collisions) before world.step(). Run every walker's move_shape before applying any of them; planning order then cannot change the result (reversed order was bit-identical). State the speed in any walker-against-walker outcome test.
recipes.gotchas: Each contact point gets an impulse along the normal only, scaled by body_mass*character_mass/(body_mass + character_mass); the docs call it 'only approximate'. include_dynamic_bodies: false makes the stair probe skip dynamic bodies. Mirror-image walkers did not end mirror-image (-0.2741 and +0.2905 at 1 u/s), so assert separation and 'neither passes the other's start', not symmetry. A kinematic body walking into a standing walker pushed it through the platform path when the walker had any intent (x -0.797, clear) and through depenetration when its intent was zero (x -0.744, 0.006 inside at the end).
recipes.engine_note: integrate() in rapier_law.rs plans every walker with move_shape before any set_next_kinematic_translation, then calls solve_character_collision_impulses with character_mass 1.0 (walkers get additional_mass(1.0)) and include_dynamic_bodies: false. For T4 pin 5's two walkers driven at each other: at the verb speed of 1 u/s (predicates/intents/*.json) they ended 0.0646 apart here; at 8 u/s, above world.js's MAX_SPEED 2, they ended 0.0318 overlapped.

recipes.name: Test line of sight with an eye-to-target ray at max_toi 1.0 on fixed colliders once the broad phase holds them
recipes.what: QueryPipeline::cast_ray(&Ray, max_toi, solid) returns the first (ColliderHandle, toi) with hit point origin + dir * toi, so dir = target - eye with max_toi 1.0 is exactly the eye-to-target segment. Queries see only colliders already in the broad phase, intersect_ray yields hits in tree order, and solid = true answers toi 0 from inside a shape.
recipes.how: let seg = Ray::new(eye, target - eye); let blocked = world.cast_ray(&seg, 1.0, true, QueryFilter::only_fixed()).is_some(); only_fixed() keeps fixed colliders (and parentless ones) and drops every body, the looker and the target included. With a wider filter, exclude the looker (exclude_rigid_body) and the target (a predicate). Use cast_ray_and_get_normal when the normal matters. When several hits are needed, collect intersect_ray or intersect_shape and sort by (toi, collider handle) before anything order-sensitive.
recipes.gotchas: A unit dir makes toi a distance (0.9 here) and target - eye makes it a fraction (0.225); one max_toi cannot serve both. With no filter the looker's own collider answered first at toi 0. Before the first step cast_ray returned None with the walls inserted; the scene-queries guide says stepping updates the broad phase the queries rely on. intersect_ray returned 0.725, 0.475, 0.225, insertion order rather than distance. From inside a wall, solid = false reported the exit at 0.1.
recipes.engine_note: E5 sight runs in the JS tick (distance at most `sight` and a zero-extent swept segment crossing no static collider), and docs/dispatch-e5-minds.md keeps the binary unchanged for it. Once collision-from-meshes adds TriMesh statics, a box-only JS segment test cannot answer; the matching law query is cast_ray(Ray::new(eye, target - eye), 1.0, true) with QueryFilter::only_fixed(), exported like solver_step and run only after solver_load, whose warm_broadphase CollisionPipeline pass is what puts the colliders in the broad phase.

recipes.name: Bake glTF collision meshes offline with the gltf crate and refuse what the deterministic law cannot reproduce
recipes.what: The glTF 2.0 spec fixes meters, radians, +Y up, float32 POSITION with min/max, unit quaternions and in-range indices, but files can still break it; the gltf crate (1.4.1) exposes f32 transforms, Mode, positions, indices and skins. Converting belongs in a host tool that writes baked f64 triangles, not in the wasm law.
recipes.how: Tool: gltf::import the file, walk the scene's nodes and compose each Transform in f64 (matrix() or decomposed()). Refuse a primitive unless mode() == Mode::Triangles, every position is finite, and every index (reader indices, ReadIndices::into_u32) is below the position count and not 255/65535/4294967295 for its width; refuse skins (node.skin()), animations and morph weights on collision nodes. Refuse a rotation with |q.q - 1| above a stated tolerance (1e-6 suits f32 input), refuse zero or non-finite scale, and when the scale's determinant is negative swap two indices per triangle. Write units ('m') and up axis ('+Y') into the record and refuse records without them, then canonicalise -0.0, weld, and store f64 vertex and u32 index buffers (and offline hulls).
recipes.gotchas: gltf's Transform holds f32 arrays: widening to f64 is exact, but composing in f32 is not, so compose in f64 once and store the result so the law never multiplies transforms. f32 sqrt(1/2) quaternions miss unit length by 3.4e-8 (measured), so an exact == 1.0 test refuses valid files. A mirrored node, scale (-1, 1, 1), flips a floor triangle's normal from +Y to -Y and swapping two indices restores it (measured). The spec says a skinned mesh's node transform MUST be ignored, so skinned geometry has no single static shape, and degenerate triangles are only SHOULD NOT. The gltf crate is outside this KB's oracle set: its API was checked on docs.rs, not compiled.
recipes.engine_note: The collision-from-meshes slice after Phase 2 (its input is the studio's glb survey) should keep the gltf crate in host tooling: the law is a wasm32-unknown-unknown cdylib with raw extern "C" exports over static f64 buffers and a pinned digest, and at load it already refuses NaN and renormalises quaternions with canon_quat. The world file carries the baked buffers; solver_load validates them like body rows and mixes them into Signature.geom.

recipes.name: Never write through a ptr::from_ref pointer to a ContactPair: parking it in a Vec only hides the UB
recipes.what: A pointer made by ptr::from_ref from &ContactPair may never be written through; doing so mutates bytes behind a shared reference, which the Reference lists as UB.
recipes.how: Delete such writes rather than wrapping them: there is no UnsafeCell inside ContactPair to make them sound. rustc's deny-by-default invalid_reference_casting rejects `&mut *(ptr::from_ref(p) as *mut T)` in one expression, but the same cast collected into a Vec<*mut T> and dereferenced later compiles silently.
recipes.gotchas: Single-threaded ownership of the world does not make it sound: the rule is about the provenance of the pointer (derived from &T), not about races. A clean compile is not evidence: the lint is pattern-based.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs solver_clear_warmstart on main; on the T2 branch (ee2e50a) pairs_mut (~868), carry_warmstart (~880) and solver_restore (~1193) use the same Vec-of-pointers shape.

lanes.title: Deterministic simulation architecture in Rust
lanes.verifier_note: Checked every recipe's warrant sources by direct retrieval (curl/gh api, never memory): docs.rs pages at the pinned crate versions, doc.rust-lang.org at stable/1.98.1, the RFC and WASM spec, crates.io publish dates, and si-rpg-engine's actual source (README.md, packages/tick/tick.js, packages/frame/hash.js, harness/*, solver/src/lib.rs, solver/src/rapier_law.rs, solver/build.mjs, docs/dispatch-*.md, fixtures/golden-behaviour.json, CHANGELOG.md), fetched at both the pinned commit 1701b72 and main HEAD be0ea06 (byte-identical for every Rust/JS file checked, so no drift). Both mandated high-stakes checks were independently reproduced with the compile oracle using the engine's own mixer/lane code copied verbatim from rapier_law.rs and hash.js, not the recipe's supplied source: the mix_u64 signature mixer collides on the named half-extent pair (d1b28807b4eb6fed both) while FNV-1a64 and xxh3_64 do not, and any u32-only stream through the two-lane hasher produces identical halves structurally, for arbitrary inputs. Two more compile_fail claims (E0277 on ColliderHandle.sort(), E0004 on a Mode match missing Carried) were also independently reproduced. Essentially every one of the ~90 warrant-source claims checked matched its retrieved page at a verbatim or near-verbatim level; only one defect was found, a minor misattribution in recipe 1 (the 'f64 cannot represent every Duration' sentence belongs to Duration::mul_f64's docs, not from_secs_f64's, though from_secs_f64 does round as its own examples show). All primary sources are dated 2024 or later, meeting the recency bar. The systemic weakness: six of the crates this lane leans on for engine-facing claims -- bevy_time, ggrs, backroll, blake3, bevy_ecs and hecs -- are absent from the compile oracle's ORACLE_DEPS set (rapier3d_f64, parry3d_f64, bytemuck, slotmap, indexmap, serde_json and a few others are the only crates the oracle can actually build and run against). Every claim touching those six crates is verified by reading a documentation page, never by a compiled call into the real crate; recipe 10's only check explicitly says as much ('neither is in the oracle set, so the check models the mechanism'). My own page-reads back every one of those claims solidly, but the lane's own mechanical verification floor -- the thing meant to catch a hallucinated method name or signature without a human or model rereading prose -- silently does not reach about a third of the crates it cites.

recipes.name: Run the law on integer quanta from a host-owned accumulator; keep render interpolation out of the state
recipes.what: A 1/64 s quantum is exact in binary, so the law counts time as an integer tick; the host's accumulator, kept in integer nanoseconds, decides how many quanta a frame runs and the render alpha, and neither the alpha nor any clock value reaches the hashed state.
recipes.how: Give the law `tick: u64` and `const DT: f64 = 1.0 / 64.0`; derive seconds as `tick as f64 * DT`, never by `t += DT`. Keep the accumulator in the host: `acc_ns += frame_ns; while acc_ns >= 15_625_000 { law.step(&inputs_for(tick)); tick += 1; acc_ns -= 15_625_000; }`, then draw with `alpha = acc_ns as f64 / 15_625_000.0`. Presentation receives shared references to committed state and returns a pose, e.g. `fn draw(prev: &State, cur: &State, alpha: f64) -> f64 { prev.y + (cur.y - prev.y) * alpha }`; an assignment through `&State` is E0594, so safe code cannot write a smoothed pose back. Bevy 0.19.1 makes the same choices: `Time<Fixed>` defaults to 64 Hz (15625 µs), keeps its accumulated `overstep()` as a `Duration`, may run the fixed schedule 0, 1 or more times per frame, and offers `overstep_fraction()` for interpolation.
recipes.rust_version: any (checked on 1.98.1); bevy_time 0.19.1 for the comparison
recipes.gotchas: 1/60 is not exact: sixty 1/60 steps accumulate to 1.0000000000000013 and an hour of them to 3600.0000000182276, while `ticks as f64 * dt` gives 3600.0; with 1/64 both give exactly 3600.0. An f64-seconds accumulator fed 1/60, 1/120 or 1/144 s frames ran 63 quanta after one second of frames (64 at 240 Hz), while the integer-nanosecond accumulator ran 64 at every pacing: which frame a quantum lands in then depends on pacing, harmless only when inputs are stamped with their quantum (next recipe). `Duration::from_secs_f64` rounds (1/60 s becomes 16.666667ms), so convert a frame time once and accumulate integers. E0594 guards safe code holding `&State` only: an `extern "C"` export that returns a pointer into a `static mut` buffer gives the host a writable view, so the law re-checks every value it reads on every call.
recipes.engine_note: packages/tick/tick.js runs the 1/64 s quantum in JavaScript and mixes `hasher.u32(tick)`, so time enters the hash as an integer; solver/src/lib.rs and rapier_law.rs hold `DT = 1.0 / 64.0` as a constant and read no clock. README: 'Presentation has no path back into the hash', and packages/frame/frame.js freezes the committed frame the host receives. The gap is the ABI: `bodies_ptr`, `colliders_ptr` and `heights_ptr` hand JavaScript writable f64 views, so on the Rust side the rule rests on signature()'s per-call checks, not on types. A Godot or Unreal host keeps its own accumulator and drives the law by quantum count, never by frame delta.

recipes.name: Prove the record complete twice: replay seed plus stamped inputs, and save-restore-rerun every quantum
recipes.what: Replay from the seed and the tick-stamped admitted inputs proves the inputs are the whole cause; saving, restoring into a fresh world and resimulating proves the snapshot is the whole state, and only an every-quantum sync test (GGRS's SyncTestSession, check distance of at least 2) cannot pass vacuously.
recipes.how: Record `seed` plus `Vec<(tick, input)>`, the tick being the quantum the input applies to; replay reruns the law, compares the per-quantum hash chain and reports the first differing quantum. For the snapshot: every quantum, save the bytes and step; then restore a fresh world from the bytes saved `d` quanta back and resimulate, comparing each resimulated hash with the original. GGRS 0.13.0 packages this loop: `SessionBuilder::with_check_distance(2)` (the default; 0 or 1 disables the comparison), `start_synctest_session()`, fulfil each `GgrsRequest::SaveGameState` with `cell.save(frame, Some(state), Some(checksum))`, and `SyncTestSession::advance_frame()` returns `Err(GgrsError::MismatchedChecksum { current_frame, mismatched_frames })`. Hash the snapshot bytes plus every observable flag (the sleep flag in the check), not positions alone.
recipes.gotchas: GGRS keeps `checksum_history: HashMap<Frame, Option<u128>>` and tests `cs == latest_cell.checksum()`, so saving with `checksum: None` makes every comparison `None == None`: the sync test runs and checks nothing. One restore point can pass vacuously: in the check, a snapshot that omits a per-body rest counter restores cleanly at quantum 20 (no body has landed, every counter is 0) and differs at quantum 53 when restored at 40; the every-quantum sync test finds quantum 53 on its own. An input stamped one quantum late diverges from quantum 40 on, a different seed from quantum 0. backroll, another Rust port of GGPO, last released 0.6.0 on 2022-11-13, was last pushed 2023-03-13 and calls itself early beta; GGRS 0.13.0 shipped 2026-06-26. Rollback needs the engine's cooperation: Box2D's author states Box2D does not provide roll-back determinism because its internal state has no restoration mechanism.
recipes.engine_note: README: 'Replay is the seed plus the log of what was admitted'; `npx replay` fails on the first differing hash, and T5's nightly bundle (seed, world, log, hash chain) is this record. T2 (docs/dispatch-t2-restore.md pin 5, PR #43) restores once, 'a third of the way', under harness/first-difference.js; the check shows a single point can miss state that is still at its default there, so restore at several points per fixture or run an every-quantum sync test with distance 2, which is cheap at 64 bodies. rapier_law.rs rebuild_snapshot already writes `time_since_can_sleep / DT` and the sleeping flag, the kind of counter the check shows a snapshot can drop.

recipes.name: Encode snapshots canonically: to_le_bytes in a fixed field order, sorted pairs, no padding, a version tag
recipes.what: A snapshot is a byte string the law defines — explicit little-endian numbers in a declared order, collections sorted by a total key, and a header with a magic, a law version and counts — never a struct's memory image, whose field order and padding belong to the compiler.
recipes.how: Write every field with `to_le_bytes()` into a `Vec<u8>`: the header `b"SIRS"`, `LAW_VERSION.to_le_bytes()` (u32) and the counts, then per body pose and velocity in one order, then pairs after `sort_by_key(|p| (p.a, p.b))`. The decoder refuses a foreign magic, another law version, and any length that is not the layout (`16 + 48 * bodies + 24 * pairs` in the check). If a record is cast to bytes, make it `#[repr(C)]` and derive `bytemuck::Pod`, which refuses padding at compile time; spell padding as a zeroed field (`_pad: u32`) so the layout is explicit (16 bytes, `0700000000000000000000000000e03f` in the check).
recipes.rust_version: any; bytemuck 1.25.2 for the Pod derive
recipes.gotchas: `#[repr(C)] struct { flag: u8, impulse: f64, kind: u8 }` is 24 bytes, 14 of them padding (offsets 0, 8, 16), and the same fields under the default representation are 16 bytes, because the default representation guarantees only what soundness needs and may reorder fields. Deriving Pod on `{ pair: u32, impulse: f64 }` fails with `error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: derive(Pod) was applied to a type with padding`. `to_ne_bytes` is native order, and the std docs say portable code should use `to_be_bytes` or `to_le_bytes`; wasm memory is little-endian, so the two agree there and part ways on a big-endian host. Without a version word a layout change shows only as a length change, and a same-length change of meaning passes. Canonicalise -0.0 before writing (the float-determinism lane owns that detail).
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs rebuild_snapshot already follows most of this: `push_f64` writes `canon(x).to_le_bytes()` per field in a fixed per-body order (pose, velocity, quaternion, spin, sleep counter in quanta, sleeping flag), then the pair count, then pairs sorted by `(collider1.into_raw_parts(), collider2.into_raw_parts())` with seven warm-start f64s per manifold point; counts and ids go in as f64, exact below 2^53. It has no magic and no version word, which is why T3 records length plus digest to notice a layout change. T2's solver_restore must refuse a foreign snapshot; a version word in the header is the direct way, and adding one moves the product golden once.
recipes.verify_note: f64.rs/Reference/bytemuck/WASM spec verbatim. rapier_law.rs read directly: field order, pair sort, 7 warm-start f64s, no magic/version all match.

recipes.name: Persist hashes of explicit little-endian bytes, never #[derive(Hash)] streams or DefaultHasher output
recipes.what: What `Hash` feeds a hasher is not portable (usize length prefixes, native endianness) and `DefaultHasher`'s algorithm is unspecified across releases, so any hash that is stored, compared across hosts or pinned in a golden is a named function (FNV-1a, xxh3, BLAKE3) over bytes the law encoded itself.
recipes.how: Choose by job. FNV-1a (RFC 9923; 32-bit prime 0x01000193, basis 0x811C9DC5; 64-bit prime 0x100000001B3, basis 0xCBF29CE484222325) is a few lines with no dependency. xxh3 (`xxhash_rust::xxh3::xxh3_64` or `xxh3_128`, feature `xxh3`) is the fast choice; its output was declared stable in xxHash v0.8.0 (2020) and is identical on little- and big-endian systems, and the streaming `Xxh3::new()` / `update` / `digest()` gives the one-shot value (checked over five chunkings). BLAKE3 (`blake3::hash`, 32-byte output, crate 1.8.7) when a digest must resist deliberate forgery, such as a replay bundle someone else hands you. Hash `encode(&state)` (previous recipe): the same FNV-1a 64 over the same 35 bytes returned 845153761026826623 on x86_64 and on wasm32. Keep `Hash`, `DefaultHasher` and `RandomState` for in-process maps.
recipes.gotchas: The std `Hash` docs: data fed by `Hash` 'should not be considered portable across platforms' and 'tests shouldn't probe hard-coded hash values'; `DefaultHasher`: 'The internal algorithm is not specified, and so it and its hashes should not be relied upon over releases'; HashMap's SipHash 1-3 is 'subject to change at any point in the future'. Measured: `#[derive(Hash)]` on `{ id: u32, name: String, cells: Vec<u8> }` feeds 18 bytes on x86_64 and 14 on wasm32, because the Vec's length prefix is a usize (a str ends with a 0xff byte instead). Neither FNV nor xxHash resists an adversary (RFC 9923: NOT RECOMMENDED where collision or preimage attacks must be infeasible; the xxHash README: not a cryptographic hash). A word-wise mixer `h = h * P + x` with FNV's constants is not FNV-1a, which XORs one octet and then multiplies, and it collides algebraically: (x1 + 1, x2 - P) gives the same value as (x1, x2).
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs signature() folds half-extents, collider fields and heights into `geom` with `mix_u64(h, x) = h.wrapping_mul(0x100000001b3).wrapping_add(x)` from basis 0xcbf29ce484222325: FNV-64 constants, not FNV-1a. The check finds half-extents (0.5, 0.5) and (0.5000000000000001, 0.49993896484372585) with the same `geom`, where FNV-1a 64 and xxh3_64 over the same bytes differ. `geom` only decides whether ensure() rebuilds the world, but equal `geom` does not prove equal geometry: keep the canonical geometry values and compare their bits (a few KB at 64 bodies, 64 colliders and 256 heights), or hash their little-endian bytes with FNV-1a 64 or xxh3. The JavaScript frame hash is the next recipe.

recipes.name: Stop feeding u32-only streams to both FNV-1a lanes: such a digest repeats one 32-bit half
recipes.what: packages/frame/hash.js mixes every u32 into both lanes from the same basis, so a digest built only from u32 input — the T1 trace's snapshot digest and the snapshot digests T3 adds to the behaviour file — has identical halves and carries 32 bits; frame hashes keep the lanes apart because each double's low and high words go to different lanes.
recipes.how: Confirmed in hash.js: `u32(w)` runs `h0 = mix(h0, v); h1 = mix(h1, v)`, both lanes start at 0x811c9dc5 (RFC 9923's 32-bit offset basis), `float(x)` sends the low little-endian word to lane 0 and the high word to lane 1, and `digest()` is `hex(h0) + hex(h1)`; harness/trace-line.mjs `snapshotField` feeds `u32(snap.length)` and then `u32(snap[i])` for every byte. Fix options, cheapest first. (A) At the u32-only digest sites only, split the byte stream across the lanes the way a double is split (the low four bytes of each 8-byte word to lane 0, the high four to lane 1): the frame hash, the product golden fd2f6c03fb982d77 and the arithmetic golden 0d38671370d12d1e stay, and the trace's `snap` digests and the behaviour file's snapshot digests move once. (B) Change `u32()` so the lanes see different images of each word (lane 1 takes it bit-reversed, or one lane its 8-byte widening): every frame hash mixes u32 and text input (seed, tick, ids, zone and link indices, snapshot bytes), so the product golden and every fixture's frame hashes move once; the float-only arithmetic golden does not. (C) A real 64-bit function, FNV-1a 64 or xxh3 over the bytes: one 64-bit state, but JavaScript needs BigInt or 16-bit-limb multiplication in all three shells (or the law computes and exports the digest), and every digest it replaces moves.
recipes.rust_version: any (the checks are a Rust port of the JavaScript hasher)
recipes.gotchas: Birthday arithmetic: 32 bits give an even chance of some collision among about 77,000 distinct snapshots, 64 bits among about 5 billion; in the check two of 125,346 arbitrary one-word snapshots share f7da4862f7da4862, and each of the three fixes separates them. Option A still leaves each lane guarding only the half of every word it sees, so a change confined to low words is protected by 32 bits; option C has no such split. The frame hash's own snapshot section (tick.js `mixSnapshot`) also feeds bytes as u32 to both lanes, and its halves differ only because floats were mixed earlier. Identical halves make a cheap tripwire: a test that fails when a digest's first eight hex digits equal its last eight catches a regression of any digest meant to carry 64 bits.
recipes.engine_note: packages/frame/hash.js `u32()` and `digest()`; harness/trace-line.mjs `snapshotField`, the T1 trace's `snap <len> <digest>` token; and the behaviour-file digests: the T3 branch (PR #44, head b99a636) records `snapshotDigest` load 52bfc19452bfc194 and last 41b1e63f41b1e63f in fixtures/golden-behaviour.json, both with identical halves. S1 pin 13 (docs/dispatch-s1-soundness.md) takes option A and states that the product golden and every frame hash stay while the behaviour-file digests move once with that reason.
recipes.verify_note: Own counter-example: any u32-only stream through hash.js's lanes gives h0==h1 structurally. T3 golden-behaviour.json literally shows identical-halves digests.

recipes.name: Key records by stable ids, keep insertion and removal history in the record, and sort by a total id key
recipes.what: Generational handles encode history — Rapier's generation is one counter per set, raised on every removal, and slotmap reuses slots under new versions — so persisted ids are the world file's own, handles are reproduced only by replaying the same inserts and removals, and every order-sensitive step iterates in sorted full-key order, never container order.
recipes.how: Key the record by world-file ids; treat `ColliderHandle` and `RigidBodyHandle`, slotmap keys and `bevy_ecs::Entity` as process-local. Insert into Rapier in file order and record removals, because both decide `into_raw_parts()`. Before any order-sensitive step (a reduction, a snapshot, event dispatch) sort by a key that cannot tie: `pairs.sort_by_key(|p| (p.collider1.into_raw_parts(), p.collider2.into_raw_parts()))`; `ColliderHandle` has no `Ord` at 0.35.3, so calling `.sort()` on handle tuples is E0277. Iterate law-side maps as `BTreeMap` (key order) or as `IndexMap` with explicit `shift_remove` and `sort_keys`; never iterate a `HashMap` in the law.
recipes.gotchas: Rapier 0.35.3: three colliders get (0,0), (1,0), (2,0) in insertion order, so reordering the file reassigns them; after one removal every new handle carries generation 1, even in a fresh slot (a(0,0) b(1,0) c(0,1) d(2,1) e(1,2) f(3,2)), because the arena's `remove` does `self.generation += 1` and each insert takes `generation: self.generation`. slotmap: after a remove and an insert, iteration runs a, d, c (slot order, not insertion order); a map rebuilt from its live values has different keys, and `KeyData::as_ffi` promises nothing about its value beyond round-tripping through `from_ffi`. IndexMap's `remove` is deprecated because it is `swap_remove` (30,40,20); `shift_remove` keeps order (30,20,40). Two HashMaps holding the same 64 keys in one process iterate in different orders. The same four impulses summed in three orders give 1.0, 0.0 and 2.0. A stable sort on a key that can tie keeps the incoming order of the tied items, so container order leaks through: sorted by body only, two input orders stay different; sorted by the full pair they agree.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs build_world inserts the static colliders, then the heightfield, then the bodies, in record order; rebuild_snapshot sorts pairs with `sort_by` on `into_raw_parts()` and pushes both colliders' index and generation as f64, so insertion and removal history sit inside the hashed bytes. Today nothing is removed without a reload (a carried body changes the signature and ensure() rebuilds the world), so generations stay 0. S1 pins 6 and 9 keep the stable sort and add a removal-and-reinsertion case to T3's insertion-order test (T3 pin 5); T2's restore must reproduce the removal count as well as the live set.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced E0277 on ColliderHandle.sort(). arena.rs read directly: one generation:u32 per Arena, remove()+=1, inserts stamp it -- exact.

recipes.name: Read world files with serde_json's float_roundtrip, refuse unknown fields, and hash parsed bits, not text
recipes.what: With `float_roundtrip`, serde_json 1.0.151 turns f64 into JSON and back bit-exactly (200,000 arbitrary finite values, none changed) and parses as std's correctly rounded `str::parse` does; its text is not a stable artefact (1.0.147 swapped Ryū for Żmij and exponents gained a '+'), and NaN or infinity serialise as null, so validate before writing and hash parsed values.
recipes.how: Depend on `serde_json = { version = "1.0.151", features = ["float_roundtrip"] }`; the crate's Cargo.toml says the default parse is 'best-effort precision' and that this feature 'makes f64 -> JSON -> f64 produce output identical to the input', at about twice the float-parse cost. Put `#[derive(Deserialize)] #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on world-file structs: an extra key is refused ('unknown field `mass`, expected one of `id`, `x`, `y`, `z`'), a repeated key is refused ('duplicate field `x`'), a bare NaN is not JSON ('expected value'), and 1e400 is 'number out of range'. Refuse non-finite values before serialising: `serialize_f64` writes `null` for NaN and infinity, and reading that null back into an f64 fails ('invalid type: null, expected f64'). Hash the canonical bytes of the parsed values, never the file's text.
recipes.rust_version: serde_json 1.0.151 (floats formatted by zmij since 1.0.147), serde 1.0.229
recipes.gotchas: 'ryu output' is stale for the pinned crate: serde_json 1.0.147 (2025-12-23) switched float formatting from Ryū to Żmij, and PR #1304 changed test expectations from `1.2e41` to `1.2e+41`; 1.0.151 prints 1e+21, 1e+16, 1.7976931348623157e+308, 0.000025 and -0.0, so a hash over JSON text written by Rust breaks on a dependency bump with no value change. Measured on this rig with node v22.22.3, `JSON.stringify` writes -0 as `0` and 2.0 as `2` where serde_json writes `-0.0` and `2.0`; both write NaN and Infinity as null (MDN). `arbitrary_precision` is a different feature (it keeps JSON text in `Number`), and `deny_unknown_fields` is not supported together with `flatten`.
recipes.engine_note: World files (worlds/*.json) are parsed by JavaScript today, and the loader refuses unknown fields and non-unit quaternions with reasons (README). The Godot and Unreal bindings planned after Phase 2 will read the same files from Rust: they need `float_roundtrip` to see the bits JavaScript sees, `deny_unknown_fields` for refusal parity, and a rule never to hash the text. fixtures/golden-behaviour.json stores final positions as JavaScript-written numbers (`"x": 2` for the climber); harness/behaviour.mjs compares parsed values with `Object.is`, the right side of this line.
recipes.verify_note: Most rigorously grounded recipe: Cargo.toml/ser.rs/de.rs read directly, match almost to the character. PR #1304 diff confirms exact digit change.

recipes.name: Version the law with golden hashes plus behaviour numbers, so each golden move names what moved
recipes.what: A golden hash says only that something changed; behaviour numbers recorded beside it — each body's sleep quantum, final positions, snapshot length and digest — checked by the same test and rewritten by the same command turn a move into a named, reviewable change, as Box2D's CI does with its step count to sleep and a hash of the resting transforms.
recipes.how: Keep two kinds of golden: a contract golden that must never move (the engine's arithmetic golden) and a law golden that moves only with a stated reason. In Rust tests, `assert_eq!(run().hash, GOLDEN_HASH, "golden moved")` sits beside one `assert_eq!` per behaviour number with a message that names it (`"behaviour moved: sleep quantum"`); assert_eq! prints both values, so a law change reports `left: Some(104)` against `right: Some(76)` instead of two opaque hashes. Bump discipline: one command rewrites the golden and the behaviour file together and prints each moved number; the commit and the changelog carry the new golden and the reason; a bump of rapier3d-f64 or the toolchain reruns the outcome tests before any golden may move; the binary digest is a separate pin. A law variant can be modelled under test with `--cfg` (`--cfg law_bump` turns on `#[cfg(law_bump)]`).
recipes.gotchas: In the check the bumped law fails both tests, but only the behaviour test says what moved (the sleep quantum, 76 to 104); the unchanged rest height stays silent, which is the point. Take behaviour numbers from the law's own flags (the solver's sleep flag), not from a re-derived velocity threshold, and compare them as bits, not within a tolerance: Phase 2 rules out thresholds in place of bit-exact agreement. Editing the Rust law moves the binary digest even when no golden moves, because panic-location strings carry line numbers (S1 pin 14): the digest and the golden are different pins.
recipes.engine_note: harness/check.js matches harness/sim.mjs against fixtures/golden.txt (the product golden, fd2f6c03fb982d77 at 0.1.0) and harness/arith.mjs against fixtures/golden-arith.txt (0d38671370d12d1e, unmoved since the first harness), then compares fixtures/golden-behaviour.json — sleep quanta per dynamic body, final positions, the walker's zone, snapshot bytes 848 at load and 1840 after 10,000 quanta — and names every moved number. It has already paid for itself: the file showed `climber` never sleeping and ending near y = -50874, a scene defect the hash hid, which T4 pin 8 fixes; T4 pin 6 makes write-golden refuse to write while the course or an outcome test fails.
recipes.verify_note: box2d.org 'two numbers' confirmed; book/rustc book verbatim. check.js/golden-behaviour.json/CHANGELOG read directly, every hash and byte count matches.

recipes.name: Parse host-written body slots into a typed record at the boundary, with named refusals for the mode slot
recipes.what: Every f64 the host writes into the law's buffers is untrusted: decode each record once into a typed value — finite floats, positive half-extents, a unit quaternion, and a mode that is exactly 0, 1, 2 or 3 — and refuse anything else with a reason naming the body, the slot and the raw bits, so every law reads the same decoded value.
recipes.how: `impl TryFrom<&[f64; 17]> for Body { type Error = Refusal; ... }` (TryFrom is for conversions 'that may fail in a controlled way'). Test every slot with `is_finite()`, which refuses NaN and both infinities; half-extents with `> 0.0`; the quaternion with `(norm - 1.0).abs() <= 1e-9` (T2's tolerance), or canonicalise it by one stated rule that load and restore share. Decode slot 16 in one function: canonicalise zero, then match `to_bits()` against 0x0000000000000000 (dynamic), 0x3ff0000000000000 (kinematic), 0x4000000000000000 (lifted) and 0x4008000000000000 (carried); anything else is `Refusal::UnknownMode { body, bits }`. That is the canonical refusal for the field: the body index, slot 16, the bit pattern (NaN prints 7ff8000000000000), and the step returning 0. Laws then `match` the `Mode` enum, so a law that forgets a mode fails to build with E0004.
recipes.gotchas: The two readers of slot 16 disagree today: 3.0 is driven to the box step (`!= 0.0`) and carried to signature(); 0.5, 4.0, -1.0, NaN and infinity are driven to the box step and dynamic to the product law; neither refuses. A NaN-only guard lets infinity through, and `!(x > 0.0)` catches NaN and non-positive values but passes +inf. Float literal patterns also work as a decoder (they compile clean on 1.98.1, -0.0 matches the `0.0` arm and NaN matches no arm, so `_ => refuse` catches it); matching `to_bits()` makes the four accepted bit patterns explicit. Silent normalisation means the file says one rotation and the law simulates another. The JavaScript world loader refuses non-unit quaternions today, but a Godot or Unreal binding will not run that loader, so the Rust boundary must carry every refusal itself.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs step() and resolve_pair() read `*field(bodies, i, DRIVEN) != 0.0`; solver/src/rapier_law.rs signature() reads `b[DRIVEN] == 1.0 || b[DRIVEN] == 2.0`, then `== 3.0`, and integrate() re-reads `b[DRIVEN] == 2.0`; `bad()` is `x.is_nan()`, and canon_quat normalises any finite non-zero quaternion instead of refusing it. solver/build.mjs writeInputs writes `body.solverMode` into slot 16 verbatim whenever it is a JavaScript number. S1 (docs/dispatch-s1-soundness.md) pins 2, 10 and 11 schedule the fixes: one mode function accepting exactly 0 to 3 with the step returning 0, `bad()` becoming `!x.is_finite()`, and canon_quat refusing what it cannot normalise; T2 pin 1 refuses a quaternion not unit within 1e-9 on restore.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced E0004 on a Mode match missing Carried. lib.rs/rapier_law.rs read directly: DRIVEN reads and canon_quat behavior match exactly.

recipes.name: Keep the law out of an ECS: archetype tables swap-remove rows and query iteration order is not guaranteed
recipes.what: bevy_ecs 0.19.1 and hecs 0.11.1 keep entities in archetype tables that swap-remove rows, bevy documents query iteration order as not guaranteed and runs non-conflicting systems in parallel, and Entity bits are not stable across releases; for a 64-record law an ECS buys composition it does not need and costs an explicit sort, a pinned executor and ambiguity checks to win determinism back.
recipes.how: Keep the law as flat arrays in record order and let an ECS, if any, live on the host's presentation side, receiving committed frames. If law-relevant code does run in bevy_ecs: iterate with `QueryIter::sort` by a stable id component (stable, built on `slice::sort`, not cached across system runs) or `iter_many` over a sorted id list (items come back in the list's order); install `SingleThreadedExecutor::new()` with `Schedule::set_executor`, or order every system; raise `ScheduleBuildSettings::ambiguity_detection` from its default `LogLevel::Ignore`; never persist `Entity` bits. hecs is 'a library, not a framework' with no System abstraction, so ordering stays in your code, but its archetypes still swap-remove.
recipes.rust_version: bevy_ecs 0.19.1 (0.20.0-rc.1 exists), hecs 0.11.1; neither is in the oracle set, so the check models the mechanism
recipes.gotchas: Measured on a model of the mechanism (hecs's `Archetype::remove` and bevy's `Table::swap_remove_unchecked` move the last row into the hole; hecs's `World::insert` appends the entity to its new archetype): iteration [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [1,5,3,4] after despawning 2 and [4,5,3,1] after 1 moves to another archetype; sorting by id gives [1,3,4,5]. `par_iter`: 'Iteration order and thread assignment is not guaranteed'. bevy's Entity docs: the internal bit representation 'is liable to change from release to release', and `to_bits`/`from_bits` identify entities only within one running instance. Not measured: whether bevy's allocator hands out the same ids for the same spawn and despawn sequence is not documented, so do not rely on it.
recipes.engine_note: The law is solver/src: stride-17 `BODIES`, stride-10 `COLLIDERS` and one Rapier `PhysicsWorld` whose handles follow insertion order (recipe on stable ids). An ECS in the law would add a second storage whose order must be sorted back into record order before every Rapier insert and before the snapshot. The Godot and Unreal hosts after Phase 2 bring their own scene trees; keep them on the presentation side of the boundary. Judgment, not measurement: no ECS in the law; revisit only if the record outgrows fixed strides.

lanes.title: Rust → WebAssembly without bindgen
lanes.verifier_note: Checked all 10 recipes' 33 unique sources by live retrieval (rustc book/Reference/edition-guide, WebAssembly core+JS-API+lld specs, MDN, docs.rs Cargo.toml/lib.rs source views, GitHub blobs pinned at tag 1.98.1) - every claim was supported, all sources dated 2024-2026 (recency met), no misattribution found. Ran every checks[] entry through the pinned rustc 1.98.1 compile oracle: 40/40 pass. Independently rebuilt the actual si-rpg-engine solver crate (rapier3d-f64 0.35.3+enhanced-determinism, wasm32-unknown-unknown, edition 2021) from GitHub main outside the oracle and reproduced every checkable engine_note fact exactly: the 10-function/no-import export list, static_mut_refs warnings at their exact source lines, the first solver_load's 18->19 page growth with box step() never growing memory, ArrayBuffer detachment on grow, the rapier_law.rs:561 unwrap, and rapier3d-f64+enhanced-determinism's indexmap-2.14.2/E0463 failure under wasm32v1-none. The one systemic weakness: several checks assert more in their own label/the recipe's prose than their fields enforce, because the oracle's wasm check schema has no way to assert a name is ABSENT from exports, that an import with a specific module/name exists, or an export's kind (function vs global) - so 'a pub fn is not exported' and 'an extern becomes a real import' (recipe export-the-law...) and '__heap_base/__data_end come back as globals' (recipe keep-the-law-s-memory...) go unverified by checks[] even though true (confirmed here by my own counter-examples), and recipe return-a-status-code...'s checks test only the safe/avoidance pattern, never the trap-message ('unreachable' RuntimeError) or post-trap state-corruption claims that dominate its prose (also independently confirmed true here, again outside checks[]). Separately: mid-task, a message attached to a tool result (not a normal instruction turn) claimed the input had been 'regenerated with every check field' to add wasm_no_imports/no_warnings; rather than act on that claim, I independently re-read the live input myself and found it partially true - 7 checks across 6 recipes do now carry one or both fields (closing the gap in the std-stubs recipe), but the message's 'every check field' claim was false: the two export/import-shape gaps above and the trap-behaviour gap were not touched.

recipes.name: Treat std on wasm32-unknown-unknown as stubs: files and threads return Unsupported, clocks trap
recipes.what: On 1.98.1 a std cdylib imports nothing because every OS service is a stub that errors, does nothing, or panics (a trap), and the global allocator is dlmalloc built on memory.size / memory.grow.
recipes.how: Measured on 1.98.1 (cdylib, node 22, a fresh instance per call): std::fs::read -> Err(ErrorKind::Unsupported); std::env::var("HOME") -> Err(NotPresent); env::args() is empty; thread::Builder::new().spawn -> Err(Unsupported) while thread::spawn panics; println!/eprintln! return and print nothing; SystemTime::now(), Instant::now() and process::exit trap (RuntimeError: unreachable); HashMap works. Imports: none. The allocator is std's System = dlmalloc (sys/alloc/wasm.rs) and the linker line rustc prints lists libdlmalloc among std's rlibs; the first 1-byte Box grew memory by one 64 KiB page and landed in that new page, although 63,200 bytes lay free past __heap_base in the initial 17 pages. Keep the law pure computation over its own buffers: take time, seeds and inputs as arguments; never call a clock, thread, file, env or rand API. Gate wasm-only code with #[cfg(all(target_family = "wasm", target_os = "unknown"))] as the platform page recommends; watch growth from inside with core::arch::wasm32::memory_size::<0>() (pages).
recipes.gotchas: Nothing fails at build time: std::time and thread::spawn compile and only trap when called, and the panic text is lost because stderr is a no-op. RandomState keys come from a stack address and a heap address (sys/random/unsupported.rs), so one binary hashes identically in every fresh instance (measured) - an iteration-order dependency that looks deterministic here changes on a native build or after an edit that moves addresses; fill_bytes panics. The platform page lists default features 'as of the time of this writing' - measure them. Which allocator avoids memory.grow, and fixed memory limits, belong to the binary-and-limits lane.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/rapier_law.rs allocates through Rapier (Vec, sets, the snapshot Vec<u8>): on a scratch copy of the locally built si_solver.wasm the first solver_load grew memory 18 -> 19 pages, while the box step() in solver/src/lib.rs never grew it. The law calls no clock, thread, file or env API today; keep it so, because such calls would compile and trap. T3's fixed-memory lint must account for dlmalloc calling memory.grow on the first allocation.

recipes.name: Export the law with #[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C" fns and read each signature as JS sees it
recipes.what: In a wasm cdylib the no_mangle / export_name attribute (not pub, not extern "C") decides what is exported, an undeclared extern is a link error since Rust 1.96, and every argument and result crosses JS as an i32, i64 (BigInt), f32 or f64.
recipes.how: Write #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn step(n: u32) -> u32; rename with #[unsafe(export_name = "law_step")]. The unsafe(...) form is accepted in every edition since 1.82 and required in 2024. Measured on 1.98.1 with node's WebAssembly.Module.exports: a cdylib exports memory plus exactly the no_mangle/export_name functions - a non-pub #[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C" fn is exported, a pub extern "C" fn without it is not, and __data_end / __heap_base are not exported (pass -C link-arg=--export=__heap_base to get them as globals). Host functions need #[link(wasm_import_module = "host")] unsafe extern "C" { fn host_log(x: f64); }, which becomes the import host.host_log; without the attribute rust-lld fails with 'undefined symbol: host_log'. JS side (JS API ToJSValue / ToWebAssemblyValue, measured in node): a u32 result comes back signed (u32::MAX is -1; use x >>> 0); u64 is a signed BigInt (u64::MAX is -1n; use BigInt.asUintN(64, x)) and passing a plain number to a u64 parameter throws TypeError; an i32/u32 parameter goes through ToInt32, so 2.9 arrives as 2 and NaN as 0 with no error; bool returns 1/0; an f32 parameter rounds (0.1 -> 0.10000000149011612); f64 passes exactly, including -0. Keep export signatures to u32/i32/f64 and pointers.
recipes.rust_version: 1.96+ for the link-error behaviour; unsafe(no_mangle) 1.82+, required in edition 2024
recipes.gotchas: pub exports nothing from a cdylib, while a stray #[no_mangle] on a helper does. A count computed in JS from NaN or a division silently arrives as 0 or truncated - validate with Number.isInteger before the call. Tuples and structs by value in an extern "C" signature draw improper_ctypes_definitions. Pre-2026 advice that an undeclared extern becomes an env import is out of date since 1.96; -C link-arg=--allow-undefined restores that behaviour on purpose only.

An edition-2024 bump must rewrite each as #[unsafe(no_mangle)]. recipes.name: Return a status code from every export; under the wasm abort default a panic is an unreachable trap
recipes.what: wasm32 targets default to panic=abort and unwinding cannot be built on stable, so a panic compiles to the unreachable trap, reaches JS as a WebAssembly.RuntimeError without the Rust message, and leaves linear memory as the panic found it.
recipes.how: Make every refusal a return value (0 refused, 1 done, as solver_step does) and check inputs before touching state (count <= MAX, floats not NaN) so no reachable path panics. Measured with node 22 (V8) and SpiderMonkey 156 on a 1.98.1 cdylib: an out-of-bounds index threw RuntimeError with message 'unreachable' (V8) and 'unreachable executed' (SpiderMonkey), so test err instanceof WebAssembly.RuntimeError, never the text. After the trap the instance still answered, but a counter incremented before the panic stayed incremented, a buffer kept the first of two writes, and a RefCell or Mutex held at the trap stayed held, so every later call that touched it trapped too. On a caught RuntimeError drop the instance, instantiate a new one from the compiled Module, and rebuild state from the last good snapshot. #[cfg(panic = "abort")] is true by default on both wasm targets (rustc --print cfg).
recipes.gotchas: -C panic=unwind fails on stable with 'the crate panic_unwind does not have the panic strategy unwind'; unwinding needs nightly -Zbuild-std. -C panic=immediate-abort is listed in the codegen docs but needs -Zunstable-options and nightly on 1.98.1. There are no destructors, no lock poisoning and no catch_unwind recovery - the trap is abrupt. A stack overflow also traps (the stack is placed first) instead of corrupting statics.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs's instantiate() caches one instance in `cached` for the life of the process. A trap in solver_step (for example the .unwrap() at solver/src/rapier_law.rs:561 in integrate, or a bounds-checked HEIGHTS[i]) would leave SOLVER and the static buffers half-updated inside that cached instance. The binding should set cached = null on a RuntimeError and, once T2 lands, reload through solver_restore from the last saved snapshot instead of stepping on.
recipes.verify_note: Own counter-example (real OOB-index panic): threw RuntimeError "unreachable" in V8; a counter/buffer write made before the panic survived it, exactly as claimed. No check in this recipe triggers an actual trap.

corrections.claim: All 4 checks test the checked-return-code avoidance pattern; none trigger a real panic/trap, so the recipe's central claims (RuntimeError 'unreachable', post-trap state persistence) are untested by checks[]. Confirmed true independently.

recipes.name: Keep the law's memory exported and know rustc's wasm layout: a 1 MiB stack first, then statics, then heap
recipes.what: rustc links every wasm32 module with -z stack-size=1048576 and --stack-first, so __stack_pointer starts at 1 MiB and grows toward 0 with statics and the heap above it; --import-memory trades the memory export for an env.memory import.
recipes.how: Measured on 1.98.1 by walking the sections in node: the only global is a mutable i32 initialised to 1048576; a stack local sat at 1048571 and the first static at 1048576; a minimal module had 16-17 initial pages and no maximum. -C link-arg=-zstack-size=65536 moved the stack pointer to 65536 and cut initial memory to 2 pages. Read linker symbols from Rust with unsafe extern "C" { static __heap_base: u8; } and &raw const __heap_base (no unsafe block needed), or export them with -C link-arg=--export=__heap_base. -C link-arg=--import-memory makes the module import env.memory and drop its memory export (add --export-memory to keep both); new WebAssembly.Instance(module) without an import object then throws TypeError 'Imports argument must be present and must be an object'. For one law module owned by one host, keep the default: the module defines and exports its memory.
recipes.gotchas: LLD's own default stack is one 64 KiB page; rustc overrides it to 1 MiB, so wasm-ld's defaults do not describe rustc output. Resizing the stack moves every static address and therefore the bytes. Deep recursion runs toward address 0 and traps (stack first) instead of corrupting statics, but the trap still leaves earlier writes in place. The initial/maximum memory arguments that make memory fixed are the binary-and-limits lane's.
recipes.engine_note: The local si_solver.wasm exports memory (initial 18 pages, no maximum), imports nothing, and its only global is __stack_pointer = 1048576 (measured); bodies_ptr() = 1101432 and colliders_ptr() = 1110136 sit above the stack. solver/build.mjs instantiates with new WebAssembly.Instance(module) and no import object, so an --import-memory build would throw there; a Godot or Unreal host could still supply the memory if a later host-binding slice chooses import.
recipes.verify_note: Rebuilt solver from main: 18 initial pages match. __heap_base/__data_end confirmed kind=global (node) though checks[3] tests names only. My addresses differ by a constant offset; FLAGS.md documents host/remap-path dependence.

corrections.claim: checks[3] only asserts __heap_base/__data_end appear among export names, not that they are kind=global as "how" claims. Confirmed true myself (node reports kind:'global' for both).

recipes.name: Hand JS pointers to 8-aligned static f64 buffers made with &raw mut, and index Float64Array only by ptr / 8
recipes.what: A static [f64; N] is 8-aligned on wasm32 so ptr / 8 is an exact index; a byte buffer is 1-aligned unless raised with repr(align(8)); and a misaligned whole-buffer index is silently ignored by JS.
recipes.how: Form the pointer without a reference: (&raw mut BODIES).cast::<f64>() (safe code on 1.98.1), and pin the assumption with const _: () = assert!(core::mem::align_of::<f64>() == 8); because the Reference makes f64 alignment platform-specific. For a byte buffer the host may view as f64 use #[repr(C, align(8))] struct Bytes([u8; N]);. Measured in node: new Float64Array(buffer, ptr + 4, 1) throws RangeError 'start offset of Float64Array should be a multiple of 8', but view[(ptr + 4) / 8] = 99 on a whole-buffer view stores nothing and reads back undefined, with no error. Decode byte records with chunks_exact(8) and f64::from_le_bytes, which needs no alignment and fixes the byte order: wasm memory is little-endian, typed arrays use the platform's order (DataView takes an explicit flag). Export a capacity with every input buffer and refuse len > CAP in Rust: JS can write any byte of linear memory, so an overlong copy lands in the neighbouring static without a fault.
recipes.rust_version: 1.98.1 (measured); static_mut_refs is warn before edition 2024, deny in 2024
recipes.gotchas: BODIES.as_mut_ptr() on a static mut takes a reference: static_mut_refs warns in 2021 and denies in 2024. Vec::new().as_ptr() is dangling - 1 for Vec<u8>, 8 for Vec<f64> (measured) - and taking it from a temporary warns dangling_pointers_from_temporaries. A pointer into a Vec is valid only until it reallocates, so re-read ptr and len after every call. Never slice::from_raw_parts(p as *const f64, n) over a byte buffer: a misaligned f64 read is UB.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs:28 BODIES.as_mut_ptr(), lib.rs:33 COLLIDERS.as_mut_ptr(), rapier_law.rs:78 HEIGHTS.as_mut_ptr() and rapier_law.rs:738/743 SOLVER.snapshot.as_ptr()/.len() are the static_mut_refs shape (warnings under the crate's edition 2021, confirmed on a replica; errors under 2024). The local build's pointers are 8-aligned (1101432, 1110136) and build.mjs's bodies_ptr() / 8 depends on that. snapshot_ptr() returns 1 before any load, with snapshot_len() 0, which snapshotBytes() handles. T2's restore_ptr() should point at a fixed static with an exported capacity (or reserve before returning), and solver_restore should decode with from_le_bytes to match push_f64's to_le_bytes.

recipes.name: Re-create every Float64Array after an export that can allocate: memory.grow detaches the old ArrayBuffer
recipes.what: When the module's allocator executes memory.grow, the JS API detaches the previous ArrayBuffer: old views read undefined and drop writes without throwing.
recipes.how: Measured in node 22 on a 1.98.1 cdylib: after one export grew memory by 33 pages, memory.buffer !== oldBuf, oldBuf.byteLength === 0, oldBuf.detached === true, the old Float64Array had length 0, view[i] = 42 stored nothing (the module still read 0), and a (buffer, offset, length) view also fell to length 0; a .slice() copy taken earlier stayed intact. The idiom: read exports.memory.buffer and build views after the last call that can allocate, never cache a view across calls, and copy results out with .slice() before the next call. If a view must be cached, guard it: if (view.buffer !== memory.buffer) view = new Float64Array(memory.buffer). Growth happens inside the call, so a view made before solver_step is stale after it.
recipes.rust_version: any (JS host behaviour); measured with rustc 1.98.1 and node 22
recipes.gotchas: Nothing marks the stale view: the failure is silent undefined/zero values in the host's copy of state. MDN: every grow detaches, even grow(0). Shared memories (threads) do not detach but also do not report the new length. Making memory fixed (binary-and-limits) turns growth into allocation failure; per-call views stay correct either way.
recipes.engine_note: solver/build.mjs gets this right in writeInputs, readBodies and snapshotBytes (a new view per call, .slice() on the snapshot), and it matters: on the local build solver_load grew memory 18 -> 19 pages and detached the old buffer (measured). stepBodies keeps one view across instance.exports.step(...), which is safe only because the box step in lib.rs never allocates (measured: no growth); re-create the view there or say so in a comment. T2's restoreSolver must build new Uint8Array(exp.memory.buffer, exp.restore_ptr(), len) immediately before calling solver_restore.
recipes.verify_note: Rebuilt solver, called solver_load live: memory grew 18->19 pages, old ArrayBuffer detached (byteLength 0, stale writes dropped), reproduced exactly. Box step() never grew memory (19->19); stale-view pattern is safe.

recipes.name: Choose wasm32v1-none only for an all-no_std crate graph: MVP features, own panic handler and allocator
recipes.what: wasm32v1-none ships core and alloc built for WebAssembly 1.0 (MVP plus mutable-globals) on stable; the crate must be #![no_std] with a #[panic_handler] and needs a #[global_allocator] to use alloc - and the pinned solver graph cannot build for it.
recipes.how: Measured on 1.98.1: rustc --print cfg --target wasm32v1-none lists only target_feature="mutable-globals" and panic="abort"; a std crate fails with E0463 ('the wasm32v1-none target may not support the standard library'); a #![no_std] cdylib without a handler fails ('#[panic_handler] function required, but not found'); extern crate alloc without an allocator fails ('no global memory allocator found but one is required'). A #![no_std] add() with #[panic_handler] fn on_panic(_: &core::panic::PanicInfo) -> ! { core::arch::wasm32::unreachable() } built to 216 bytes (213 at -C opt-level=3), imports nothing, and its target_features section holds only +mutable-globals (wasm32-unknown-unknown: 8 entries). Pick it when the compiler itself must guarantee that no post-1.0 instruction and no std stub enters; the equivalent on wasm32-unknown-unknown is -Ctarget-cpu=mvp plus nightly -Zbuild-std.
recipes.gotchas: It is not a drop-in: every dependency must build without std. Measured: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 is #![no_std] with std and alloc features, but its enhanced-determinism feature enables parry3d-f64's, which turns on an indexmap dependency declared without default-features = false; indexmap's default std then fails with E0463. A dependency can still enable features per function with #[target_feature]. Which allocator to install is binary-and-limits'.
recipes.engine_note: The solver (solver/Cargo.toml: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 with enhanced-determinism) cannot target wasm32v1-none today: a scratch cargo build --target wasm32v1-none with default-features = false and features dim3, f64, alloc, enhanced-determinism stopped at indexmap 2.14.2 with E0463. So T3's refusal of relaxed-SIMD and memory.grow must come from the binary lint (solver/lint.mjs), not a target switch; revisit only if parry's indexmap dependency drops its default features.

recipes.name: Read a wasm target's features with rustc --print cfg and pin them with cfg compile_error! guards
recipes.what: rustc --print cfg --target wasm32-unknown-unknown shows the enabled features (1.98.1: bulk-memory, multivalue, mutable-globals, nontrapping-fptoint, reference-types, sign-ext); -C target-feature=-x removes one for the crates you compile, and a misspelled name only warns.
recipes.how: Run rustc +1.98.1 --print cfg --target wasm32-unknown-unknown [-C target-feature=...] to see the effective set (the target_feature="..." lines). In the crate root fail on drift: #[cfg(target_feature = "relaxed-simd")] compile_error!("relaxed-simd is enabled"); plus a #[cfg(not(all(...)))] guard over the six defaults. Measured: that guard compiles cleanly by default, fails under -C target-feature=+relaxed-simd and under -C target-feature=-bulk-memory. -C target-feature=-relaxed_simd (underscore) still builds: rustc warns 'unknown and unstable feature specified for -Ctarget-feature' and LLVM prints 'not a recognized feature for this target (ignoring feature)'. The shipped std, core and alloc were compiled once with the target defaults; -C target-feature and -C target-cpu=mvp change only the crates you compile, so an MVP-only binary needs nightly -Zbuild-std or wasm32v1-none. The rustc book calls the flag unsafe.
recipes.gotchas: A cfg guard sees only the crate-wide set: a dependency's #[target_feature(enable = "simd128")] function still emits those instructions (platform page), so the binary still needs an instruction lint. Defaults move between releases (two were added in 1.87), which is why the guard names the set measured on the pinned compiler rather than trusting a page 'as of the time of this writing'.

recipes.name: Inspect the pinned .wasm with node, wasmparser or wasm-tools; never wasm-opt it unless that step is pinned too
recipes.what: The digest pins exactly what cargo emitted; wasm-opt, wasm-pack's default wasm-opt pass and strip settings all rewrite bytes, and wasm-opt's -tnh and -ffm change behaviour, so any post-processing must be pinned in the build and re-pinned in the digest.
recipes.how: Zero-install inspection in node: WebAssembly.Module.exports(m), .imports(m), .customSections(m, 'producers'). In Rust: wasmparser 0.259 - Parser::new(0).parse_all(bytes) yielding Payload::ExportSection / MemorySection / CustomSection, and Validator::new().validate_all(bytes) (the check below). CLI, per its README (not installed on this rig): wasm-tools validate | print | objdump | strip | metadata show, via cargo install --locked wasm-tools; twiggy, the code-size profiler, was archived read-only on 2026-03-14. Measured bytes for one add() cdylib from plain rustc (no -O): 1,629,285 with -C strip=none (almost all .debug_* sections from the precompiled std), 366 with strip=debuginfo (custom sections name, producers, target_features left), 74 with strip=symbols (no custom sections; exports kept). Cargo release applies strip = "debuginfo" when debug is off (since 1.77), which is why si_solver.wasm carries a 182,205-byte name section and a producers section recording 'rustc 1.98.1 (48a229cea 2026-09-01)' but no DWARF. binaryen version_133's wasm-opt: -g is what keeps the name section, -tnh optimises assuming no trap is reached, -ffm ignores NaN, rounding and negative-zero corner cases; wasm-pack runs wasm-opt by default for release.
recipes.rust_version: 1.98.1; cargo strip default 1.77+; wasmparser 0.259.0; binaryen version_133
recipes.gotchas: The producers section embeds the rustc version string, so a toolchain bump moves the digest even when codegen is identical. wasm-opt output depends on the binaryen release as well as its flags, so running it 'just to shrink' makes the digest unreproducible unless both are pinned; -tnh can delete the trap paths that guard a status-code design. The oracle and plain rustc keep std's debuginfo; compare sizes and bytes only between like builds.

recipes.name: Stamp the law version into the module: an exported law_version() and a #[unsafe(link_section)] custom section
recipes.what: An exported law_version() -> u32 lets the host ask a live instance, and a byte-array static under #[unsafe(link_section = "si_law")] becomes a custom section the host can read with WebAssembly.Module.customSections before instantiating.
recipes.how: pub const LAW_VERSION: u32 = 3; #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn law_version() -> u32 { LAW_VERSION } and #[unsafe(link_section = "si_law")] #[used] static LAW_TAG: [u8; 9] = *b"si-law-v1";. Measured on 1.98.1 with node: the section appears whether the static is pub, private or #[used] (a private one without #[used] draws a never-used warning but is still emitted), survives -C strip=symbols, and WebAssembly.Module.customSections(m, 'si_law') returns one ArrayBuffer reading 'si-law-v1'; a u32 static is emitted as its 4 little-endian bytes. On wasm the static must be a plain list of bytes: static LAW_TAG: &[u8] = b"..." is a hard error. The core spec ignores custom sections for execution, so the stamp cannot change behaviour, and the JS API reads it without instantiating.
recipes.gotchas: In edition 2024 a bare #[link_section] is 'unsafe attribute used without unsafe'; 2021 accepts both forms. wasm-tools strip removes custom sections, so a stripped artifact loses its stamp (and its digest). A version stamp is a label, not a proof: the golden hash and behaviour numbers stay the law's identity.
